description: Learn how to use the Network panel to see what a webpage requests, what comes back, whether a request succeeded, and how network evidence helps explain frontend problems.
mastery: The learner can open the Network panel, identify requests made by a page, inspect a request's URL, method, status, and response information, and use that evidence to explain a simple failed or missing request.
learningObjectives: Explain what the Network panel records and why frontend developers use it.
Identify a request's URL, method, status, and basic response information.
Distinguish a successful request from a failed request using its status.
Use Network activity to investigate a simple case where a page is missing data or a resource fails to load.
Trace a request from the user action that triggered it to the response the browser received.

sections.text: When the UI Says 'Nothing Happened'
A user clicks Search. Nothing appears. The button looks fine. There is no obvious JavaScript error. The UI just sits there, quietly pretending the problem does not exist.
This is where the Network panel becomes useful. It lets you see the requests the page is making and what comes back from those requests.

sections.title: A useful mental model
sections.text: Think of Network as the browser's delivery tracker. It shows what the page asked for, where it asked, what the server said, and useful details about the trip.
Open Network Before You Trigger the Action
Open DevTools and switch to Network before performing the action you want to investigate. Then reload the page or trigger the interaction. The panel records requests as they happen.

steps.title: 1. Open Network
steps.description: Open the Network panel before triggering the request you want to observe.

steps.title: 2. Reload or interact
steps.description: Reload the page or perform an action such as submitting a search form.

steps.title: 3. Find the request
steps.description: Look through the recorded requests for the resource or API call associated with the action.

steps.title: 4. Inspect the request
steps.description: Look at the request URL, method, status, and other available details.

steps.title: 5. Inspect the response
steps.description: Check what came back from the server and whether the returned information matches what the frontend expected.

sections.text: What Is a Request?
A request is the browser asking another system for something or asking it to perform an operation. The Network panel records those requests so you can inspect what the browser actually sent.

sections.title: A simplified request
sections.code:
GET /api/courses HTTP/1.1
Host: forge.example

sections.text: For this lesson, focus on the parts you can use while debugging: what URL was requested, what method was used, and what response came back.
The URL Tells You Where the Browser Went
The request URL tells you the destination the browser contacted. When an API call is going to the wrong path or domain, the URL is often the first clue.

sections.title: Common mistake
sections.text: Seeing a request in Network does not automatically mean the request was correct. A request can successfully reach the wrong endpoint. Always inspect where it actually went.
The Method Describes the Request

HTTP methods communicate the general kind of operation being requested. You will learn the methods in detail later, but you should recognize common ones such as GET for retrieving information and POST for sending data for processing.

sections.title: Two common methods
sections.code:
GET /api/courses

POST /api/login

sections.text: Do not try to memorize every HTTP method yet. At this stage, simply recognize that the method is part of the request information and can help explain what the browser was trying to do.
The Status Tells You What Came Back

The response status gives you an important clue about the outcome. A 2xx status generally indicates success, while a 4xx status indicates a client-side request problem and a 5xx status indicates a server-side failure.

sections.title: Useful status categories
sections.code:
200 → successful response

404 → requested resource was not found

401 → authentication is required or missing

403 → access is forbidden

500 → server encountered an error

sections.text: You do not need to memorize every status code. Learn to recognize the pattern and use the exact status as evidence while investigating a problem.
A status code is a clue, not the whole diagnosis. A 404 tells you something was not found. You still need to inspect the request URL and the rest of the response to understand why.
Inspect the Response
A request can succeed and still return data the frontend did not expect. That is why the response matters too.

sections.title: Example API response

sections.text: If the interface expects a courses array but the server instead returns an error object or a differently shaped response, the Network panel gives you evidence that can explain why the UI is not behaving as expected.
Network Helps You Stop Guessing

Suppose a learner says, 'The courses are not loading.' That sentence describes the symptom, not the cause. Network lets you ask better questions: Did the request happen? Which URL did it use? What method did it use? What status came back? What did the response contain?

sections.title: Turn a symptom into an investigation
sections.code:
Symptom:
Courses do not appear.

Questions:
1. Was a request sent?
2. What URL was requested?
3. What status came back?
4. What did the response contain?
5. Did the response match what the frontend expected?

sections.text: Interactive Practice: Trace the Request
Now practice the investigation sequence. Before revealing the answer, predict which network detail would be most useful for each problem.

sections.title: Network Detective
sections.instructions: Read each scenario and decide which Network detail you would inspect first. Focus on evidence: request URL, method, status, or response. Then reveal the explanation.

sections.text: Practice: Investigate a Failed Request
Imagine a search button does nothing. The Console is quiet. Open Network, trigger the search, and imagine you find this request:

sections.title: The evidence
sections.code:
Request URL: /api/search
Method: GET
Status: 404

Expected endpoint:
/api/searches

sections.text: The correct conclusion is not simply 'the API is broken.' The evidence shows the browser requested a path that does not match the expected endpoint. Your next step would be to verify and correct the URL in the frontend code.
One More Important Habit
Clear the Network panel before reproducing a problem when the request list is noisy. Otherwise you may end up investigating yesterday's request while today's bug sits quietly in the corner.

Network debugging is about tracing evidence. Start with the user action, find the request it triggered, inspect the request, inspect the response, and compare what actually happened with what the frontend expected.

sections.label: Use the Network panel to trace a request from a user action, identify its URL, method, and status, and inspect the response to explain a simple failure or unexpected result.
sections.hint: Ask: Did the request happen? Where did it go? What status came back? What did the response contain?

sections.text: Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'An API-powered page is not showing data. How would you debug it?' A strong beginner answer is: 'I would open Network, reproduce the problem, find the relevant request, inspect its URL and method, check the status code, and inspect the response. That tells me whether the request was sent, whether it succeeded, and whether the returned data matches what the frontend expects.'
Notice what you are not doing: immediately rewriting the API call because the page looks broken. First find the evidence.
Reflect

Think of one website feature that depends on data from a server. Before you leave this lesson, describe what request you would expect to see in Network and what evidence would convince you that the problem was on the client side, the server side, or in the response data.
What You Should Take Away

The Network panel records the requests a webpage makes and provides evidence about where requests went, how they were made, what status came back, and what the response contained. Effective network debugging starts from a user action, finds the relevant request, and compares the actual request and response with what the frontend expected.

exercises.title: Trace a Network Request
exercises.brief: Open the Network panel on a real webpage, trigger an action that causes a request, and record the request URL, method, status, and response type. Then explain what the evidence tells you about the request.

quiz.question: What is the main purpose of the Network panel?
options: Inspecting requests and responses made by the webpage.
Editing the browser's operating system.
Replacing the DOM shown in Elements.
Permanently changing backend source code.
quiz.explanation: The Network panel records requests and provides information about their URLs, methods, statuses, timing, responses, and related details.

quiz.question: A request appears in Network with status 404. What does that immediately tell you?
options: The request was never sent.
The requested resource was not found.
The browser successfully stored the response.
The server definitely crashed.
quiz.explanation: A 404 response indicates that the requested resource could not be found. You should then inspect the request details to understand why.

quiz.question: A request returns 200, but the UI still cannot display the expected data. What should you inspect next?
options: Only the browser's font settings.
The response content and whether its shape matches what the frontend expects.
Only the page title.
The user's keyboard layout.
quiz.explanation: A successful HTTP status only tells you about the request outcome at that level. The actual response data may still be missing, malformed, or different from what the frontend expects.

quiz.question: Why can clearing the Network panel before reproducing a problem be useful?
options: It permanently deletes the server logs.
It reduces unrelated requests so the request associated with the current problem is easier to identify.
It makes failed requests automatically succeed.
It changes the API endpoint.
quiz.explanation: Clearing old entries reduces noise and makes it easier to identify the request generated by the interaction you are currently investigating.

summary: The Network panel helps frontend developers see what a page requests and what comes back. URL, method, status, and response information provide evidence when a feature fails or data does not appear. Rather than guessing from the UI symptom, reproduce the problem, locate the request, inspect the request and response, and compare them with what the frontend expected.
interviewQuestions: What is the Network panel used for?
How would you investigate an API request that returns 404?
What would you inspect if a request returns 200 but the UI still shows no data?
How would you trace a user action to the network request it triggered?
Why is network evidence more useful than simply guessing from the visible UI?

title: Your First Debugging Exercise
description: Put Elements and Console together in a guided debugging drill: inspect the page, identify evidence, explain the cause, and make the smallest fix instead of guessing.
mastery: The learner can independently complete a first debugging pass by inspecting the live DOM and CSS with Elements, using the Console to identify a JavaScript problem, explaining the root cause before changing code, and applying the smallest reasonable fix.
learningObjectives: Combine Elements and Console evidence during a single debugging investigation.
Distinguish a visible symptom from the underlying cause of a bug.
Inspect the live page before changing the source code.
Use a Console error or logged value to narrow down a JavaScript problem.
Explain the cause of a bug before applying a fix.
Apply the smallest reasonable fix and verify that the behavior now matches the requirement.

sections.text: Now We Debug

You have now met the tools separately. Elements lets you inspect the live page and CSS. Console lets you inspect JavaScript output and errors. This lesson is where those tools stop being separate topics and become a debugging workflow.
You are not being asked to become a debugging wizard in twenty minutes. You are learning the first professional habit: do not guess at the fix before you understand the cause.
Debugging is detective work. The page is the crime scene, DevTools is your evidence kit, and changing five things at once is the fastest way to make the detective regret taking the case.
The First Debugging Pass
When something looks broken, start by describing the symptom precisely. Then inspect the evidence that could explain it. Only after you have a likely cause should you change the code.

sections.title: The workflow
sections.code:
1. Reproduce the problem.
2. Describe the symptom.
3. Inspect the live DOM and styles.
4. Check the Console for errors or useful values.
5. Form a hypothesis about the cause.
6. Make the smallest fix.
7. Reproduce the problem again.
8. Verify the fix.

sections.text: Notice that 'change the code' appears after inspection and hypothesis. That order matters.
Debugging Drill 1: A Visual Bug
The learner profile card below is supposed to have comfortable spacing around its content. Instead, everything is pressed against the edge.

sections.title: The page
sections.code:
Frontend Foundations

Learn how the browser works.

sections.title: The current styles

sections.text: Your first job is not to edit the stylesheet. Inspect the card in Elements. Find the padding declaration. Temporarily change it in DevTools and observe whether the symptom disappears.
If the temporary change fixes the spacing, you now have evidence for your hypothesis: the padding value is part of the problem. Only then should you make the real source-code change.

sections.title: Debug Drill 1 — Find the Visual Cause
sections.instructions: Inspect the card and identify the declaration responsible for the cramped spacing. Predict what will happen if you increase padding, then change the value in the sandbox and verify your prediction. Your goal is to explain the cause before changing it.
sections.initialCode:
Frontend Foundations

Learn how the browser works.

sections.text: Debugging Drill 2: A Logic Bug
Now the problem is less visible. The button is supposed to update its label when clicked, but nothing changes.

sections.title: The broken behavior

sections.text: If you run this code and click the button, the Console gives you a clue. The function being called does not exist in the current example.

sections.title: The evidence
sections.code: ReferenceError: startLesson is not defined

sections.text: That error is more useful than the symptom 'the button does nothing.' It tells you that JavaScript tried to call startLesson and could not find that function.

Do not fix a JavaScript error by randomly adding code until the red message disappears. First translate the error into plain language: 'I called something that does not exist here.' Then inspect the code and decide what the application actually intended to call.

sections.title: Debug Drill 2 — Find the JavaScript Cause
sections.instructions: Run the example and inspect the Console. Identify the first meaningful error. Explain what it means before changing the code. Then make the smallest change that produces the intended button behavior.

sections.text: Debugging Drill 3: Use Both Tools
Now combine the two skills. The page has a button that appears correct, but clicking it produces an error and the interface does not update.

sections.title: The complete example
sections.code: HTML Foundations

sections.text: Start with Elements. Confirm that the button and heading actually exist in the live DOM. Then click the button and inspect the Console. You should now have two pieces of evidence that work together.
The Console tells you that the JavaScript is trying to work with a value that does not exist. Elements lets you compare the selector in the code with the actual id in the live DOM.

sections.title: Combine the Evidence
sections.description: Visible symptom → Elements: confirm the relevant DOM exists and inspect its attributes → Console: inspect the runtime error → Compare the selector with the live DOM → Form a hypothesis → Make the smallest fix → Test again.

sections.title: Debug Drill 3 — Elements + Console
sections.instructions: Reproduce the bug. First inspect the live DOM and confirm the heading's actual id. Then click the button and read the Console error. Explain the mismatch before changing the code. Fix only the cause you have evidence for, then verify that the title changes to 'Lesson complete'.
sections.initialCode: HTML Foundations

sections.text: The Rule: Explain Before You Fix

A debugging fix is stronger when you can explain why it works. In the final drill, you should be able to say exactly what was wrong, what evidence revealed it, what you changed, and why the change solves the original symptom.

sections.title: A professional debugging note
sections.code:
Symptom:
Clicking Complete lesson does nothing.

Evidence:
Console reports an error because the queried element is null.

Cause:
The JavaScript selector uses #lesson-titel, but the DOM contains #lesson-title.

Fix:
Correct the selector.

Verification:
Clicking the button now updates the heading to "Lesson complete".

sections.text: That last step—verification—is part of the fix. 'I changed something and the red error disappeared' is not the same as 'I confirmed the original requirement now works.'

sections.label: Complete all three debugging drills. For each bug, identify the symptom, inspect evidence before changing code, explain the root cause, apply the smallest reasonable fix, and verify the expected behavior.
sections.hint: Use the workflow: reproduce → inspect → read evidence → hypothesize → fix → verify.

sections.text: Interview Mode
Imagine an interviewer gives you a broken interface and asks, 'What would you do first?' Do not immediately say, 'I would fix the code.' Say what evidence you would gather first.

A strong beginner answer is: 'I would reproduce the bug, inspect the affected element in DevTools, check the Console for runtime errors, form a hypothesis from the evidence, make the smallest fix, and then reproduce the original action to verify the fix.'
Reflect

Think about your natural debugging instinct. When something breaks, do you immediately start changing code, or do you first try to understand what happened? The second habit is the one you want to build.
You are not expected to solve every bug immediately. Professional debugging is not 'I always know the answer.' It is 'I know how to gather evidence and narrow the problem.'
What You Should Take Away

A first debugging pass should be evidence-driven: reproduce the problem, inspect the live page, check the Console, identify the root cause, make the smallest reasonable change, and verify the original behavior. Elements and Console become much more powerful when you use them together instead of treating them as separate tools.

exercises.title: Debug Drill 1 — Visual Bug
exercises.brief: Use Elements to identify why a card has inadequate spacing. Test your hypothesis in DevTools, explain the cause, and apply the smallest reasonable fix.

exercises.title: Debug Drill 2 — Logic Bug
exercises.brief: Use the Console to identify why a button click throws a JavaScript error. Explain the first relevant error, determine the cause, and make the smallest fix that restores the intended behavior.

exercises.title: Debug Drill 3 — Full First Pass
exercises.brief: Combine Elements and Console to diagnose a broken lesson-completion button. Inspect the live DOM, reproduce the runtime error, identify the selector mismatch, fix it, and verify the UI update.

quiz.question: What should you generally do before changing code to fix a bug?
options: Change several unrelated values at once.
Gather evidence and form a hypothesis about the cause.
Delete the feature and rebuild it.
Ignore the error and wait for it to disappear.
quiz.explanation: A strong debugging workflow starts with reproduction and evidence gathering. You then form a hypothesis before making a targeted change.

quiz.question: A button appears visually correct, but clicking it throws a JavaScript error because a queried element is null. Which DevTools combination is most useful?
options: Network only.
Elements to inspect the actual DOM and Console to inspect the runtime error.
Sources only without reproducing the problem.
The browser's bookmarks panel.
quiz.explanation: Elements lets you verify the live DOM and its attributes, while Console provides the runtime error explaining what the JavaScript failed to find or use.

quiz.question: Why is verification part of the debugging process?
options: Because changing any line of code automatically proves the bug is fixed.
Because you need to confirm that the original behavior now works and that the fix addressed the actual problem.
Because browsers cannot run code without a second refresh.
Because verification is only useful for backend developers.
quiz.explanation: A fix is not complete until you reproduce the original scenario and confirm that the expected behavior now occurs.

summary: Your first debugging pass combines the evidence from Elements and Console. Reproduce the problem, inspect the live DOM and styles, read the relevant Console output, form a hypothesis, make the smallest reasonable fix, and verify the original behavior. The goal is not to know every answer immediately; it is to build the habit of investigating before changing code.
interviewQuestions: What is your first step when debugging a frontend bug?
How would you use Elements and Console together to investigate a broken UI interaction?
Why should you form a hypothesis before changing code?
What does it mean to verify a bug fix?
How would you explain the difference between a symptom and a root cause?

title: HTML: The Structure of the Web
description: Understand HTML as the semantic structure of a webpage and learn how the browser turns a document into a meaningful tree of elements.
mastery: The learner can explain HTML as the semantic structure of a webpage, distinguish structure from presentation, identify the main parts of a simple HTML document, and build a small page using meaningful HTML elements rather than treating tags as visual containers.
learningObjectives: Explain HTML as the language used to describe the structure and meaning of webpage content.
Distinguish HTML structure and semantics from CSS presentation.
Identify the basic structure of a simple HTML document.
Explain that HTML documents form a tree of nested elements.
Build a small HTML page using appropriate elements for its content.

sections.text: Welcome to HTML

You already know what frontend development is, how browsers communicate with servers, how DevTools helps you inspect a page, and how to approach your first debugging problem. Now we are ready to build the thing the browser actually renders.

HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language. It describes the structure and meaning of content in a web document. HTML tells the browser, 'This is a heading,' 'This is a paragraph,' 'This is a link,' or 'This is a form.'

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: Think of HTML as the structure of a building. It defines the rooms, doors, stairs, and relationships between them. CSS will later decide what those rooms look like. If you try to use HTML as your paintbrush, the browser will allow the chaos but your future self may file a complaint.
HTML Describes Meaning, Not Appearance

A heading is a heading because the content is a heading, not because the browser makes it large. A paragraph is a paragraph because it represents a paragraph of text, not because it happens to appear underneath another element.

sections.title: HTML describes the content
sections.code:
Frontend Engineering

Learn how browsers turn structured documents into interfaces.

Start learning

sections.text: The HTML tells the browser what these pieces of content are. Later, CSS can change their colors, sizes, spacing, and layout without changing the fact that one is a heading, one is a paragraph, and one is a link.
A Webpage Is a Tree
HTML elements can contain other elements. That nesting creates a tree-like structure. The browser uses this structure to understand how pieces of content relate to each other.

sections.title: A simple HTML tree
sections.code:
Forge Academy

Learn frontend engineering.

sections.title: From HTML to a Tree
sections.description: main → section → h1 and p. The main element contains the section. The section contains the heading and paragraph. These parent-child relationships form the document structure the browser represents as the DOM.

sections.text: In this example, main is the parent of section, while h1 and p are children of section. Thinking in these relationships becomes extremely useful later when you work with CSS, JavaScript, accessibility, and the DOM.
The Basic HTML Document
A complete HTML document has a standard outer structure. You do not need to memorize every detail yet, but you should recognize the major pieces.

sections.title: A basic document
sections.code:
Welcome to Forge

Your frontend engineering journey starts here.

sections.text: The doctype tells the browser to use modern HTML parsing rules. The html element wraps the document. The head contains metadata and information about the document, while the body contains the content rendered as part of the page.
You do not need to memorize the entire document skeleton like you're preparing for an HTML spelling bee. Learn what each major region is responsible for. The details will become familiar through use.
HTML Elements Build the Document

Most of the HTML you write will consist of elements. An element represents a piece of content or structure. Some elements contain content between an opening and closing tag. Others, such as images, are void elements and do not wrap content.

sections.title: Elements in a document
sections.code:
Forge Academy

Build real frontend skills.

sections.text: You will learn exactly how tags, attributes, nesting, and different element types work in the next lesson. For now, focus on the bigger idea: HTML is a system of elements used to describe the structure and meaning of a document.
Why Semantics Matter

The browser is not the only thing consuming your HTML. Assistive technologies, search engines, developer tools, JavaScript, and other parts of the web platform rely on the structure and meaning expressed by your markup.
That is why 'it looks right' is not enough. Two pieces of markup can look identical while communicating very different meanings to the browser and to users who rely on assistive technology.

sections.title: Common mistake
sections.text: Treating HTML tags as decorative boxes. If your first question when choosing an element is 'Which one looks right?', stop. Ask what the content actually is. Visual appearance is CSS territory; semantic structure belongs in HTML.
Interact: Read the Structure
Look at the example below and identify the parent and child relationships before revealing the explanation.

sections.title: HTML Tree Detective
sections.instructions: Inspect the markup and identify the parent of each element. Then predict what the structure would look like as a tree. Use the controls to reveal the relationships.

sections.text: Practice: Build a Tiny Page

Create a small HTML document for a fictional Forge lesson. Give it one main heading, one paragraph explaining the lesson, and one link to another page. Your goal is not visual design. Your goal is to choose elements that accurately represent the content.

sections.title: Build Your First HTML Structure
sections.instructions: Create a simple document with a main heading, a paragraph, and a link. Start with semantic structure. Do not add CSS yet. When finished, inspect the result and explain what each element represents.
sections.initialCode:
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <title>My Forge Lesson</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <!-- Build your page here -->
  </body>
</html>

sections.text: Practice: Structure Before Styling

Imagine you are given a design showing a large title, a block of explanatory text, and a clickable 'Learn more' control. Before thinking about colors or font sizes, identify the HTML elements you would use and explain why.

sections.title: Your planning notes
sections.code:
Main title:
____________________

Supporting text:
____________________

Navigation to another page:
____________________

sections.label: Explain HTML as the semantic structure of a webpage, identify the main regions of a basic HTML document, explain one parent-child relationship in an HTML tree, and build a small page using meaningful HTML elements rather than styling-oriented choices.
sections.hint: Think structure and meaning first. Appearance comes later.

sections.text: Interview Mode
Imagine an interviewer asks: 'What is HTML?' Avoid saying only 'HTML is the skeleton of a website.' That analogy is useful, but give the technical idea too.

A strong beginner answer is: 'HTML is the markup language used to describe the structure and meaning of content in a web document. The browser parses that markup into a document tree that other parts of the web platform can work with.'
Reflect

Look at the page you just built. Temporarily ignore how it looks. Can you explain what each element means and how the elements relate to one another? If you can, you are beginning to think in HTML instead of simply typing tags.
The goal is not to memorize hundreds of HTML elements. The goal is to build the habit of choosing markup because it describes the content correctly. The vocabulary will grow as you build.
What You Should Take Away

HTML describes the structure and meaning of web content. Elements form a nested document tree, and the browser uses that structure when building the page. HTML is not primarily a visual styling language: it tells the browser what the content is. The next lesson zooms in on the pieces you use to construct that structure—elements, tags, and attributes.

exercises.title: Build a Tiny HTML Page
exercises.brief: Create a small HTML document containing a meaningful main heading, a supporting paragraph, and a link. Explain why you selected each element and describe the parent-child relationships in your document.

quiz.question: What is HTML primarily used for?
options: Describing the structure and meaning of content in a web document.
Controlling all visual styling and animations.
Storing application data in a database.
Sending network requests directly to a server.
quiz.explanation: HTML describes the structure and meaning of content. CSS handles presentation, while JavaScript can provide behavior and application logic.

quiz.question: What does it mean to say that an HTML document has a tree structure?
options: Every element must have exactly one sibling.
Elements can be nested inside other elements, creating parent-child relationships.
HTML pages can only contain text.
The browser stores every element as a separate webpage.

Elements can be nested to form a document tree, and the browser uses that structure when building the page. HTML should describe what content is rather than how it should look; CSS handles presentation. The next lesson introduces elements, tags, and attributes in more detail.

title: Elements, Tags, and Attributes
description: Learn how HTML elements are written, how opening and closing tags create structure, and how attributes provide additional information or configuration.
mastery: The learner can identify an HTML element, distinguish an opening tag from a closing tag, explain the role of an attribute, correctly nest and close common elements, and build a small page containing valid elements with correctly written attributes.
learningObjectives: Distinguish an HTML element from its opening and closing tags.
Identify the opening tag, closing tag, and content of a basic HTML element.
Explain what HTML attributes are and what additional information they provide.
Write correctly formatted attributes with quoted values.
Correct simple nesting, closing-tag, and attribute-syntax mistakes in HTML.

sections.text: Zoom In: What Actually Makes Up an Element?

In the previous lesson, you learned the big picture: HTML describes the structure and meaning of a webpage. Now we are going one level deeper and looking at the pieces you use to build that structure.
You will see three terms constantly in frontend development: element, tag, and attribute. They are related, but they are not interchangeable.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: Think of an HTML element as the complete thing. Tags are the markup that opens and closes it. Attributes add extra information to the element. Once you separate those three ideas, HTML syntax becomes much less mysterious.
An Element Can Contain Content

sections.title: A basic element
sections.code: Learn frontend engineering.

sections.text: The complete element here is the paragraph element. It contains an opening tag, the text content, and a closing tag.

sections.title: Anatomy of an HTML Element

Opening tag →

sections.text: The opening tag tells the browser where the element starts. The closing tag tells the browser where it ends. The content sits between them.
Tags Are the Markup

In

Learn frontend engineering.

and the closing tag is

sections.title: Common mistake
sections.text: Forgetting a closing tag can produce confusing markup and unexpected nesting. HTML is surprisingly forgiving in some cases, which is convenient until the browser politely fixes your mistake in a way you did not expect.
Attributes Add Information
Attributes provide additional information about an element. They are written inside the opening tag and usually follow the pattern attribute="value".

sections.title: An attribute on a link
sections.code: Start learning

sections.text: Here, href is the attribute name and /learn is its value. The href tells the browser where the link should navigate.

sections.title: An attribute on an image

sections.text: The img element uses src to identify the image resource and alt to provide alternative text. Attributes allow the same basic element type to carry additional information.
Attributes Belong to the Opening Tag
When you write attributes, place them inside the opening tag. You do not put them after the closing tag or inside the element's text content.

sections.title: Correct attribute placement
sections.code:

sections.text: The class attribute belongs inside the opening p tag, and href belongs inside the opening a tag.
Quote Attribute Values
For normal HTML authoring, quote attribute values so the browser can clearly identify where the value begins and ends.

sections.code:

Start learning

sections.text: If you are writing HTML inside a JSON string, there is an extra rule: the quotation marks must be escaped for JSON. That is a data-format requirement, not an HTML requirement. The HTML itself still uses ordinary quotes around attribute values.
One Element Can Have Multiple Attributes

sections.title: Multiple attributes
sections.code:
<input
  id="email"
  class="form-control"
  type="email"
  name="email"
>

sections.text: An element can have several attributes. Each attribute contributes additional information or configuration. The exact attributes available depend on the element.
Attributes Do Not Replace Meaning
An attribute can describe or configure an element, but it does not give a generic element the meaning of a completely different element. A class named button does not turn a div into a native button.

sections.title: Appearance is not semantics
sections.code: Save

sections.text: The class can be useful for CSS, but the second example is actually a button element. The element itself communicates the semantic role.
Attributes add information. They do not give you permission to ignore the meaning of the element. HTML is not a costume party where a div puts on a button class and suddenly becomes a button.
Nesting Elements Correctly
HTML elements are often nested inside one another. When elements overlap, close them in the reverse order in which they were opened.

sections.title: Correct nesting
sections.code: Learn frontend engineering today.

sections.text: The strong element opens and closes entirely inside the paragraph. This keeps the nesting relationships clear.

sections.title: Incorrect nesting

sections.text: This example closes the paragraph before closing strong. The tags overlap incorrectly. Build the habit of closing the most recently opened element first.
Some Elements Do Not Wrap Content
Not every HTML element has a closing tag. Elements such as img and input are void elements: they cannot contain child content in the normal HTML structure.

sections.title: Void elements

sections.text: You will encounter more void elements as you learn HTML. For now, recognize that an element can be either a container for content or a standalone element with attributes.

sections.text: Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'What's the difference between an HTML element, a tag, and an attribute?' A strong beginner answer is: 'An element is the complete HTML structure, such as a paragraph. Tags are the opening and closing markup used to define that element, and attributes provide additional information or configuration inside the opening tag.'
Then be ready for the follow-up: 'Can an element have multiple attributes?' Yes. A single element can have multiple attributes when the element supports them.
Reflect

Look at one HTML element you wrote today and point out the complete element, its opening tag, its closing tag if it has one, and every attribute. If you can name those pieces without guessing, the syntax is starting to become something you understand rather than something you copy.

HTML syntax looks small, but tiny syntax mistakes can change the structure the browser builds. Learn to read your markup like the browser does: element by element, attribute by attribute, relationship by relationship.
What You Should Take Away

An HTML element is the complete structure represented by its markup. Tags define where an element starts and ends, while attributes provide additional information or configuration in the opening tag. Correct closing, nesting, and attribute syntax help the browser build the structure you intended. The next lesson shifts from syntax to the most basic text structures: headings and paragraphs.

summary: HTML elements are complete structures made from markup such as opening and closing tags and, when applicable, content between them. Attributes live in opening tags and provide additional information or configuration. Correct nesting, closing tags, and quoted attribute values help the browser build the structure you intended. The next lesson applies these building blocks to headings and paragraphs.

title: Headings, Paragraphs, and Text
description: Practice using HTML headings and paragraphs to create a clear document structure that communicates hierarchy to both people and the browser.
mastery: The learner can choose appropriate heading levels and paragraph elements for a given content outline, correct a poorly structured heading hierarchy, and build a short document whose HTML structure communicates the intended content hierarchy without using heading tags merely to control visual size.
learningObjectives: Choose appropriate heading elements for different levels of content.
Use paragraphs to represent blocks of ordinary text.
Explain why heading levels should reflect document hierarchy rather than desired visual size.
Identify and correct common heading-structure mistakes.
Build a short, readable HTML document with a logical heading hierarchy.

sections.text: Now Let's Give the Document a Shape
You already know how HTML elements, tags, and attributes work. Now we are going to use a few of those elements to create something readers actually care about: a document whose structure makes sense.
Headings and paragraphs are among the simplest HTML elements you will write, but they are also foundational. A good heading structure makes a page easier to scan, understand, navigate, and maintain.
Think of headings as the table of contents of your page. If your headings are chaotic, the content may technically exist, but your document is making everyone work overtime to understand it.
Headings Describe Hierarchy
HTML provides six heading levels: h1 through h6. The number represents the heading's level in the document hierarchy, not how large you want the text to appear.

sections.title: A simple document hierarchy
sections.code:

Subsections Go Deeper
When a section contains a distinct subsection, you can move to the next appropriate level.

sections.title: The classic beginner mistake
sections.text: Do not choose h3 because h3 looks smaller and happens to fit your design. If you need smaller text, that is a CSS problem. Heading levels describe structure.
What Makes a Good Heading Hierarchy?
A useful heading hierarchy reflects the relationships between ideas. You should be able to read the headings alone and get a rough outline of what the page contains.

Paragraphs Hold Ordinary Text
The p element represents a paragraph of text. Use it for ordinary blocks of prose rather than creating a collection of generic elements just to separate lines.

A better structure might use paragraphs for those descriptions or, if they truly represent subsections, choose the appropriate heading level based on the actual content relationship.

sections.title: Important distinction
sections.text: There is no rule saying a page becomes invalid because it contains h4 after h2. The real question is whether the heading level accurately represents the document hierarchy. Do not turn heading rules into a superstition.
Why This Matters Beyond the Browser
A clear heading structure helps people scan content and helps assistive technologies communicate the structure of a document. It also gives developers a predictable outline when maintaining a page.
The important skill is not memorizing an accessibility checklist. It is learning to make the HTML describe the content honestly.
Practice Drill 4: Build a Lesson Page

sections.text: Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'How do you decide which heading level to use?' A strong answer is: 'I choose the heading level based on the document hierarchy and relationship between sections, not based on the visual size I want. If the heading needs to look different, I use CSS for presentation.'
A useful follow-up answer is that paragraphs represent ordinary blocks of prose, while headings identify sections or subsections in the document structure.
Reflect

Take any article or webpage you know well and imagine reading only its headings. Could you understand the major structure of the page? That is the kind of question you should start asking when writing your own HTML.

If your heading hierarchy makes sense without the CSS, your HTML is doing its job. If it only makes sense because you remember which heading looked big on screen, the stylesheet is doing all the thinking.
What You Should Take Away

Headings create document hierarchy, while paragraphs represent ordinary blocks of text. Choose heading levels based on the relationship between sections, not on the visual size you want. A strong HTML document should communicate its structure even before CSS is added.

summary: HTML headings communicate document hierarchy, while paragraphs represent ordinary blocks of text. Use h1 through h6 according to the relationship between sections and subsections, not according to the visual size you want. CSS can change appearance without changing the underlying document structure. The next lesson applies the same structural thinking to links, images, and resource paths.

title: Links, Images, and Paths
description: Practice using anchors and images correctly, understand how href and src point to resources, and learn how relative and absolute paths are resolved by the browser.
mastery: The learner can create working links and images, choose appropriate href and src values, distinguish relative and absolute URLs, explain how the browser resolves a relative path, and diagnose a simple broken-link or missing-image problem without guessing.
learningObjectives: Create links with the anchor element and an appropriate href value.
Add images with the img element using meaningful src and alt attributes.
Distinguish relative paths from absolute URLs.
Predict how a relative path will be resolved from the current document location.
Diagnose and correct a simple broken link or missing image caused by an incorrect path.

sections.text: Now Let's Make the Page Go Somewhere

Your HTML can now describe a document with a sensible heading hierarchy and readable paragraphs. Useful pages, however, rarely exist in isolation. They connect to other pages, load images, link to documents, and reference resources.
That is where links, images, and paths come in. The elements themselves are straightforward. The part that causes beginners grief is usually the path.
A broken path is one of those bugs where the browser is actually doing exactly what you told it to do. Unfortunately, what you told it to do was nonsense.
Links With the Anchor Element
The a element creates a hyperlink. Its href attribute tells the browser where the link should go.

sections.title: A link to another page
sections.code: HTML course

sections.text: The visible text is 'HTML course'. The href contains the destination. When a user activates the link, the browser uses that destination to navigate.
Absolute URLs
An absolute URL identifies a complete destination, including the scheme and domain.

sections.title: An absolute URL
sections.code: Visit MDN

sections.text: This tells the browser to navigate to a specific address on the web. Absolute URLs are useful when linking to a resource on another site.
Relative Paths
A relative path is resolved in relation to the current document or URL. This is extremely common when linking pages and local assets inside the same website.

sections.title: A simple project structure
sections.code:
project/
├── index.html
├── courses/
│   └── html.html
└── images/
    └── forge-logo.png

sections.title: Relative links from index.html
sections.code: HTML course

sections.text: Because index.html is at the project root, courses/html.html points into the courses folder and images/forge-logo.png points into the images folder.
The Browser Resolves the Path

Relative paths are not magic. The browser resolves them against the current document's location. That means the same relative path can point somewhere different when the current page is in a different folder.

sections.title: Same path, different starting point
sections.code:
project/
├── index.html
├── lessons/
│   ├── html.html
│   └── css.html
└── images/
    └── logo.png

From index.html:
images/logo.png
→ project/images/logo.png

From lessons/html.html:
../images/logo.png
→ project/images/logo.png

sections.text: The ../ means 'go up one directory.' Once you understand that, paths become a small navigation problem rather than mysterious punctuation.

sections.title: Path vocabulary
sections.text: ./ means the current directory. ../ means the parent directory. A deeper path such as images/logo.png means enter the images directory and look for logo.png.
Images With img
The img element embeds an image resource into the document. It uses src to identify the image and alt to provide alternative text.

sections.title: A basic image

sections.text: src tells the browser which image resource to request. alt provides a text alternative that can be useful when the image cannot be seen or loaded.

sections.title: Common mistake
sections.text: A common beginner move is using an absolute local computer path such as C:\Users\You\Desktop\logo.png. That path describes your computer, not your deployed website. It is basically telling the browser, 'Please look on my laptop.' The internet does not live there.
Why Relative Paths Matter in Real Projects

Projects contain many interconnected resources: pages link to other pages, stylesheets reference images, scripts load modules, and HTML documents reference assets. Relative paths let those resources travel with the project instead of depending on one developer's local filesystem.

sections.text: Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'What's the difference between an absolute URL and a relative path?' A strong answer is: 'An absolute URL identifies a complete destination, such as https://developer.mozilla.org/. A relative path is resolved from the current document location, such as ../images/logo.png. Relative paths are commonly used for resources within the same project.'

A likely follow-up is: 'How would you debug a broken image?' Start with the actual file location, compare it with the src value, determine what URL the browser will resolve, and then inspect the resulting request if necessary.
Reflect

Take one local file path from a project and manually walk it from the current document to the target. If you can explain every ../ and directory name without guessing, you are no longer treating paths as random punctuation.
The browser does not know where you meant to point. It only knows where the path resolves. When a link or image breaks, trace the path instead of blaming the browser. The browser has receipts.
What You Should Take Away

Links use a to navigate to destinations through href. Images use img with src to reference image resources and alt to provide alternative text. Absolute URLs identify complete destinations, while relative paths are resolved from the current document location. When a resource breaks, compare the current file location, the written path, and the actual resource location before changing anything.

title: Lists and Tables
description: Practice using HTML lists to represent ordered or unordered collections and tables to represent genuine tabular data.
mastery: The learner can choose between unordered and ordered lists based on the meaning of the content, build correctly nested list structures, create a basic accessible table with headings and data cells, and explain why tables should represent tabular data rather than page layout.
learningObjectives: Choose between unordered and ordered lists based on the meaning and order of the content.
Build correctly nested ul, ol, and li structures.
Identify the purpose of table, tr, th, and td elements.
Build a simple table that represents genuine tabular data.
Distinguish tabular data from page layout and explain why tables should not be used as a layout system.

sections.text: Structure the Stuff That Comes in Groups

Webpages are full of collections: navigation links, shopping items, steps in a tutorial, search results, feature lists, schedules, prices, scores, and probably at least one list nobody bothered to clean up after 2017.
HTML gives you specific structures for these cases. Lists represent collections of related items. Tables represent information whose meaning comes from the relationship between rows and columns.

sections.title: The important distinction
sections.text: A list is a collection. A table is a relationship between data points arranged in rows and columns. Choose the structure based on what the content means, not on how you want the browser to arrange it.
Unordered Lists
Use an unordered list when the items belong together but their order does not communicate a meaningful sequence.

sections.title: An unordered list
sections.code:
• HTML
  • CSS
  • JavaScript

sections.text: The ul element represents the list as a whole. Each li element represents one item in that list.
Ordered Lists
Use an ordered list when the sequence or ranking of the items matters.

sections.title: An ordered list
sections.code:
1. Open the project.
  2. Run the application.
  3. Inspect the page.

sections.text: Here the order matters. Step 1 comes before step 2, and step 2 comes before step 3. Changing the order changes the meaning of the instructions.

sections.title: Common mistake
sections.text: Choosing ul or ol because you prefer bullets or numbers is backwards. The list type should describe the meaning of the content. CSS can later change how the list looks.
List Items Belong Inside the List
The li element represents an individual list item and normally belongs inside a ul or ol.

sections.title: Correct structure
sections.code:
• Semantic HTML
  • Accessible forms
  • Responsive layout

sections.text: The relationship is clear: the list contains the items. That structure is useful to browsers, assistive technologies, and developers.
Nested Lists
A list item can contain another list when the content has a hierarchy of its own.

sections.title: A nested list
sections.code:
• Frontend
    • HTML
    • CSS
    • JavaScript
  • Backend

sections.text: The nested list belongs inside the relevant li. That preserves the relationship between the parent item and its sub-items.
Practice Drill 1: Choose the Right List
For each set of content, decide whether an unordered or ordered list better communicates its meaning. Do not think about the default bullets or numbers. Think about whether sequence matters.

sections.title: List Type Detective
sections.instructions: Choose the correct list type for each scenario. Reveal the explanation only after you have made your choice.

sections.text: Tables Represent Data Relationships
Tables solve a different problem from lists. A table represents data where the relationship between columns and rows carries meaning.

sections.title: A simple data table
sections.code:
Course Lessons
HTML 8
CSS 7

sections.text: The table represents a relationship between courses and their lesson counts. Each row represents one record, while the columns identify what each value means.
The Table Building Blocks
A basic table uses table for the overall structure, tr for a row, th for a header cell, and td for a data cell.

sections.title: Table Structure
sections.description: table → tr (row) → th or td (cell). A header cell identifies the meaning of a column or row. A data cell contains the corresponding value.

sections.title: Reading a table structurally
sections.code:
Lesson Duration
HTML Foundations 25 min

sections.text: The header cells tell us what the data underneath represents. Without that relationship, a group of numbers and words becomes much harder to interpret.
Tables Are Not for Page Layout

Older websites sometimes used tables to position parts of a page. Modern HTML should not use tables as a generic layout tool. Tables communicate tabular relationships; CSS layout systems handle page structure.

sections.title: Do not use a table for this
sections.code:
Logo Navigation
Sidebar Main content

sections.text: This is not tabular data. It is page layout. Using a table communicates the wrong meaning and can make the page harder to understand and navigate.

sections.title: Common mistake
sections.text: If your table contains 'sidebar', 'header', or 'main content' as layout regions, you probably have a CSS problem, not a table problem. A table is not Flexbox wearing a tie.

sections.text: Practice Drill 4: Lists or Tables?
Now classify the content before writing any HTML. Your goal is to identify the data model first and choose the HTML structure second.

sections.title: Choose the structure
sections.code:
A. Steps for deploying a website.
B. A list of skills on a developer profile.
C. Monthly revenue grouped by month and product.
D. Navigation links for a website.

sections.text: A and B are list-shaped problems, although A needs an ordered list because sequence matters. C is tabular data because the relationship between rows and columns carries meaning. D is a collection of navigation links and can be represented as a list within a navigation structure.

sections.label: Choose ul or ol based on content meaning, correctly build nested list structures, create a basic table using table/tr/th/td, and explain why a table is appropriate for tabular data but not for page layout.
sections.hint: Ask what relationship the content communicates. Sequence → ol. Collection → ul. Row/column data relationships → table.

sections.text: Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'When would you use a table instead of a list?' A strong answer is: 'I use a list when I have a collection of related items, choosing ordered or unordered based on whether sequence matters. I use a table when the relationship between rows and columns represents meaningful tabular data.'
A likely follow-up is: 'Would you ever use a table for page layout?' No. Page layout should be handled by CSS layout systems, while tables should communicate tabular data.
Reflect

Look at a real interface you use. Find one collection of items and one place where information is presented in rows and columns. Decide whether each should be represented as a list or a table, and explain the meaning that led to your choice.
Good HTML starts with the data model. Before asking 'Which tag should I use?', ask 'What kind of information am I representing?' The right element usually becomes much easier to see.
What You Should Take Away

Use ul for unordered collections and ol when sequence matters. Each list contains li elements, and nested lists belong inside the relevant list item. Use tables when rows and columns represent meaningful relationships between data, with table, tr, th, and td providing the basic structure. Do not use tables as a page-layout system; CSS handles layout.

quiz.question: Why should you not use a table to create a page layout?
options: Tables cannot contain text.
Tables only work with numbers.
A table communicates tabular data relationships, while page layout is a CSS responsibility.
Browsers refuse to display tables with more than one row.
quiz.explanation: Tables are semantic structures for tabular data. Using them as generic layout containers communicates the wrong meaning and can hurt accessibility.

summary: Lists represent collections, while tables represent meaningful relationships between rows and columns. Use ul when order does not matter and ol when sequence matters; list items belong inside li elements. Build basic tables with table, tr, th, and td. Do not use tables for page layout because CSS is responsible for layout and tables should communicate tabular data.

Why should tables not be used for page layout?

title: Forms and User Input
description: Build forms that collect user input using labels, inputs, and a submit action, and learn why associating labels with controls is essential for usable HTML.
mastery: The learner can build a small HTML form with correctly associated labels and inputs, choose appropriate basic input types, provide a submit control, explain what happens when a form is submitted, and identify a form whose labels are not correctly associated.
learningObjectives: Explain what an HTML form is used for.
Build a form containing labels and input controls.
Associate each label with its corresponding form control using matching for and id values.
Choose appropriate basic input types for common kinds of user input.
Create a submit control and explain its role in the form.
Identify and fix a basic form-structure or label-association mistake.

sections.text: Now Let the User Talk Back

So far, your HTML pages have mostly been talking at the user. Headings explain things. Paragraphs explain more things. Links send the user somewhere else. Forms are where the page says, 'Okay, your turn.'
A form collects information or actions from a user. Login details, search terms, contact information, feedback, settings, and checkout details can all be gathered through form controls.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: Think of a form as a conversation with a structure: the page asks for specific information, the user provides it through controls, and submitting the form sends that information for processing.
The Form Element
The form element groups controls that belong to the same user-input task.

sections.title: A tiny form
sections.code:
<form>
  <input type="text">
  <button type="submit">Save</button>
</form>

sections.text: The form contains an input control and a submit button. That is enough to demonstrate the basic idea, but it is not yet a good user experience because the input has no visible label.
Labels Tell the User What a Control Means
A label gives a form control a human-readable description. Instead of asking the user to guess what an empty box is for, tell them.

sections.title: A labeled input
sections.code:
<label for="email">Email address</label>
<input id="email" type="email">

sections.text: The label's for value matches the input's id. That association tells the browser which control the label describes.
The matching pair is the important part: label for="email" and input id="email". They are basically saying, 'Yes, this label belongs to that box.'
Why Label Association Matters

The label is not just decoration sitting above the input. Proper association improves usability and gives assistive technologies information about what the control is for. It can also make the label itself an interactive way to focus the associated control.
Without the association, a user may see the words 'Email address' while the browser and assistive technology have less explicit information connecting those words to the input.

sections.title: Common mistake
sections.text: Writing the label next to the input and assuming that is enough. Visually placing the words nearby does not create the semantic association. The for and id values need to match.
Choose the Right Input Type
The input element supports different types of user input. Choosing the appropriate type communicates what kind of value the control expects and lets the browser provide useful behavior.

sections.title: Common input types
sections.code:
<input type="text">
<input type="email">
<input type="password">
<input type="number">
<input type="date">

sections.text: These controls all collect user input, but they communicate different expectations. An email field is different from a password field, which is different from a date field.
Use the input type that matches the data. If you are asking for an email address, use type="email" instead of a generic text input and hoping JavaScript figures out the rest later.
The Submit Control
A form needs a way for the user to say, 'I'm done. Send this.' A button with type="submit" provides the form's submit action.

sections.title: A complete small form
sections.code:
<form>
  <label for="name">Name</label>
  <input id="name" type="text">

  <label for="email">Email</label>
  <input id="email" type="email">

  <button type="submit">Create account</button>
</form>

sections.text: Now the page has a clear interaction: ask for a name, ask for an email address, and provide a submit action.
What Happens When the Form Is Submitted?

Submitting a form can cause the browser to send the form's data according to the form's configuration. In a real application, the result may involve a server request, validation, success feedback, an error state, or some combination of those things.

For this lesson, do not worry about building the entire server-side submission flow. The important idea is that the form collects the user's input and the submit action starts the process of handling that input.

sections.text: Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'Why is label association important in HTML forms?' A strong answer is: 'A label gives a form control a meaningful description and explicitly associates that description with the control. Matching the label's for attribute with the input's id improves usability and helps assistive technologies understand what the control is for.'
A likely follow-up is: 'Why not just put text next to the input?' Because visual proximity is not the same thing as a semantic label-control relationship.
Reflect

Look at a login or signup form you use. Pick one field and trace the relationship from the visible label to the control. Then ask what would happen if the label and control were not explicitly connected.

A form can look perfectly fine while still being poorly structured. HTML is not judged only by whether your eyes are happy. The browser and the people using assistive technology need the relationships to be explicit too.
What You Should Take Away

Forms collect user input through controls such as inputs and provide a submit action for processing that input. Every control should have a meaningful label, and label associations should be explicit by matching the label's for value with the control's id. Choose input types that match the data being requested. Good forms communicate their structure and purpose before CSS or JavaScript enters the picture.

quiz.question: How is a label explicitly associated with an input?
options: The label's for value matches the input's id.
The label's class matches the input's name.
The input's type matches the label's text.
The label appears above the input visually.
quiz.explanation: The label's for attribute should match the id of the input it describes.

email
password
number
quiz.explanation: type="email" communicates that the field expects an email address and enables browser behavior appropriate to that kind of input.

quiz.question: What is the role of a button with type="submit" inside a form?
options: It identifies the form's heading.
It provides a control for submitting the form.
It automatically validates every possible business rule.
It replaces all input fields.
quiz.explanation: A submit button provides the form's submit action, allowing the collected input to enter the form submission process.

summary: HTML forms collect user input through controls such as input elements and provide a submit action for processing that input. Labels should be explicitly associated with controls by matching for and id values, and input types should match the kind of data being requested. These relationships are part of the HTML structure, not merely visual styling.

title: Semantic HTML
description: Learn how semantic HTML elements communicate the role of page regions and content, then refactor generic markup into meaningful structure that is easier to navigate, maintain, and understand.
mastery: The learner can identify when a semantic HTML element is more appropriate than a generic div, explain the roles of header, nav, main, article, section, and footer at a beginner level, refactor a small page into semantic markup, and justify the structural choices without relying on visual appearance.
learningObjectives: Explain what semantic HTML means and why element meaning matters.
Identify appropriate uses for header, nav, main, article, section, and footer.
Distinguish semantic elements from generic containers such as div.
Refactor a small block of generic markup into meaningful semantic HTML.
Explain how semantic structure can support accessibility, navigation, and maintainability.

sections.text: Stop Making Every Box a div

You have now learned the mechanics of HTML: elements, attributes, headings, links, lists, tables, and forms. There is one more habit that separates meaningful HTML from a pile of generic containers: choosing elements because they describe what the content actually is.
That is semantic HTML. Instead of using a generic div for every region and hoping the class names explain everything, you use elements whose names communicate the role of the content.

sections.title: The div-everything trap
sections.text: A div is useful. It is not evil. The problem is using it for everything. If every region of your page is a div, your markup starts looking like a cardboard box factory where nobody labeled the boxes.
What Makes HTML Semantic?

An element is semantic when its name communicates something about the role or meaning of the content it contains. Elements such as nav, main, article, header, and footer tell the browser and other tools more than a generic div does.

sections.title: Generic structure
sections.code:
...
...
...

sections.title: Meaningful structure
sections.code:
<header>
  <nav>...</nav>
</header>

<main>
  ...
</main>

<footer>
  ...
</footer>

sections.text: Both structures can be styled to look identical. The second one communicates more about what each region represents.
header
The header element represents introductory content for a page or section. It can contain things such as a heading, logo, introductory information, or navigation associated with that region.

sections.text: nav
The nav element represents a section whose purpose is navigation: a collection of important links that help users move around the site or application.

sections.title: Navigation
sections.code:

sections.text: main
The main element represents the dominant content of the page. It identifies the part of the document that is directly related to the page's primary purpose.

sections.title: Main content

Build the structure of the web.

sections.text: article

An article represents a self-contained piece of content that can stand on its own or potentially be distributed independently. Blog posts, news stories, forum posts, and some learning content can be good candidates.

sections.title: A self-contained article
sections.code:
What Is Semantic HTML?

Semantic HTML communicates the meaning of page content.

sections.text: section
The section element represents a thematic grouping of content. A section commonly has its own heading and helps divide a larger document into meaningful parts.

sections.title: A content section
sections.code:
HTML Foundations

Start with the structure of web documents.

sections.text: A useful beginner distinction is that article is about a self-contained piece of content, while section is about grouping related content into a thematic part of a larger document. The exact choice depends on what the content means.
footer
The footer element represents footer content for a page or section. It can contain information such as related links, author information, copyright information, or other supporting content.

sections.title: A page footer
sections.code: © Forge Academy

sections.text: Why Semantic HTML Matters

Semantic HTML gives the structure of a page meaning that can be understood beyond visual appearance. Browsers, assistive technologies, search systems, and developers can use that structure to better understand what different regions represent.

For accessibility, meaningful landmarks can help users navigate large pages more efficiently. For maintainability, semantic markup makes the intent of a document easier for another developer to understand. For search, meaningful structure can also help systems interpret the page.

sections.title: Important boundary
sections.text: Semantic HTML improves structure and can provide useful accessibility information, but it does not magically make an entire interface accessible. Good accessibility also involves labels, keyboard interaction, focus behavior, contrast, states, and more. You will build those skills progressively.

The goal is not 'replace every div.' The goal is 'use a meaningful element when one exists, and use a generic container when you genuinely need one.' Semantic HTML should be intentional, not performative.

sections.hint: Choose the element by the role of the content. Do not choose it because its default appearance looks convenient.

sections.text: Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'Why is semantic HTML better than using div for everything?' A strong answer is: 'Semantic elements communicate the role and structure of content more clearly to browsers, assistive technologies, search systems, and developers. That can improve navigation, accessibility, and maintainability. I would still use div when no more specific semantic element fits.'

A likely follow-up is: 'Does semantic HTML automatically make a page accessible?' No. It provides important structural information, but accessibility also depends on things such as keyboard behavior, labels, focus management, contrast, and interaction design.
Reflect
Look at a real page and pick three regions. Ignore their colors and layout. Identify what each region is for and choose the HTML element that best communicates that purpose.

Semantic HTML is one of those skills that looks small in code and enormous in the long run. Good element choices make the document easier for people, browsers, assistive technology, and future-you to understand.
What You Should Take Away

Semantic HTML uses meaningful elements to describe the role of page content. header, nav, main, article, section, and footer communicate different structural purposes, while div remains useful as a generic container when no specific semantic meaning fits. Semantic structure can improve accessibility, navigation, search understanding, and maintainability, but it is only one part of building an accessible interface.

title: HTML Challenge: Build a Real Page
description: Bring the HTML module together by building a complete page that uses headings, text, links, images, lists, forms, and semantic structure in one coherent document.
mastery: The learner can independently build a complete HTML page that satisfies the project requirements, uses meaningful semantic structure, contains correctly associated form controls, uses working links and image paths, represents lists and tabular data appropriately, and can explain the structural decisions made.
learningObjectives: Plan the semantic structure of a complete HTML page before writing all of its markup.
Combine headings, paragraphs, links, images, lists, forms, and semantic elements into one coherent document.
Apply correct nesting and attribute syntax across a larger HTML document.
Choose HTML structures based on content meaning rather than visual appearance.
Inspect the finished document for common structural, semantic, and accessibility mistakes.
Explain the major structural decisions made in the completed page.

sections.text: Time to Stop Collecting Tags

You have spent the module learning individual pieces of HTML. You know how headings work, how elements and attributes fit together, how links and images use paths, how lists and tables represent different kinds of information, how forms collect user input, and why semantic elements matter.
Now you have to do the slightly uncomfortable thing: use all of that without someone pointing at the exact tag you should type next.

sections.title: This is a build, not a typing test
sections.text: The goal is not to remember every HTML element by heart. The goal is to look at a page requirement, identify what kind of content you have, and choose HTML that represents that content correctly.
The Challenge
Build a small Forge Academy learning page for a fictional lesson called 'Frontend Foundations'. The page should feel like a real page someone could use, not a random pile of HTML examples.

sections.title: Project brief
sections.code:
Page title: Frontend Foundations

The page must contain:
- A site header with the Forge Academy name.
- Navigation links for Learn, Practice, and Progress.
- One main content region.
- A page heading for Frontend Foundations.
- At least two paragraphs explaining the lesson.
- One image with meaningful alt text.
- One unordered list of learning outcomes.
- One ordered list of three steps for completing the lesson.
- One self-contained article containing a short tip.
- One form asking for the learner's name and email.
- Correctly associated labels for both form controls.
- A submit button.
- A footer.

Do not add CSS or JavaScript yet.

sections.text: Plan Before You Code
Do not immediately start typing the final HTML. First turn the brief into a structure. You already know enough HTML to sketch the page before writing the details.

sections.title: A sensible page outline
sections.code:
header
└── site name
└── nav
    └── navigation links

main
└── h1
└── introductory paragraphs
└── image
└── learning outcomes list
└── lesson steps list
└── article
    └── tip
└── form
    ├── name field
    ├── email field
    └── submit button

footer

sections.text: This is not the only possible structure. It is a reasonable starting point because each region has a clear purpose. Before writing the markup, make sure you can explain why each major element belongs where it does.
Build in Layers

sections.title: A Safer Way to Build the Page

steps.title: 1. Build the document shell
steps.description: Create the doctype, html element, head, title, and body.

steps.title: 2. Build the semantic page regions
steps.description: Add header, navigation, main, article or section where appropriate, and footer.

steps.title: 3. Add the content structure
steps.description: Add headings, paragraphs, links, images, lists, and form controls based on the project requirements.

steps.title: 4. Check relationships
steps.description: Verify nesting, heading hierarchy, label-to-input associations, and local resource paths.

steps.title: 5. Inspect the result
steps.description: Open the page in the browser and use DevTools to inspect the resulting DOM. Look for structural mistakes rather than styling problems.

sections.text: Checkpoint 1: Build the Structure
Start with the page shell and semantic regions. Do not worry about making every detail perfect yet. Get the document's structure correct first.

sections.title: Project Stage 1 — Page Structure
sections.instructions: Build the document shell and semantic regions for the challenge. Create the html, head, and body structure, then add header, nav, main, and footer. Keep the structure meaningful and do not add CSS or JavaScript.

<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <title>Frontend Foundations</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <!-- Build the page structure here. -->
  </body>
</html>

sections.text: Checkpoint 2: Add the Content
Now add the actual lesson content. Use your previous lessons as references when you are unsure about the correct element. The important part is making the content structure reflect the brief.

sections.title: Project Stage 2 — Content Structure
sections.instructions: Complete the main content requirements: a logical h1, explanatory paragraphs, an image with meaningful alt text, an unordered list of learning outcomes, an ordered list of lesson steps, and a self-contained article containing a short tip.

  <!-- Add an image with appropriate alt text. -->

  <!-- Add an unordered list of learning outcomes. -->

  <!-- Add an ordered list of three lesson steps. -->

  <!-- Add a self-contained article containing a short tip. -->
</main>

sections.text: Checkpoint 3: Add the Form
Now add a small learner form asking for a name and email address. Both controls need visible labels and explicit label-to-input associations. Use the appropriate input types.

sections.title: Project Stage 3 — Learner Form
sections.instructions: Add the form to the page. Include a name field, an email field, correctly associated labels, and a submit button. Inspect your own markup and confirm that every label's for value matches exactly one input id.
