  <!-- Add the learner name field. -->

  <!-- Add the email field. -->

  <!-- Add the submit button. -->
</form>

sections.text: Checkpoint 4: Test Your Paths
Your image and links are only useful if the browser can resolve their destinations. Before declaring victory, inspect every href and src value.

sections.title: Path audit
sections.code:
For every local resource, ask:

1. Where is the current document?
2. Where is the target resource?
3. Is the path relative or absolute?
4. How will the browser resolve it?
5. Does the resource actually load?

sections.text: You already learned this in the previous lesson. This time you are applying it inside a larger document where several relationships have to work at once.
Checkpoint 5: Perform an HTML Quality Pass
Before you call the page finished, inspect it like an engineer rather than its proud parent.

sections.title: Your quality checklist
sections.code:
STRUCTURE
[ ] One clear page structure
[ ] Semantic regions used appropriately
[ ] Elements nested correctly

CONTENT
[ ] Heading hierarchy makes sense
[ ] Paragraphs are used for ordinary prose
[ ] Lists match the meaning of the content
[ ] Article content is self-contained

LINKS & MEDIA
[ ] href values point to intended destinations
[ ] src values point to real resources
[ ] Images have meaningful alt text

FORMS
[ ] Every control has a label
[ ] label[for] matches input[id]
[ ] Input types match the requested data
[ ] Submit button exists

CODE QUALITY
[ ] No obvious malformed tags
[ ] No unnecessary layout tables
[ ] No styling-driven heading choices

sections.title: Do not skip the inspection pass
sections.text: The page working in your browser does not automatically mean the HTML is well structured. Browsers are extremely tolerant. They will often recover from your mistakes instead of filing a formal complaint.
Final Project Workspace

sections.title: HTML Challenge — Build the Real Page
sections.instructions: Build the complete page from the project brief. Do not copy a finished solution. Work from the requirements, use the previous lessons as references when needed, and complete the quality checklist before considering the project finished.

<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <title>Frontend Foundations</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <!--
      Build the complete Forge Academy lesson page here.

      Requirements:
      - header + navigation
      - main content
      - h1 + paragraphs
      - image + alt text
      - unordered learning outcomes list
      - ordered lesson steps list
      - self-contained article with a tip
      - name + email form
      - correctly associated labels
      - submit button
      - footer
    -->
  </body>
</html>

sections.text: Self-Review: Explain Your Decisions

A project is not complete just because the browser displays something. Explain five decisions you made: one semantic choice, one heading decision, one list decision, one form decision, and one path decision.
For each decision, explain what the content meant, which HTML structure you chose, and why that structure was appropriate.

sections.label: Complete the full HTML project, satisfy every requirement in the brief, pass the quality checklist, and explain the major structural choices made in the final page.
sections.hint: Do not judge the project only by appearance. Check structure, semantics, relationships, paths, form associations, and content meaning.

sections.text: Project Review
Before leaving the module, compare your finished page against the original brief. Every requirement should have a visible implementation and a structurally appropriate HTML element.

Your first complete page will probably not be beautiful. That is completely fine. Right now, correct structure beats impressive decoration. We can make things pretty after we stop putting the navigation inside a table.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks you to walk through the HTML of your project. Be prepared to explain why you used semantic regions, why certain content is a list rather than a table, how your form labels connect to their controls, and how the browser resolves your local resource paths.
The important skill here is not remembering a list of tags. It is defending structural decisions based on the meaning of the content.
Module Reflection

Look back at the page you built at the beginning of the module versus what you can build now. You have moved from individual tags to a complete document with meaningful structure, navigation, media, lists, tables, forms, and semantic regions.
That is the point of the module: not to collect HTML vocabulary, but to be able to look at a page requirement and construct a sensible document from it.

sections.title: HTML module complete
sections.text: You now have enough HTML to build a real structured page from scratch. The next module changes the question from 'What is this content?' to 'How should this content look and lay out?' That is where CSS begins.
What You Should Take Away

A complete HTML page is built by combining individual semantic structures into one coherent document. You now have practice applying headings, paragraphs, links, images, paths, lists, tables, forms, and semantic regions together. The strongest habit to carry forward is to choose HTML based on content meaning first and inspect the finished document before moving on.

The learner must plan the structure, combine semantic regions and content elements, build working links and images, create lists and a form, inspect paths and relationships, and perform a final quality pass. title: What Is CSS?
description: Understand CSS as a rule-based styling language, learn the anatomy of a CSS rule, and build the mental model that styles are matched to elements and then resolved.
mastery: The learner can explain CSS as a rule-based language that selects elements and applies visual properties, identify the selector, property, and value in a CSS rule, and explain why CSS does not simply apply blindly when multiple rules target the same element.
learningObjectives: Explain CSS as a rule-based language that selects elements and applies visual properties.
Identify the selector, property, value, and declaration in a basic CSS rule.
Read a simple CSS rule as a plain-language instruction.
Explain at a high level that CSS rules are matched to elements and then resolved when multiple rules apply.
Apply one simple CSS rule to an HTML element.

sections.text: Rules, Not Magic
You spent the HTML module teaching the browser what your content is. Now we change the question: what should that content look like?
CSS stands for Cascading Style Sheets. It is a rule-based styling language that selects elements and applies visual properties to them. That sounds simple because, at the foundation, it is.
The useful part is the word rule. CSS is not a bag of random decoration commands. You write a rule that essentially says: find these elements, then give them these styles.

sections.title: A simple mental model
sections.text: HTML says what something is. CSS says how it should be presented. JavaScript can later make it behave. Three jobs, three tools. Much less chaotic than asking one language to do everyone's job and then blaming it when the project becomes a mess.
The Anatomy of a CSS Rule

sections.title: One rule, four useful ideas

sections.text: The h1 is the selector. It tells the browser which elements the rule targets. Inside the braces are declarations. Each declaration contains a property and a value: color is the property and navy is its value; font-size is the property and 2rem is its value.

sections.title: Reading a CSS Rule
sections.description: Selector → h1. Declaration → color: navy. Property → color. Value → navy. Declaration → font-size: 2rem. Property → font-size. Value → 2rem. Read the rule as: select h1 elements, then apply these style declarations.

sections.text: A good beginner habit is to read CSS rules as sentences. In the example above: 'Find every h1 element and make its text navy and its font size 2rem.'
CSS Targets HTML
CSS becomes useful because it can target the HTML structure you already built. If your page contains an h1, paragraph, and button, CSS rules can select those elements and change their presentation.

sections.title: The HTML
sections.code:
Forge Academy

Build frontend engineering skills.

sections.title: The CSS

sections.text: The HTML has not changed its meaning. The h1 is still a heading, the p is still a paragraph, and the button is still a button. CSS changes their presentation.
This separation is powerful: you can change the visual design without rewriting the document structure. The HTML tells the browser what the content means; CSS tells it how to present that meaning.
Properties Describe What You Want to Change
CSS properties describe different aspects of presentation. Some affect color, some typography, some spacing, some dimensions, and others layout or visual effects.

sections.title: A few common properties

sections.text: You do not need to memorize hundreds of properties today. You need to understand the relationship between selector, property, and value so that new properties have somewhere to fit in your mental model.
What Does 'Cascading' Mean?
Here is the part that beginners often skip: CSS does not simply find a rule and stop. Several rules can match the same element. When they disagree, the browser has to resolve the conflict.

sections.title: Two rules disagree

sections.text: Both rules target paragraphs. Both try to set color. The browser therefore has to determine which declaration wins. The exact mechanics involve the cascade, specificity, and source order.

sections.title: Important boundary
sections.text: You do not need to master specificity or the full cascade algorithm in this lesson. You only need to stop thinking of CSS as 'the browser applies my styles somehow.' CSS rules are matched to elements and, when rules conflict, the browser resolves those conflicts using a defined process. The next lesson is where we study that process.
Interact: Read the Rule
Before touching the CSS, translate each rule into plain English. The goal is to understand what the browser has been told to do.

sections.title: CSS Rule Detective
sections.instructions: Inspect the CSS rule and explain it in plain language before revealing the answer. Identify the selector, property, and value. Then change one value and predict what will happen to the page.

sections.text: Practice: Write Your First CSS Rule
Take the HTML below and write a CSS rule that changes the h1 color and font size. Do not touch the HTML. Your job is to describe the desired presentation using CSS.

sections.title: The HTML
sections.code:
Learn Frontend Engineering

Start with the browser and build from first principles.

sections.title: Write a CSS Rule
sections.instructions: Add a CSS rule that targets the h1. Make its color #2563eb and its font-size 2rem. Then explain which part of your rule is the selector, which parts are properties, and which parts are values.
sections.initialCode:
Learn Frontend Engineering

Start with the browser and build from first principles.

sections.text: Practice: Predict Before You Change
Consider these two rules. Before deciding what the paragraph looks like, identify the fact that both rules match the same element.

sections.title: Which value wins?

sections.text: Both selectors have the same basic specificity, so source order becomes relevant here. The later declaration wins and the paragraph is red. You will learn the complete mechanics next.

This is the first CSS mystery you should refuse to solve with vibes. When two rules disagree, there is a reason one wins. Your job as a developer is to learn the rules instead of adding another declaration and hoping the browser feels generous.

sections.label: Explain CSS as a rule-based language, identify the selector, property, value, and declaration in a CSS rule, write one simple rule that styles an HTML element, and explain at a high level why conflicting CSS rules require a resolution process.
sections.hint: Think: select something → declare a property/value → browser matches the rule → conflicts are resolved by the cascade.

sections.text: Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'What is CSS?' A strong beginner answer is: 'CSS is a rule-based styling language used to select elements and apply visual properties to them. A rule contains a selector and declarations, and when multiple rules match the same element, the browser resolves conflicts through the cascade.'

A likely follow-up is: 'What is the difference between a property and a value?' A property describes what aspect you are changing, such as color, while the value specifies what you want it to be, such as blue.
Reflect

Look at any CSS rule you have written and read it as a sentence: 'Find these elements and change this property to this value.' If that sentence makes sense, you are beginning to read CSS as a system instead of memorizing decorative commands.

CSS gets complicated later, but the foundation does not change: selectors identify what you are styling, declarations describe what to change, and the cascade resolves conflicts when multiple rules apply.
What You Should Take Away

CSS is a rule-based styling language. A selector identifies the elements a rule targets, and declarations specify properties and values that control their presentation. Multiple rules can target the same element, so the browser must resolve conflicts through the cascade. The next lesson examines selectors and specificity more closely.

Storing application data in a database.

summary: CSS is a rule-based language for controlling the presentation of HTML. A CSS rule contains a selector and declarations; each declaration pairs a property with a value. The browser matches rules to elements, and when multiple rules conflict, the cascade determines which declaration wins. The next lesson goes deeper into selectors and specificity.

title: Selectors and Specificity
description: Learn how CSS identifies elements with type, class, ID, attribute, and descendant selectors, then understand why conflicting rules do not all have equal priority.
mastery: The learner can choose an appropriate selector for a simple styling requirement, explain the difference between type, class, and ID selectors, combine selectors to target elements more precisely, calculate basic specificity comparisons, and diagnose a simple case where an expected CSS rule does not win.
learningObjectives: Use type, class, and ID selectors to target HTML elements.
Use descendant selectors to target elements based on their relationship in the document.
Explain why classes are generally useful for reusable styling while IDs are more specific.
Compare the specificity of simple competing selectors.
Diagnose a basic selector conflict by identifying which rule has greater specificity or appears later when specificity is equal.

sections.text: CSS Needs to Find Something First
In the previous lesson, CSS was the rulebook: select something, then apply declarations. The question now is obvious: how does CSS decide exactly which elements a rule should target?
Selectors are the answer. They are the part of the rule that tells the browser which elements should receive the declarations.

sections.title: A useful mental model
sections.text: Think of selectors as filters. A broad filter can match lots of elements. A more specific filter narrows the target. Specificity matters when multiple filters match the same element and disagree about how it should be styled.
Type Selectors
A type selector targets every element of a particular HTML type.
This rule targets paragraph elements. If the page contains ten p elements, all ten can match the selector.
Class Selectors
A class selector targets elements that have a particular class attribute. Classes are especially useful when the same styling should be reusable across multiple elements.

sections.title: HTML with classes
sections.code:
Secondary information.

Another secondary note.

sections.title: Class selectors

sections.text: The period identifies a class selector. Multiple elements can share the same class, which makes classes useful for reusable styling patterns.
ID Selectors
An ID selector targets an element by its id attribute.

sections.title: An element with an id
sections.code: Frontend Foundations

sections.title: An ID selector

sections.text: The hash symbol identifies an ID selector. IDs are intended to identify a particular element, and ID selectors have greater specificity than class or type selectors.

sections.title: Don't reach for IDs just because they are stronger
sections.text: An ID selector being more specific does not make it automatically better. Reusable component styling is usually easier to manage with classes. Strong selectors can become difficult to override later, which is why CSS developers should use specificity intentionally rather than treating it like a volume knob.
Descendant Selectors
Selectors can also describe relationships between elements. A descendant selector targets elements that occur somewhere inside another element.

sections.title: A descendant selector

sections.text: This targets p elements that are descendants of an element with the card class. It is more targeted than selecting every paragraph on the page.

sections.title: Which paragraphs match?
sections.code:
Outside the card.

Inside the card.

sections.text: Only the paragraph inside the card matches .card p.
Specificity: When Rules Disagree
Now we reach the reason specificity matters. Imagine two rules target the same element and assign different values to the same property.

sections.title: Two competing rules
The element being styled
sections.code: Important update.

sections.text: Both rules match the paragraph. The type selector p is less specific than the class selector .notice, so the class rule wins for the color property.
A Beginner Specificity Model
For the selector types in this lesson, you can use a simple comparison: ID selectors are more specific than class selectors, and class selectors are more specific than type selectors.

sections.title: Basic specificity order
sections.code:
ID selector
    ↓
Class / attribute / pseudo-class selector
    ↓
Type / element selector

sections.text: This is a simplified mental model for the selector types introduced here. Later, you will learn the full specificity calculation and how combinations of selectors affect the result.
What If Specificity Is Equal?
If two matching declarations have the same specificity, source order becomes relevant. When otherwise equivalent rules conflict, the later declaration wins.

sections.title: Equal specificity

sections.text: Both selectors have the same specificity. The later declaration wins, so the message becomes green.

sections.title: The 'my CSS isn't working' trap
sections.text: When a rule does not seem to work, do not immediately add !important or make the selector uglier. First ask: does my selector match the element? Is another selector more specific? If specificity is equal, does another declaration appear later?
Practice Drill 1: Which Elements Match?
Predict which elements each selector matches before revealing the answer. This is the fastest way to stop guessing what selectors do.

sections.title: Selector Matching Lab
sections.instructions: For each selector, predict which elements match. Then reveal the explanation. Pay attention to whether the selector targets every element of a type or only elements with a particular class or relationship.

The paragraph below matches all three selectors. Predict which color the browser uses and explain why.

sections.code: Deployment failed.

sections.instructions: Change the selectors and declaration order to create different specificity conflicts. Before each change, predict which color should win. Then verify your prediction in the browser.

sections.text: Practice Drill 3: Fix the Rule That 'Doesn't Work'
The developer expects the button to be blue, but it is red. Do not immediately rewrite the CSS. Find out why the red declaration wins.

sections.code: <button id="save" class="primary">Save changes</button>

sections.title: The stylesheet

sections.text: The issue is not that the blue rule is broken. It matches the element. The red rule simply has greater specificity because it uses an ID selector.

sections.title: Diagnose the Specificity Bug
sections.instructions: Inspect the three matching rules and explain why the expected blue background does not win. Then choose a reasonable way to produce the intended result without using !important. Prefer reducing unnecessary specificity rather than escalating it.

    background: blue;
    color: white;
  }

  }

    background: red;
  }
</style>

sections.text: Specificity Is a Tool, Not a Competition
A common beginner reaction to a CSS conflict is to write an even stronger selector. That can solve today's problem while creating tomorrow's problem.

sections.title: Escalating specificity

sections.text: This selector is much harder to override than a simple reusable class. As CSS grows, unnecessary specificity can turn small changes into a negotiation with your own stylesheet.
When you need to win a specificity battle, first ask why you are in the battle. A clean stylesheet usually benefits more from sensible selector design than from increasingly dramatic selectors.

sections.label: Choose appropriate type, class, ID, and descendant selectors; compare competing selectors using the basic specificity model; and diagnose a simple conflict by explaining why one rule wins.
sections.hint: First determine which rules actually match. Then compare their specificity. If specificity is equal, use source order.

sections.text: Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'What is CSS specificity?' A strong beginner answer is: 'Specificity is part of how the browser decides which conflicting CSS declaration wins when multiple selectors match the same element. In the basic cases, ID selectors are more specific than class selectors, which are more specific than type selectors. If specificity is equal, source order matters.'
A likely follow-up is: 'Which is more specific, .card or #card?' The ID selector #card is more specific.
Reflect

Take one CSS rule that did not behave as you expected. Instead of adding more CSS, ask three questions: did the selector match, did another selector have greater specificity, and if specificity was equal, did another rule appear later?

You now have the beginning of a real CSS debugging skill: when a style does not win, investigate the selector and the cascade before changing the code. Later lessons will make that reasoning more precise.
What You Should Take Away

Selectors determine which elements CSS rules target. Type selectors target elements by tag name, class selectors target reusable classes, ID selectors target elements by id, and descendant selectors express relationships between elements. When matching rules conflict, specificity and then source order help determine which declaration wins. The goal is to use selectors precisely without creating unnecessary specificity.

title: The Cascade and Inheritance
description: Understand how the CSS cascade resolves competing declarations, how inherited properties flow from parent to child, and why !important should not be your first response to a styling conflict.
mastery: The learner can explain the basic cascade order between competing declarations, identify when a property is inherited, distinguish inherited styles from directly matched styles, and diagnose a simple styling conflict without reaching for !important.
learningObjectives: Explain what the CSS cascade does when multiple declarations match the same element.
Use specificity and source order as part of a basic cascade decision.
Explain inheritance as the flow of certain property values from a parent to descendants.

sections.text: When CSS Has Opinions
In the last lesson, you learned that selectors decide which elements a rule matches and specificity helps decide which conflicting rule wins. Now we take one step deeper.

The cascade is the browser's process for resolving competing CSS declarations. Inheritance is a related idea: some properties can take their value from an ancestor when the child has not explicitly received its own value.

sections.title: The beginner mental model
sections.text: Think of the cascade as the browser sorting out competing instructions. Think of inheritance as certain instructions naturally flowing down the family tree. CSS has drama, but at least it has rules for the drama.
The Cascade Is About Competing Declarations
Suppose two rules target the same paragraph and both set its color.

sections.title: Two competing declarations
The matching element
sections.code: Server is temporarily unavailable.

sections.text: Both declarations match the same element. The browser cannot use both values for the same property at once, so it resolves the conflict. In this example, the class selector is more specific than the type selector, so red wins.
What If Specificity Is Equal?
When relevant specificity is equal, source order can decide the winner.

sections.title: Later wins when specificity ties

sections.text: Both selectors have the same specificity. The later declaration wins, so the text becomes green.
The Cascade Is Bigger Than Specificity

Specificity is important, but it is not the entire cascade. The browser considers several factors when deciding which declaration applies, including the origin and importance of the declaration, specificity, and source order.

For now, Forge is keeping the mental model focused: first make sure the selector matches, then consider which competing declaration has the relevant priority, then use source order when otherwise equivalent declarations tie.

sections.title: Do not memorize a giant cascade chart yet
sections.text: There is a much bigger cascade system than what you need for today's problems. You will meet important and advanced cascade behavior later. The goal here is to understand why a browser can legitimately choose one declaration over another.
Inheritance Is Different
Inheritance is not the browser choosing between competing rules. It is the browser allowing certain properties to take their value from an ancestor when the descendant does not have its own value.

sections.title: A parent value inherited by children
The descendants
sections.code:
Frontend Foundations

Learn CSS.

sections.text: The h2 and p can inherit the body's color because color is an inheritable property and neither descendant has supplied its own color.
Not Everything Inherits
Inheritance is property-specific. Some properties commonly inherit, such as color and font-related properties. Many layout and box properties do not automatically inherit.

sections.title: Do not assume every property flows down

sections.text: A child can inherit the body's color, but you should not assume it automatically receives the body's padding as its own padding.

sections.title: Common mistake
sections.text: Inheritance does not mean 'all CSS values travel down.' It only applies to properties that inherit, and even then a child can provide its own value and stop relying on the inherited one.
Direct Styling Can Override Inheritance

sections.title: The child gets its own value

sections.text: Now the card has its own color declaration, so its descendants can inherit from the card's blue value instead of the body's original value.
This gives you an important relationship: inheritance can provide a value, but a directly applicable declaration can establish a different value for the element.

!important Is Not a Debugging Button
When a style does not win, beginners often reach for !important. It can change the result, but using it as a first response usually hides the reason the existing CSS lost.

sections.title: The shortcut to avoid

sections.text: Important declarations participate in the cascade with higher priority than ordinary declarations. That makes them powerful, but repeated use can make future overrides harder to reason about.

sections.title: The !important reflex

sections.text: A Better Debugging Question
When a style seems wrong, ask a more precise question than 'Why isn't CSS working?' Ask: 'Where is this value coming from?'

sections.title: Trace the value
sections.code:
1. Does a selector directly match the element?
2. Do multiple declarations match?
3. Which declaration wins?
4. If nothing directly supplies the value, is it inherited?
5. Is there an unnecessary !important making the situation harder?

sections.text: That question turns a vague visual problem into something you can investigate with DevTools and the CSS rules in front of you.

sections.label: Explain why a declaration wins in a simple cascade conflict, distinguish inherited values from directly matched declarations, and fix a basic cascade or inheritance problem without using !important as the first solution.
sections.hint: Follow the value: matching rules → priority/specificity → source order when applicable → inheritance when the element does not have its own applicable value.

sections.text: Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'What is the difference between the cascade and inheritance?' A strong beginner answer is: 'The cascade resolves conflicts between declarations that apply to an element, while inheritance allows certain properties to receive their value from an ancestor when the element does not have its own value.'

A likely follow-up is: 'Why shouldn't you use !important everywhere?' Because it changes the priority of a declaration and can make the stylesheet harder to override and reason about. It is better to understand the underlying cascade conflict first.
Reflect

Think about a CSS bug that initially looked random. Ask yourself whether you were actually missing information about where a value came from. That is one of the first big shifts from 'trying CSS' to debugging CSS.
The browser is not picking styles out of a hat. If a value surprised you, there is a rule explaining it. Your job is to find the rule.
What You Should Take Away

The cascade resolves competing CSS declarations, using factors such as priority, specificity, and source order. Inheritance is different: certain properties can flow from an ancestor to a descendant when the descendant does not have its own applicable value. When CSS behaves unexpectedly, trace where the value comes from before reaching for !important.

quiz.explanation: !important changes the priority of a declaration. Using it indiscriminately can make CSS conflicts harder to manage rather than solving the underlying design.

summary: The CSS cascade resolves conflicts between declarations that apply to the same element, while inheritance allows certain properties to flow from ancestors to descendants when the descendant has no applicable value of its own. Priority, specificity, and source order all contribute to cascade decisions. When a style behaves unexpectedly, trace where the value comes from before using !important.

title: The CSS Box Model
description: Understand how every HTML element becomes a box made of content, padding, border, and margin, and learn how the browser calculates the space that element occupies.
mastery: The learner can identify the four parts of the CSS box model, distinguish padding from margin, calculate a basic element's rendered size, explain content-box versus border-box sizing, and diagnose a simple spacing or sizing problem using the box model.
learningObjectives: Explain the four parts of the CSS box model: content, padding, border, and margin.
Distinguish padding from margin based on where the space appears.
Calculate the rendered width of a simple element using content-box sizing.
Explain how border-box changes the meaning of a declared width or height.
Use DevTools to inspect an element's box model and diagnose a basic spacing problem.

sections.text: Every Element Is a Box
You have learned how CSS finds an element and decides which declarations apply to it. Now we need to understand something more physical: how much space that element actually takes up.
The CSS box model describes every element as a rectangular box made from four layers: content, padding, border, and margin.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: Picture a package. The content is what's inside. Padding is the bubble wrap around it. Border is the box itself. Margin is the empty space separating your package from everyone else's. CSS has basically turned shipping logistics into a layout system.

sections.title: The Four Layers
sections.description: Center: content. Around it: padding. Around padding: border. Outside the border: margin. Content, padding, and border contribute to the element's box; margin creates space outside the box.

sections.text: Content

The content box is where the element's actual content lives: text, an image, or the children of a container. If you set width: 200px with the default content-box sizing, that 200px refers to the content area.

sections.title: A content width

sections.text: At this point, the content area is 200px wide. Padding and border can make the total visible box wider.
Padding
Padding is space between an element's content and its border. Increasing padding makes the content breathe inside the element.

sections.title: Add internal space

sections.text: With 20px of left and right padding, the visible width is now larger than the original 200px content width when using the default content-box sizing.
A quick memory trick: padding is inside the border. If you increase padding, the content gets more breathing room inside the box.
Border
The border sits between padding and margin. It is part of the element's box and can have a width, style, and color.

sections.title: Add a border

sections.text: With the default box-sizing behavior, the border adds to the total rendered size as well.
Margin
Margin is space outside the border. It separates the element from surrounding content.

sections.title: Space outside the box

sections.text: Unlike padding, margin does not create breathing room around the content inside the box. It creates separation between the box and other elements.

sections.title: The classic padding-versus-margin mistake
sections.text: If text feels cramped inside a card, margin is usually not the answer. You probably want padding. If two cards are too close together, padding will not separate the boxes from each other; margin or gap is usually involved.
The Size Calculation
With the default box-sizing value of content-box, a declared width applies to the content area. Horizontal padding and borders are added outside that content width.

sections.title: Basic width calculation
sections.code:
width: 200px
padding-left: 20px
padding-right: 20px
border-left: 2px
border-right: 2px

Total rendered width:
200 + 20 + 20 + 2 + 2 = 244px

sections.text: This is one of the reasons beginners sometimes set width: 200px and wonder why the element is visibly wider than 200px.
border-box Changes the Calculation
With box-sizing: border-box, the declared width includes the content, padding, and border.

sections.title: Include padding and border in the declared width

sections.text: Now the entire border box is 200px wide. The browser fits the content, padding, and border inside that total width.

sections.title: Why developers like border-box
sections.text: border-box often makes layout calculations easier to reason about because the width you declare is the width you expect the box to occupy. The browser still has to do the internal math, but you no longer have to mentally add every layer just to know the outside size.

sections.text: Inspect the Box in DevTools
You have already learned to use Elements to inspect styles. The browser also provides a visual box-model view that lets you see content, padding, border, and margin around a selected element.
Use that view when your mental math and the screen disagree. Instead of guessing whether the extra space is padding or margin, inspect it.
The box model is one of the best places to use DevTools as a reality check. Your CSS file tells you what you wrote. The box-model visualization shows you how the browser interpreted it.

sections.label: Identify content, padding, border, and margin; calculate a basic content-box width; explain how border-box changes the calculation; and diagnose whether a spacing problem belongs inside or outside the element's border.
sections.hint: Inside the border → padding. Outside the border → margin. Width behavior depends on box-sizing.

sections.text: Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'Explain the CSS box model.' A strong beginner answer is: 'Every element is laid out as a box with content, padding, border, and margin. Padding creates space inside the border, margin creates space outside it, and the box-sizing property affects how declared width and height relate to those layers.'

A likely follow-up is: 'What is the difference between content-box and border-box?' With content-box, the declared width applies to the content area and padding and border add to the outside size. With border-box, the declared width includes content, padding, and border.
Reflect

Look at a card component you have built before. If the text feels cramped inside it, which box-model layer should you investigate? If two cards are too close together, which layer should you investigate?
Once you can look at a spacing problem and immediately ask 'inside or outside the border?', a lot of CSS layout confusion starts becoming ordinary arithmetic.
What You Should Take Away

The CSS box model describes every element as content, padding, border, and margin. Padding creates space inside the border; margin creates space outside it. With content-box sizing, padding and border add to a declared width or height. With border-box, they fit inside the declared size. The next lesson builds on this by applying the box model to real layout relationships.

summary: The CSS box model describes every element as content, padding, border, and margin. Padding creates internal space, margin creates external space, and border sits between them. With content-box, declared width and height apply to the content area; with border-box, padding and border are included inside the declared size. title: Spacing, Sizing, and Layout
description: Turn the box model into practical layout skills by controlling width, height, spacing, and gaps while learning to distinguish element size from the space around it.
mastery: The learner can control a component's size and spacing with appropriate CSS properties, distinguish margin from padding and gap, explain why fixed dimensions can create layout problems, and reproduce a simple card layout with predictable spacing.
learningObjectives: Use width and height appropriately for simple UI components.
Distinguish padding, margin, and gap when solving spacing problems.
Explain why fixed dimensions can create problems when content or available space changes.
Use min-width, max-width, min-height, and max-height at a basic level to create safer sizing constraints.
Build a simple repeated component layout with consistent internal and external spacing.

sections.text: The Box Model Was the Math. Now We Use It.

You now know that every element has content, padding, border, and margin. That explains where the space comes from. This lesson is about using that knowledge to build layouts that do not immediately collapse the moment someone puts real content inside them.

Real interfaces need predictable sizing and spacing. Cards need breathing room, buttons need usable dimensions, sections need separation, and containers need to adapt when the available space changes.

sections.title: The practical mental model
sections.text: Use padding for space inside a component, margin for space outside a component, and gap for consistent space between items in a layout container. Use width and height to control size, but avoid pretending every screen and every piece of content is exactly the same size.
Width and Height
The width and height properties let you control the size of an element's box. They are useful, but fixed dimensions can become dangerous when the content is dynamic or the available space changes.

sections.title: A fixed-size card

sections.text: This can look perfectly fine with a short title and two lines of text. Add a much longer title or larger text, and the fixed height may no longer be enough.

sections.title: The fixed-height trap
sections.text: A fixed height is not automatically wrong. It is wrong when the content is expected to grow but the box refuses to make room. If your paragraph gets cut off because the card was declared 140px tall, the CSS did exactly what you asked. It was just a terrible request.
Let Content Breathe
For many content-driven components, it is better to control horizontal width while allowing height to grow naturally with the content.

sections.title: A safer content card

sections.text: The card has a predictable width but no forced height. If the paragraph becomes longer, the card can become taller.
min-width and max-width
Minimum and maximum constraints can make components more flexible than a single hard width.

sections.title: Use a range instead of one rigid width

sections.text: Here, the element can use the available width up to a maximum of 720px. This is often more useful for content containers than saying 'this must always be exactly 720px.'
A max-width often says something more useful than a fixed width: 'You may grow, but please stop before becoming a ridiculously long sentence across the entire monitor.'
Padding vs Margin vs Gap
You already know padding and margin from the box model. There is another spacing tool you will use constantly in layouts: gap.

sections.title: Three different jobs

sections.text: Padding creates space inside the card. Margin creates space outside an individual card. Gap creates consistent space between children in a layout container.
Use the Spacing Tool That Matches the Problem

sections.title: Choose the right layer
sections.code:
Content feels cramped inside a card
→ padding

Two separate components need space between them
→ margin or gap

Items inside a layout container need consistent separation
→ gap

The container itself is too wide
→ width / max-width

Content is being squeezed by a forced size
→ reconsider fixed height/width or use min/max constraints

Open your browser's Elements panel and inspect one of your cards. Use the box-model visualization to identify its content size, padding, border, and margin. Then inspect the parent container and identify the available width.

sections.label: Use width, max-width, padding, margin, and gap appropriately to build a simple repeated layout. Explain why fixed heights can be fragile and distinguish the different jobs of padding, margin, and gap.
sections.hint: Inside the component → padding. Between layout items → gap. Outside an individual element → margin. Container sizing → width/max-width.

sections.text: Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'What's the difference between padding, margin, and gap?' A strong answer is: 'Padding creates space inside an element's border, margin creates space outside the element, and gap creates space between items in a layout container such as a flex or grid container.'

A likely follow-up is: 'Why can fixed heights be dangerous?' Because content can vary. If the content needs more room than the fixed height provides, it may overflow, become cramped, or otherwise create a poor layout.
Reflect

Take a card or panel you have built and identify four things: its maximum useful width, its internal padding, its spacing from neighboring components, and whether its height should be fixed or allowed to grow.
Good CSS sizing is often less about forcing a component into one exact shape and more about giving it sensible boundaries. Let the content breathe. Let the layout breathe. Everyone has a better day.
What You Should Take Away

Sizing and spacing should reflect the job of each layer. Use width and max-width to control container size, padding for internal breathing room, margin for external separation, and gap for consistent spacing between layout items. Avoid unnecessary fixed heights when content can vary, and use minimum and maximum constraints when they better express the intended limits.

exercises.title: Fix the Spacing
exercises.brief: Diagnose a cramped card layout and use padding, gap, and max-width to create consistent spacing and a sensible content width.

exercises.title: Use Size Constraints
exercises.brief: Experiment with width, max-width, and min-height as the available space and content change. Explain why constraints are sometimes safer than fixed dimensions.

exercises.title: Build a Reusable Card Row

quiz.question: Which property is most directly responsible for space between the content inside a card and the card's border?
options: margin
padding
gap
max-width
quiz.explanation: Padding creates space between an element's content and its border.

quiz.question: Which property is designed to create consistent space between children of a layout container?
options: gap
padding
width
border
quiz.explanation: gap is designed to control spacing between items in layout contexts such as flex and grid.

quiz.question: Why can a fixed height be fragile for a text-heavy card?
options: Because fixed heights automatically remove padding.
Because the content may grow beyond the available height.
Because browsers cannot render fixed-height elements.
Because fixed heights only work with images.
quiz.explanation: Text and other content can vary. A fixed height may become too small and cause overflow or cramped content.

quiz.question: What is a common benefit of max-width on a content container?
options: It forces the container to remain exactly the same width everywhere.
It lets the container use available space while preventing it from becoming excessively wide.
It prevents the container from shrinking.
It automatically creates a flex layout.
quiz.explanation: max-width sets an upper limit while allowing the element to be smaller when the available space is limited.

summary: Practical CSS layout depends on choosing the right property for the right problem. Use width and max-width for sizing, padding for internal space, margin for external separation, and gap for spacing between layout items. Fixed dimensions can be fragile when content varies, so minimum and maximum constraints often create more resilient components.

title: Typography and Text
description: Learn how CSS controls typography, including font family, size, weight, line height, alignment, and readable text width.
mastery: The learner can style text using appropriate font properties, explain why line-height and readable line length matter, distinguish font size from font weight, and build a simple text block with a clear and readable typographic hierarchy.
learningObjectives: Use font-family, font-size, font-weight, and line-height to control text presentation.
Explain the difference between font size and font weight.
Use text-align and related text properties appropriately.
Explain why line-height and readable line length affect usability.
Create a simple typographic hierarchy for headings, body text, and supporting text.

sections.text: Make the Words Comfortable to Read
A page can have perfect HTML and technically correct CSS while still being unpleasant to read. Typography is what turns a wall of technically valid text into something a human can actually survive.
CSS gives you control over the appearance and rhythm of text. The most important beginner properties are font-family, font-size, font-weight, line-height, and text-align.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: Typography is not just making text look fancy. You are controlling hierarchy, readability, rhythm, and emphasis so the reader knows what matters and can comfortably read the content.
font-family
font-family controls which typeface the browser should use. A font stack can provide fallbacks in case the first choice is unavailable.

sections.title: A font stack

sections.text: The browser tries Arial first. If it is unavailable, it can try Helvetica, and then a generic sans-serif font.
font-size
font-size controls how large the text is.

sections.title: Different text sizes

sections.text: The exact values are design decisions. The important distinction is simple: font-size changes size, not how bold the text is.
font-weight
font-weight controls how heavy or light the type appears.

sections.title: Weight creates hierarchy

sections.text: A common beginner mistake is thinking font-weight and font-size are basically the same thing because both can make text feel more prominent. They solve different problems.

sections.title: Common mistake
sections.text: If the heading looks too weak, changing font-size is not the only answer. You may actually want a stronger font-weight. If the text is too large, making it thinner will not magically make the typography comfortable.
line-height
line-height controls the vertical space between lines of text. It has a major effect on readability, especially for paragraphs.

sections.title: Give body text room

sections.text: Text with a very tight line-height can feel crowded. Text with excessive line-height can feel disconnected. Good typography gives the reader enough breathing room without turning each sentence into its own postal address.
text-align
text-align controls horizontal alignment of inline content inside its containing block.

sections.title: Common alignment

sections.text: Left-aligned body text is usually easier to read for long passages in left-to-right languages, while centered alignment can be useful for short headings or hero content.
Readable Line Length
Typography is affected by the width of the text block as well as the font itself. Very long lines force the eyes to travel far across the page and can make reading harder.

sections.title: Limit the reading width

sections.text: The ch unit relates to the width of the '0' glyph of the current font. Using a character-based max-width can provide a useful starting point for readable text blocks.
Build a Typographic Hierarchy
A page should not make every piece of text equally loud. A useful hierarchy makes the heading prominent, supporting text quieter, and body copy comfortable to read.

sections.title: A simple hierarchy

sections.text: The values are not sacred. What matters is that the roles are distinct and the hierarchy is intentional.

sections.text: A Quick Reminder About Web Fonts

The browser can use fonts available on the system or fonts provided by the application. In production interfaces, font loading deserves its own performance considerations, but you do not need to solve those today.

sections.title: Boundary for beginners
sections.text: Do not turn every typography lesson into a font-loading project. First learn how typography behaves. Later, when performance and design systems arrive, you will learn how teams manage fonts deliberately.
Practice Drill 3: Diagnose the Ugly Text
The designer says, 'The text technically fits, but the page feels exhausting to read.' Use the CSS below to identify the most likely causes.

sections.title: The suspicious typography

sections.text: Several things are working against readability: the body copy is tightly spaced, the text block is extremely wide, and the heading has almost no typographic distinction from the body text.

sections.label: Style a text block with a clear typographic hierarchy, explain the roles of font-family, font-size, font-weight, line-height, and text alignment, and diagnose a basic readability problem using those properties.
sections.hint: Ask which property controls size, emphasis, vertical rhythm, horizontal alignment, and reading width.

sections.text: Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'What CSS properties would you look at if text was difficult to read?' A strong beginner answer is: 'I would look at font family, font size, font weight, line height, and the width of the text container. I would also check alignment and whether the hierarchy makes sense between headings and body text.'
A likely follow-up is: 'What is the difference between font-size and line-height?' font-size controls the size of the glyphs. line-height controls the vertical space allocated to each line.
Reflect
Look at a page you find easy to read. Identify one thing that creates hierarchy, one thing that creates comfortable line spacing, and one thing that keeps the text from becoming too wide.
Good typography should feel almost invisible. When readers are thinking about your font choices instead of the content, your typography may be trying a little too hard.
What You Should Take Away

CSS typography controls how text looks and reads. font-family chooses the typeface, font-size controls size, font-weight controls visual weight, line-height controls vertical rhythm, and text-align controls horizontal alignment. Readable typography also depends on sensible text width and clear hierarchy.

quiz.question: Which CSS property controls the size of text?
options: font-weight
font-size
line-height
font-family
quiz.explanation: font-size controls how large the text appears.

quiz.question: What does line-height primarily control?
options: The typeface being used.
The horizontal alignment of the paragraph.
The vertical space allocated to each line of text.
The thickness of the border around the text.
quiz.explanation: line-height controls the vertical rhythm and spacing between lines.

quiz.question: Why can an extremely wide text container hurt readability?
options: Because the browser stops rendering text after 500px.
Because the reader's eyes have to travel farther across each line.
Because wide containers automatically change font-weight.
Because CSS cannot center wide containers.
quiz.explanation: Very long lines can make it harder for the eyes to track from the end of one line back to the beginning of the next.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes font-weight?
options: It controls how heavy or light the type appears.
It controls the width of the text container.
It controls the vertical distance between lines.
It controls the font family.
quiz.explanation: font-weight controls the visual weight of text, such as normal or bold.

summary: Typography is a core part of readable interface design. Use font-family for the typeface, font-size for text size, font-weight for emphasis, line-height for vertical rhythm, and text-align for alignment. Keep text blocks reasonably narrow and create a clear hierarchy so readers can understand content without fighting the typography.

title: Colors, Backgrounds, and Borders
description: Learn how CSS controls foreground and background colors, borders, rounded corners, and simple visual surfaces while keeping contrast and content accessibility in mind.
mastery: The learner can apply common color values, create backgrounds and borders, use border-radius for rounded corners, combine these properties into a simple component style, and identify a basic contrast or background-image accessibility problem.
learningObjectives: Apply CSS foreground and background colors using common color formats.
Use border width, style, color, and shorthand declarations.
Use border-radius to create rounded corners.
Apply a background image with a sensible fallback color and basic positioning or sizing.
Explain why decorative background images should not contain essential information.
Recognize when a color combination may create a basic readability or contrast problem.

sections.text: Now We Make the Boxes Look Like Something
You have learned how CSS selects elements, resolves conflicts, controls spacing and size, and shapes readable typography. Now we can start giving those boxes some visual personality.

Colors, backgrounds, and borders are simple properties individually, but together they are what turn a collection of boxes into an interface. They are also very capable of turning an interface into a crime scene if you use all three without a plan.

sections.title: A useful mental model
sections.text: color controls foreground text and other foreground content, background-color fills the element's background, and border draws a line around the box. border-radius changes the shape of the box's corners.
Foreground Color
The color property controls the foreground color of an element, most commonly its text.

sections.title: Named, hexadecimal, and RGB colors

sections.text: CSS supports several color formats. Named colors are easy to read, hexadecimal values are common in design systems, and RGB or other color functions give you more explicit control.
Background Color
background-color fills the background of an element.

sections.title: A simple surface

sections.text: The background and foreground should work together. A visually interesting color is not automatically a useful color if the text sitting on top of it becomes difficult to read.

sections.title: Contrast matters
sections.text: Do not choose text and background colors independently. The user has to read the result. If the foreground and background are too similar, your beautiful design becomes a treasure hunt for the words.
Common Color Formats

sections.title: Same idea, different syntax

sections.text: You do not need to memorize every color function today. Learn to recognize common formats and understand that they all represent color values.
Borders
A border is drawn around the element's box. The border shorthand commonly combines width, style, and color.

sections.title: The border shorthand

sections.text: Here, 1px is the border width, solid is the line style, and #d1d5db is the color.

sections.title: The longhand version

sections.text: The shorthand is convenient when you want the same style on all four sides. You can also target individual sides when the design calls for it.
border-radius
border-radius rounds the corners of an element's border box.

sections.title: Rounded corners

sections.text: A larger radius creates more rounded corners. A 50% radius can create a circle or pill-like shape when the element's dimensions allow it.
Background Images
CSS can also place an image in an element's background using background-image.

sections.title: A background image

sections.text: A background color is useful as a fallback when the image does not load or when transparent areas allow the color to show through. You can then control the background image with properties such as background-size, background-position, and background-repeat.

sections.title: A practical hero background

sections.text: cover tells the browser to scale the image so the background area is covered. Some image may be cropped as a result.

sections.title: Accessibility boundary
sections.text: A decorative background image is not a replacement for meaningful HTML content. Screen readers do not treat CSS background images as page content. If the image contains information the user needs, it should be represented in the HTML rather than hidden inside a background.

sections.text: A Small Design System Is Already Emerging
Once you style several components, you will notice repeated choices: the same border color, the same radius, the same foreground colors, the same background surfaces.

sections.title: Repeated visual decisions

sections.text: You are starting to see why design systems and reusable tokens become valuable. You do not need to build a design system yet, but notice how repeated visual decisions create consistency.

sections.label: Apply readable foreground and background colors, create a border with appropriate width/style/color, use border-radius, style a background image with a fallback color and sensible sizing, and identify a basic contrast or background-image accessibility problem.
sections.hint: Think appearance and usability together. A color is not successful if the user cannot comfortably read the content placed on it.

sections.text: Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'How would you style a simple card?' A strong beginner answer is: 'I would choose a readable foreground and background color, add a border if needed for separation, use border-radius for the desired corner shape, and use padding for internal spacing. I would also verify that the text remains readable against the background.'

A likely follow-up is: 'When would you use a CSS background image instead of an img element?' A background image is often appropriate for decorative visuals that are part of presentation rather than content. Meaningful images should generally remain represented as HTML content with appropriate alternative text.
Reflect

Choose a familiar interface component such as a card, alert, or button. Identify its foreground color, background color, border treatment, and corner treatment. Then ask which of those choices are about decoration and which affect readability or meaning.
Good visual styling is not about adding more effects. A clean border, a useful background, and readable text often beat seventeen gradients fighting for attention.
What You Should Take Away

CSS color and background properties control visual surfaces, while borders and border-radius shape and separate those surfaces. Background images can provide decorative visual treatment, with a background color serving as a useful fallback. Good styling also considers readability and accessibility: important information belongs in HTML, and foreground and background colors must work together.

summary: CSS colors, backgrounds, borders, and rounded corners provide the visual surface of an interface. Use color and background-color together with readable contrast, border shorthand to define width/style/color, and border-radius to shape corners. Background images can enhance decorative surfaces, but important content should remain in HTML rather than existing only as a background image.

title: Display and Normal Flow
description: Understand how block and inline elements participate in normal document flow, how the display property changes that behavior, and why layout bugs often begin with misunderstanding the flow.
mastery: The learner can explain normal flow, distinguish block and inline behavior, use display: block, inline, and inline-block appropriately, diagnose a basic flow-related layout problem, and explain why changing an element's display value changes how it participates in layout.
learningObjectives: Explain normal flow as the browser's default way of laying out content.
Distinguish the basic behavior of block and inline elements.
Use display: block, inline, and inline-block for simple layout changes.
Explain why changing display affects how an element participates in normal flow.
Diagnose a simple layout issue caused by misunderstanding block and inline behavior.

sections.text: Before Flexbox, the Browser Already Has a Layout System
You can write HTML and CSS without thinking about layout, and the browser will still put things somewhere. That 'somewhere' is called normal flow.

Normal flow is the default way block and inline content is laid out before you deliberately change the layout behavior. Understanding it matters because every modern layout system starts from the question: what is this element doing in the normal flow right now?

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: Normal flow is the browser saying, 'Fine, I'll arrange this in the ordinary document order.' Block content stacks through the page. Inline content sits within a line of text. CSS layout systems let you change that behavior when the default is not enough.
Block Elements

A block-level box participates in normal flow as a block. In a typical left-to-right document, block boxes appear one after another vertically and usually take available space in the inline direction.

sections.title: Block elements in normal flow
sections.code:
First block
Second block

Third block

sections.text: The browser lays these elements out one after another. You did not have to tell each one to move to a new line. Their normal display behavior already establishes that relationship.
Inline Elements
Inline boxes participate within a line of text rather than automatically starting on a new line.

sections.title: Inline content
sections.code: Learn frontend engineering with Forge.

sections.text: The strong element sits inside the paragraph's line of text. It does not create a separate block above or below the paragraph.
display Changes the Layout Behavior
The display property controls how an element participates in layout and, depending on the value, how its children are laid out.

sections.title: Three useful beginner values

sections.text: These values are related but not interchangeable. block participates as a block box, inline participates within the surrounding line, and inline-block sits alongside inline content while still behaving as a box that can have dimensions and box-model properties.
display: block
Setting an element to display: block makes it participate as a block-level box in normal flow.

sections.title: Turn spans into blocks

sections.text: This can make otherwise inline elements such as span start on their own line and behave as block boxes.
display: inline
display: inline makes an element participate in an inline formatting context. It sits alongside surrounding inline content when space allows.

sections.title: Inline navigation links

sections.text: Inline elements are useful when the content naturally belongs in the same line. You should not use inline simply because you want an element to 'look smaller.' Its layout role is the important part.
display: inline-block
inline-block is useful when you want an element to sit alongside other inline content while still behaving like a box that can have explicit dimensions and box-model properties.

sections.title: Inline blocks

sections.text: This is one reason inline-block can be useful for small controls, badges, or compact pieces of UI.

sections.title: Common mistake
sections.text: Changing display just to force something into the place you want without understanding why. CSS will happily obey. Then three weeks later you will stare at the stylesheet and wonder why a span became a tiny layout engine.
Normal Flow and Source Order

In normal flow, elements generally appear according to their order in the document. Change the HTML order and, unless another layout mechanism intervenes, the browser changes the visual order accordingly.

sections.title: Source order matters
sections.code:
First

Second

Third

sections.text: The browser starts with the heading, then the first paragraph, then the second paragraph. This predictable default is one of the reasons normal flow is useful.

sections.text: The next layout lesson will introduce the tools designed for this sort of arrangement. For now, the important skill is recognizing that normal flow itself is not broken. It is simply doing its default job.

sections.title: Do not fight the default flow yet
sections.text: If blocks stack vertically and you wanted columns, that does not mean the browser failed. It means you have reached the point where a dedicated layout system is appropriate. The next lessons will introduce those systems properly.
When Content Overflows

A constrained box can receive more content than it has room to display. That creates overflow. This is another reason understanding normal flow matters: the browser has default behavior, and CSS properties such as overflow can change what happens when content no longer fits.

sections.title: A controlled overflow area

sections.text: overflow: auto allows the browser to provide scrolling when the content exceeds the constrained box. This is different from simply hiding the content and hoping nobody notices.

sections.title: Fixed size plus real content can still bite
sections.text: If you constrain an element and then discover content spilling outside it, do not immediately hide the overflow. First ask why the size was constrained and whether the content is expected to grow.

sections.label: Explain normal flow, distinguish block and inline behavior, use block/inline/inline-block appropriately in a simple example, and diagnose a basic layout problem caused by misunderstanding display behavior.
sections.hint: Block content generally stacks in normal flow. Inline content participates within a line. display changes how an element participates in layout.

sections.text: Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'What is normal flow in CSS?' A strong beginner answer is: 'Normal flow is the browser's default layout behavior for elements before other layout or positioning rules change it. Block elements generally stack vertically, while inline elements participate within lines of text.'
A likely follow-up is: 'What is the difference between block, inline, and inline-block?' Explain the layout behavior first rather than reciting memorized definitions.
Reflect

Inspect a page in DevTools and identify one block element and one inline element. Before changing anything, predict what would happen if you changed each one to display: block, inline, and inline-block.
You do not need to defeat normal flow. You need to understand it well enough to know when you should keep it and when you should intentionally switch to another layout model.
What You Should Take Away

Normal flow is the browser's default way of laying out content. Block elements generally stack through the page, while inline elements participate within lines. The display property changes how an element participates in layout, with block, inline, and inline-block providing different behavior. Understanding normal flow is the foundation for the dedicated layout systems you will learn next.

quiz.question: What is normal flow?
options: A random layout mode chosen by the browser.
The browser's default way of laying out content before other layout or positioning rules change it.
A synonym for Flexbox.
A way to remove elements from the document.
quiz.explanation: Normal flow is the default layout behavior for content before CSS layout or positioning rules change how elements participate.

quiz.question: What generally happens to block elements in normal flow?
options: They stack one after another in the block direction.
They always appear side by side.
They are removed from the document.
They behave exactly like inline text.
quiz.explanation: Block boxes generally stack one after another in normal flow.

quiz.question: Why might width: 200px behave unexpectedly on an inline element?
options: Inline elements are always deleted by the browser.
The element's inline layout behavior does not treat width like a normal block box.
CSS width only works on images.
Width is inherited from the parent.
quiz.explanation: An inline element participates in inline layout, so it does not behave like a normal block box with explicit dimensions. Changing its display behavior can be appropriate when a box-like dimension is needed.

quiz.question: When would display: inline-block be useful?
options: When you want an element to participate alongside inline content while still behaving like a box that can have dimensions.
When you want to remove an element from the document.
When you want to disable all padding.
Only when creating a table.
quiz.explanation: inline-block combines inline-level participation with a box that can use dimensions and box-model properties.

summary: Normal flow is the browser's default layout behavior. Block elements generally stack vertically in normal flow, while inline elements participate within lines of text. The display property can change how an element participates, with block, inline, and inline-block providing different layout behavior. Understanding normal flow makes it easier to understand when and why dedicated layout systems are needed.

title: Flexbox Fundamentals
description: Learn how Flexbox arranges elements along a main axis and cross axis, and use it to build practical one-dimensional layouts with predictable alignment and spacing.
mastery: The learner can explain the main and cross axes, create a flex container, use justify-content and align-items correctly for the current flex direction, control spacing with gap, and build a simple responsive row of components without relying on arbitrary margins.
learningObjectives: Explain what Flexbox is designed to solve.
Create a flex container with display: flex.
Distinguish the main axis from the cross axis.
Use flex-direction to change the main axis.
Use justify-content and align-items correctly based on the current axes.
Use gap to create consistent spacing between flex items.
Build a simple one-dimensional responsive component layout with Flexbox.

sections.text: Meet the Layout System You've Been Waiting For

Normal flow is useful. It is also not enough for many interfaces. Eventually you want three cards in a row, a button pushed to the end of a toolbar, navigation items spaced cleanly, or a pair of elements aligned without sacrificing an afternoon to mysterious margins.
Flexbox is a CSS layout model designed for arranging items along one dimension. It gives you direct control over how items are distributed, aligned, wrapped, and spaced inside a container.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: Flexbox gives a parent container a layout job: arrange these children along an axis. The parent controls the arrangement; the children participate in that layout. Think 'container makes the rules, items live with them.'
Turn a Container Into a Flex Container
The starting point is display: flex.

sections.title: Your first flex container

sections.text: The children of .toolbar now participate in flex layout. By default, flex-direction is row, so the main axis runs horizontally.

sections.title: The children

sections.text: Instead of treating the buttons as unrelated boxes and manually pushing them around, the parent now controls how they are arranged.
The Two Axes
Flexbox has two axes: the main axis and the cross axis. The direction of the main axis is controlled by flex-direction.

sections.title: Row direction

sections.text: With row, the main axis runs horizontally and the cross axis runs vertically in the common left-to-right writing mode.

sections.title: Column direction

sections.text: With column, the main axis becomes vertical and the cross axis becomes horizontal.

sections.title: The biggest beginner trap
sections.text: justify-content does not simply mean 'horizontal alignment' and align-items does not simply mean 'vertical alignment.' Their direction depends on the current flex axes. Change flex-direction and the meaning changes with it.
justify-content Controls the Main Axis
justify-content controls how flex items are distributed along the main axis.

sections.title: Main-axis distribution

sections.text: With space-between, the first item sits at one end, the last item sits at the other, and the remaining space is distributed between the items.

sections.title: Common values

sections.text: align-items Controls the Cross Axis
align-items controls how flex items are aligned along the cross axis.

sections.title: Cross-axis alignment

sections.text: For a row flex container, this commonly means vertical alignment. For a column flex container, the cross axis changes, so the effect is different.
gap Handles the Space Between Items
The gap property creates consistent spacing between flex items.

sections.title: Clean spacing

sections.text: This is often cleaner than putting a different margin on every child. The container owns the relationship between its items.

sections.title: A useful layout habit
sections.text: When the problem is 'these siblings need consistent space between them,' start by asking whether gap belongs on the parent instead of inventing six different margins on six children.
Interactive Practice: Flexbox Axis Explorer
Change the direction, main-axis distribution, and cross-axis alignment. Before each change, predict which direction the controls affect.

sections.title: Flexbox Axis Explorer
sections.instructions: Toggle row/column, justify-content, and align-items. Before applying each value, identify the main axis and cross axis. Then explain why the result changed.

sections.text: When Flexbox Should Not Be Your Hammer
Flexbox is excellent for one-dimensional relationships: a row of controls, a vertical stack, a navigation bar, or a group of cards flowing along one primary axis.

When you need strong simultaneous control over rows and columns, another layout system is often more appropriate. You will meet that system later. For now, learn to recognize the difference between 'I need a row or column' and 'I need a full two-dimensional layout.'

sections.title: Avoid the divination ritual
sections.text: If you keep adding justify-content, align-items, margins, widths, and random transforms until the layout accidentally looks right, stop. Go back to the axes. Flexbox becomes much easier once you know which axis you are controlling.
A Note About flex-wrap
By default, flex items stay on one line. Setting flex-wrap: wrap allows them to move onto additional lines when there is not enough space.

sections.title: Allow the row to wrap

sections.text: Wrapping can make a simple flex layout more adaptable to different available widths. It is not the same thing as building a complete responsive layout system, but it is a useful first step.

sections.label: Build a Flexbox layout using display:flex, identify the main and cross axes, use justify-content and align-items according to those axes, use gap for spacing, and create a simple wrapping card layout.
sections.hint: Start with the direction. Once you know the main axis, justify-content makes sense. Once you know the cross axis, align-items makes sense.

sections.text: Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'How does Flexbox work?' A strong beginner answer is: 'Flexbox is a one-dimensional layout system. A parent becomes a flex container, its children become flex items, and the layout is controlled along a main axis and cross axis. flex-direction chooses the main axis, justify-content distributes items on the main axis, align-items controls cross-axis alignment, and gap controls spacing between items.'

A likely follow-up is: 'Why does justify-content sometimes seem to align things vertically and sometimes horizontally?' Because it controls the main axis, and flex-direction determines which direction that axis runs.
Reflect

Take one layout you have struggled with before and identify its main relationship. Is it fundamentally a row, a column, or something more two-dimensional? If it is a row or column, sketch the main and cross axes before touching the CSS.
Flexbox stops feeling like a bag of alignment tricks once you start thinking in axes. The browser is not asking you to memorize where things go. It is asking you which direction the layout flows.
What You Should Take Away

Flexbox is a one-dimensional layout system for arranging items along a main axis and cross axis. display:flex creates the flex container, flex-direction chooses the main axis, justify-content controls distribution along the main axis, align-items controls cross-axis alignment, and gap creates consistent spacing between items. flex-wrap lets items move onto additional lines when needed.
