quiz.question: What does display: flex do?
options: Turns the element into a flex container whose children participate in flex layout.
Makes every child absolutely positioned.
Creates a CSS Grid automatically.
Removes the element from normal flow.
quiz.explanation: display:flex establishes a flex container and causes its direct children to become flex items.

quiz.question: What does justify-content control?
options: The main-axis distribution of flex items.
The font weight of flex items.
The border radius of flex items.
Only the vertical position of items.
quiz.explanation: justify-content controls how flex items are distributed along the main axis.

quiz.question: What determines the direction of the flex main axis?
options: align-items
justify-content
flex-direction
gap
quiz.explanation: flex-direction determines whether the main axis is row-like or column-like.

quiz.question: Why can justify-content appear to control horizontal alignment in one example and vertical alignment in another?
options: Because justify-content is random.
Because it controls the main axis, which changes when flex-direction changes.
Because align-items secretly overrides it.
Because gap changes the axis.
quiz.explanation: justify-content works along the main axis. Changing flex-direction changes the direction of that axis.

summary: Flexbox provides one-dimensional layout control. A flex container establishes a main axis and cross axis; flex-direction determines the main axis, justify-content controls distribution along it, align-items controls cross-axis alignment, and gap controls spacing between items. flex-wrap allows items to continue onto additional lines when space is limited.

title: CSS Grid Fundamentals
description: Learn CSS Grid as a two-dimensional layout system, define rows and columns with tracks, control spacing with gaps, and place content into a predictable grid.
mastery: The learner can explain when CSS Grid is a better fit than Flexbox, create a grid container, define columns and rows, use the fr unit and gap, and build a simple two-dimensional page or card layout with predictable placement.
learningObjectives: Explain CSS Grid as a two-dimensional layout system.
Create a grid container with display: grid.
Define columns and rows using grid-template-columns and grid-template-rows.
Use the fr unit to distribute available space.
Use gap to control row and column spacing.
Place grid items using basic grid-column and grid-row values.
Distinguish a two-dimensional grid problem from a one-dimensional Flexbox problem.

sections.text: When One Axis Isn't Enough
Flexbox is excellent when your layout mainly has one direction to worry about: a row of actions, a vertical stack, or a group of items flowing along one axis.

But sometimes your design is fundamentally about rows and columns at the same time. Dashboard cards, page regions, galleries, and structured content layouts often fit that problem better. That is where CSS Grid comes in.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: Flexbox is a one-dimensional arrangement tool. Grid is a two-dimensional layout system. Think rows and columns first. If you can point at both at once, Grid is probably worth investigating.
Create a Grid Container
Like Flexbox, Grid starts by changing the display value on the parent.

sections.title: Your first grid

sections.text: Declaring display: grid creates a grid container and makes its direct children grid items. By itself, the grid starts with a simple one-column structure, so you need to define tracks before it becomes especially useful.
Columns Are Grid Tracks
You define columns with grid-template-columns. Each value describes a column track.

sections.title: Three equal columns

sections.text: This creates three flexible columns that share the available space.
The fr Unit
The fr unit represents a fraction of the available space in the grid container. It is especially useful when you want columns to share remaining space without calculating pixel values yourself.

sections.title: Flexible columns

sections.text: The second column gets twice as much of the available flexible space as the first.
Rows Are Tracks Too
You can define rows with grid-template-rows.

sections.title: Explicit rows and columns

sections.text: This lets you describe both dimensions of the layout rather than arranging everything along one axis.
Use gap for Grid Spacing

sections.title: Row and column gaps

sections.text: gap creates consistent space between the grid items in both directions. You can also use row-gap and column-gap separately when the spacing needs to differ.
repeat() Saves Repetition
When several tracks have the same definition, repeat() makes the intent easier to read.

sections.title: Three equal columns

sections.text: This means the same thing as 1fr 1fr 1fr, but it becomes more useful as layouts grow.
Grid Items Can Be Placed by Lines
Grid creates numbered lines around its tracks. You can use those lines to place an item across specific columns or rows.

sections.title: Span two columns

sections.text: The item begins at column line 1 and ends at column line 3, so it spans two column tracks.

sections.title: Span two rows

sections.text: The same idea works vertically with grid-row.
Grid lines are easier to understand if you imagine the empty lines around the cells, not the cells themselves. The numbers label boundaries. You place an item between those boundaries.
Interactive Practice: Build a Grid
Start with a stack of cards and turn it into a three-column grid. Change the number of columns and spacing before you attempt more precise placement.

sections.text: Practice Drill 3: Grid or Flexbox?
The goal is not to declare one layout system the winner of the internet. Choose the system that best matches the relationship you are trying to model.

sections.title: Choose the layout model
sections.code:
A. A toolbar with buttons arranged in one row.
→ Flexbox is a natural fit.

B. A gallery with three columns and multiple rows.
→ Grid is a natural fit.

C. A page with a sidebar and main content aligned across rows and columns.
→ Grid is a strong candidate.

D. A vertical stack of buttons that needs consistent spacing.
→ Flexbox is a natural fit.

sections.text: These are not absolute laws. Both systems can solve many problems. The useful distinction is whether the layout's main concern is one-dimensional distribution or two-dimensional placement.
A Real Page Skeleton
Grid becomes especially useful when several major page regions need to line up across both dimensions.

sections.title: Semantic page regions
sections.code:
Header
Sidebar
Main content
Footer

sections.title: A basic page grid

sections.text: The page now has a sidebar column and a flexible main column, while the header and footer span the full grid width.
The -1 line means the last grid line. It is a useful way to say 'span all the way to the other side' without counting how many columns exist.
Use DevTools to See the Grid

Modern browser DevTools can visualize grid lines and tracks directly on the page. When a grid feels mysterious, turn on the grid overlay instead of staring at the CSS and hoping the coordinates reveal themselves.
The overlay can make the relationship between tracks, lines, gaps, and placed items much easier to understand.

sections.label: Create a CSS Grid, define columns with tracks, use fr and gap, place an item across grid lines, and explain why a two-dimensional layout may be a better fit for Grid than Flexbox.
sections.hint: Think rows + columns. Start with display:grid, define the tracks, then place or let the browser auto-place the items.

sections.text: Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'When would you choose Grid instead of Flexbox?' A strong beginner answer is: 'I would consider Grid when the layout is fundamentally two-dimensional and I need to control rows and columns together. Flexbox is often a better fit when the relationship is mainly one-dimensional, such as a row or column of controls.'
A likely follow-up is: 'What is 1fr?' It represents one fraction of the available flexible space in the grid container.
Reflect

Look at one interface you have built or used. Draw its major regions as rows and columns. Then ask whether the relationships are naturally two-dimensional. If they are, Grid may describe the design more directly than a pile of nested flex containers.

Good layout code describes relationships. If your CSS is full of increasingly desperate margins because you are forcing a row-and-column design into a one-dimensional system, Grid may be trying to save you from yourself.
What You Should Take Away

CSS Grid is a two-dimensional layout system based on rows and columns. display:grid creates the container, grid-template-columns and grid-template-rows define tracks, fr distributes flexible space, gap creates gutters, and grid-column or grid-row can place items across grid lines. Grid is especially useful when the design relationship is inherently two-dimensional.

quiz.question: What kind of layout problem is CSS Grid primarily designed to solve?
options: Two-dimensional layouts involving rows and columns.
Only text styling.
Only vertical stacks of content.
Only image cropping.
quiz.explanation: Grid is a two-dimensional layout system designed to organize content across rows and columns.

quiz.question: What does the fr unit represent in a grid?
options: A fixed pixel size.
A fraction of the available flexible space.
The number of rows.
The width of the browser window.
quiz.explanation: fr represents a fraction of the available flexible space in the grid container.

quiz.question: What does grid-column: 1 / 3 mean in a three-column grid?
options: The item is hidden from columns 1 and 3.
The item starts at column line 1 and ends at column line 3, spanning two tracks.
The item is placed only in column 3.
The item creates three new columns.
quiz.explanation: Grid placement uses grid lines as boundaries. Starting at line 1 and ending at line 3 spans the two tracks between those lines.

quiz.question: Which layout is generally a natural fit for Grid?
options: A toolbar where items mainly need distribution along one row.
A two-dimensional dashboard with aligned rows and columns.
A single paragraph of text.
A simple inline link inside a sentence.
quiz.explanation: A dashboard with meaningful row-and-column relationships is a classic two-dimensional Grid problem.

summary: CSS Grid provides two-dimensional layout control across rows and columns. Define tracks with grid-template-columns and grid-template-rows, use fr for flexible space and gap for gutters, and place items with grid-column or grid-row when explicit positioning is useful. Grid is a strong fit when the layout relationship is inherently two-dimensional, while Flexbox remains a natural choice for many one-dimensional relationships.

title: Responsive Design and Media Queries
description: Learn how responsive layouts adapt to different viewport sizes using flexible sizing, media queries, and mobile-first CSS.
mastery: The learner can explain responsive design, build a layout that adapts to different viewport widths, write a basic media query, distinguish mobile-first styles from larger-screen enhancements, and diagnose a simple responsive layout problem.
learningObjectives: Explain what responsive web design means.
Distinguish fixed dimensions from flexible layout behavior.
Write a basic CSS media query using min-width or max-width.
Explain the mobile-first approach.
Adapt a simple Flexbox or Grid layout for different viewport sizes.
Test a responsive layout at multiple viewport widths and identify a basic breakpoint problem.

sections.text: The Web Does Not Know What Size Your Screen Is Going to Be

You built layouts with Flexbox and Grid. Great. Now comes the problem real interfaces have to solve: the user might be on a phone, a tablet, a laptop, a giant monitor, or a browser window that has been resized to approximately the width of a slice of toast.
Responsive design means building interfaces that adapt to different available spaces instead of assuming one screen size.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: Responsive CSS is not 'make the desktop version, then squeeze it until it fits on a phone.' It is about building rules that allow the interface to adapt as the available space changes.
Flexible Layout Comes First

Before writing a media query, ask whether your layout can already adapt through normal CSS. Flexbox, Grid, percentage widths, max-width, and flexible units can often solve part of the problem without any breakpoint at all.

sections.title: A flexible content container

sections.text: This container can shrink on a small screen while staying limited on a wider one. That is responsive behavior without a single media query.
Sometimes the Layout Needs a Breakpoint

Sometimes the design genuinely needs to change when enough space becomes available. A navigation may need to stack, a sidebar may need to disappear or move, or a multi-column card layout may need fewer columns.
Media queries let CSS apply different rules when environmental conditions match a condition such as viewport width.

sections.title: A basic media query

sections.text: The base rule uses one column. When the viewport is at least 768px wide, the media query changes the layout to three columns.
Mobile-First CSS
The example above is mobile-first: the base styles describe the smaller layout, and larger-screen changes are added with min-width media queries.

sections.title: Mobile first

sections.text: The mobile layout is the default. When more space becomes available, the layout progressively enhances.
Mobile-first does not mean 'phones are more important than desktops.' It means you start with the smallest reasonable layout and add complexity when the available space justifies it.
Breakpoints Should Come From the Layout
A breakpoint is useful when the current layout stops working well, not because a chart somewhere told you that every website must have exactly three sacred widths.

sections.title: A better breakpoint question
sections.code:
Bad question:
"What breakpoint does every developer use?"

Better question:
"At what width does this layout stop being comfortable?"

sections.text: That mindset helps you choose breakpoints based on your content and layout rather than blindly copying device categories.
Interactive Practice: Watch the Layout Adapt
Resize the available panel and observe when the layout should change. Your job is to predict the breakpoint before toggling it.

sections.title: Responsive Layout Explorer
sections.instructions: Toggle the available viewport width. Observe the one-column layout first, then the wider layout. Identify which rule is the default and which rule is activated by the media query.

The card grid works on a large screen but becomes cramped on a narrow screen. Start with one column, then introduce more columns when enough width exists.

A horizontal navigation works well when there is room but becomes cramped on a narrow screen. Build a mobile-first version that stacks the links, then changes to a horizontal layout when the viewport is wider.

sections.text: Practice Drill 3: Diagnose a Bad Breakpoint
This layout jumps to three columns at 320px. Technically it responds. Practically, it is a disaster.

sections.title: A questionable breakpoint

sections.text: The browser is following the rule. The problem is the rule itself. Three columns may not provide enough space for the content. The breakpoint should be based on when the cards can actually work comfortably.

sections.title: Responsive does not mean 'technically shrinks'
sections.text: A layout can respond to the viewport and still be terrible. Responsive design is about usability across available space, not winning a checkbox that says @media appears somewhere in the stylesheet.
Viewport Testing Is Part of the Work

When you build responsive CSS, test at widths that are actually relevant to the content. Resize the browser, use the responsive device mode in DevTools, and watch for wrapping, overflow, cramped controls, and awkward empty space.

sections.title: A simple responsive test
sections.code:
Small width:
Does content fit without horizontal scrolling?

Medium width:
Does the layout use the extra space sensibly?

Large width:
Does the content become excessively wide?

Between breakpoints:
Does the transition still make sense?

sections.text: Responsive Images and Content
The same principle applies beyond grid columns. Images should not overflow their containers, and long text should not force a component wider than the viewport.

sections.title: A common image safeguard

sections.text: max-width: 100% allows an image to shrink within its containing block instead of overflowing it.
When Media Queries Are Not Needed
Not every responsive problem requires a media query. If a flexible layout already adapts correctly, do not add a breakpoint just because you can.

sections.title: Flexible without a breakpoint

sections.text: Sometimes the best responsive CSS is the CSS that does not need to know which device the user has.
Ask the layout to adapt naturally before writing a rule that depends on a specific width. Flexible CSS ages better than a pile of device-specific exceptions.

sections.label: Build a mobile-first responsive layout, write a basic min-width media query, choose breakpoints based on content rather than device names, and test the layout at multiple viewport widths.
sections.hint: Start with the smallest reasonable layout. Add complexity only when the available space justifies it.

sections.text: Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'What is responsive design?' A strong beginner answer is: 'Responsive design means building an interface that adapts to different available viewport sizes and conditions. I would start with flexible layout rules and use media queries when the layout genuinely needs to change at a particular range.'

A likely follow-up is: 'What is mobile-first CSS?' It means the base stylesheet describes the smaller layout, and larger-screen enhancements are added progressively, often with min-width media queries.
Reflect

Take a layout you have built and resize the browser slowly from wide to narrow. Identify the exact moment when the layout stops feeling comfortable. That point is more useful than memorizing a breakpoint from a random blog post.

Responsive CSS is mostly negotiation with space. When space disappears, decide what should stack, wrap, shrink, or change. The viewport did not betray you. It simply revealed the assumptions in your layout.
What You Should Take Away

Responsive design creates interfaces that adapt to different available spaces. Flexible sizing and layout systems should do as much work as possible before media queries are introduced. Media queries let you change the layout when a condition such as viewport width is met, and a mobile-first approach starts with the smaller layout before progressively enhancing it at larger widths.

quiz.question: What does responsive design mean?
options: Making every webpage exactly the same width.
Building interfaces that adapt to different available spaces and viewport conditions.
Using only media queries and no flexible CSS.
Designing only for mobile devices.
quiz.explanation: Responsive design means creating layouts that adapt to different available spaces and conditions.

quiz.question:
What does this media query mean?

@media (min-width: 768px) { ... }
options: The rules apply when the viewport is 768px wide or smaller.
The rules apply when the viewport is at least 768px wide.
The rules apply only to printed documents.
The rules apply only to mobile phones.
quiz.explanation: min-width means the condition becomes true when the viewport reaches that width or larger.

quiz.question: What does a mobile-first approach generally mean?
options: Build only a mobile website.
Use the smallest reasonable layout as the base and add larger-screen enhancements progressively.
Start with desktop CSS and hide everything on phones.
Avoid media queries completely.
quiz.explanation: Mobile-first CSS starts with the smaller layout and typically enhances it at larger widths using tools such as min-width media queries.

quiz.question: When should you add a breakpoint?
options: Whenever a popular device reaches a particular screen size.
When the current layout stops working well and genuinely needs a different rule.
After every CSS declaration.
Only at exactly 768px.
quiz.explanation: Breakpoints should respond to the needs of the layout and content rather than blindly following device categories.

summary: Responsive design means adapting an interface to different available spaces. Start with flexible layout rules, then introduce media queries when the layout genuinely needs to change. A mobile-first approach uses the smaller layout as the base and progressively enhances it with min-width queries. Good responsive design is tested across multiple widths and is driven by content and usability rather than arbitrary device categories.

title: CSS Challenge: Build a Responsive Interface
description: Bring the CSS module together by transforming a structured HTML page into a polished, responsive interface using the cascade, box model, typography, colors, Flexbox, Grid, and responsive design.
mastery: The learner can independently style a complete HTML page using selectors, the cascade, box-model properties, typography, colors, Flexbox, Grid, and responsive rules, then inspect and refine the result across multiple viewport sizes.

Use selectors and the cascade to style different parts of a page without unnecessary specificity.

Build a responsive layout that adapts across narrow and wide viewports.

sections.text: No More Isolated CSS Tricks

You have spent this module learning how CSS actually works: selectors find elements, the cascade resolves competing declarations, the box model controls physical space, typography controls reading, visual properties shape the interface, Flexbox handles one-dimensional layouts, Grid handles two-dimensional ones, and responsive rules let the interface adapt.
Now you have to use all of that without a tutorial whispering the correct property into your ear.

sections.title: This is a build, not a property scavenger hunt
sections.text: You are not expected to use every CSS property you know. The goal is to choose the smallest set of rules that produces a clear, usable result. If you find yourself adding your seventeenth margin because the layout is 'almost right,' stop and inspect the actual layout model.
The Project Brief
You are going to style a small Forge Academy dashboard. The HTML already provides meaningful structure. Your job is to turn it into a coherent interface that works on both narrow and wide screens.

Engineering:

- Avoid unnecessary ID selectors and !important.
- Use Flexbox or Grid according to the relationship being solved.

sections.text: Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks you to walk through the project. Be ready to explain your selector strategy, how the cascade affects the result, how the box model creates spacing, how typography establishes hierarchy, why you chose Flexbox or Grid in each area, and how your responsive breakpoints were chosen.
A strong engineer can explain not only what the CSS does, but why the CSS is structured that way.
Module Reflection

You started the CSS module by learning that CSS is a system of rules. You now have a complete interface built from those rules. The important progression was not memorizing more properties. It was learning how to reason about selectors, space, hierarchy, layout, and changing available space.

sections.title: CSS module complete

What You Should Take Away

Strong CSS is a system, not a collection of random fixes. You select intentionally, understand the cascade, control the box model, establish readable typography and visual surfaces, choose the right layout model, and adapt the interface as available space changes. The final skill is being able to inspect your own CSS and explain why it works.

title: JavaScript and the Browser
description: Understand what JavaScript actually does in the browser, how it responds to events, and how it changes the live page through the DOM.
mastery: The learner can explain, in their own words, what JavaScript contributes to a browser-based interface, distinguish JavaScript from HTML and CSS, describe the event-driven nature of browser programs, and explain at a high level how JavaScript can change the DOM.
learningObjectives: Explain the role of JavaScript in a browser-based application.
Distinguish the responsibilities of HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.
Explain that browser JavaScript commonly responds to events rather than simply running once from top to bottom and stopping.
Explain at a high level how JavaScript can read and modify the DOM.
Describe a simple user interaction as a sequence of event, JavaScript logic, and visible UI change.

sections.text: The Page Can Finally Do Something
HTML gave the browser structure. CSS gave that structure appearance. JavaScript is where the page starts reacting.
Click a button and something happens. Type into a search box and results can update. Open a menu and it appears. Submit a form and the interface can respond without rebuilding the entire page.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: HTML describes what exists. CSS describes how it looks. JavaScript describes what happens when the world changes.

That last sentence is deliberately simple. JavaScript can do much more than browser UI work, but this curriculum is currently teaching JavaScript as part of frontend engineering, so the browser is our first home for the language.
The Three Layers of a Web Interface

sections.title: A tiny interface
sections.code: <button id="save-button">Save changes</button>

sections.title: What the button looks like
What the button does

sections.text: The HTML creates the button. The CSS changes its presentation. The JavaScript waits for a click and then changes what the user sees.

sections.title: A useful engineering habit
sections.text: When something on a page changes, ask which layer caused the change. If the button moved, think CSS/layout. If the button text changed after a click, think JavaScript behavior. If the button did not exist at all, think HTML or DOM generation.
JavaScript Runs in Response to Things Happening
A beginner's first mental model of a program is often: line 1 runs, then line 2, then line 3, and eventually the program ends.

That model is incomplete for browser applications. A browser program can register code that should run later when something happens: a click, a key press, an input change, a timer, a network response, or another browser event.

sections.title: Registering a response to an event

sections.text: The function passed to addEventListener is not executed simply because the browser reached that line. It is registered so the browser can call it later when a click occurs.

sections.title: The misconception to kill early
sections.text: Do not imagine browser JavaScript as a tiny script that runs once, does everything, and goes home. Browser applications spend much of their time waiting for events and responding to them.
The DOM Is the Browser's Live Page Structure
When the browser parses HTML, it creates a Document Object Model, usually called the DOM. The DOM represents the page as a tree of objects that JavaScript can inspect and change.

sections.title: The HTML
sections.code:
My Tasks

Nothing saved yet.

sections.text: JavaScript can find the paragraph and change its text.

sections.title: Changing the live DOM
sections.code:
const status = document.querySelector('#status');
status.textContent = 'Saved successfully.';

sections.text: The original HTML source file did not magically rewrite itself. JavaScript changed the live DOM currently held by the browser, which changes what is rendered on screen.

sections.title: This distinction matters
sections.text: Source HTML and the live DOM are related, but they are not the same thing. JavaScript can change the live page after the browser has loaded it.
From Click to Visible Change

steps.title: 1. The page exists
steps.description: HTML created the button and the browser turned the document into a live DOM.

steps.title: 2. JavaScript registers a listener
steps.description: JavaScript tells the browser what code should run when the button receives a click.

steps.title: 3. The user clicks
steps.description: The browser detects the click and dispatches the corresponding event.

steps.title: 4. JavaScript runs
steps.description: The registered handler executes and can read or change data, call APIs, or modify the DOM.

steps.title: 5. The page changes
steps.description: The browser updates what is rendered so the user can see the result of the JavaScript-driven change.

sections.text: This event → logic → UI-change loop is one of the most important mental models in frontend development. You will use it repeatedly throughout the rest of the JavaScript and React curriculum.
Real-World Example: A Save Button

Imagine an application with a Save button. A user clicks it. The browser receives the click event. JavaScript responds by perhaps disabling the button, showing a saving state, sending data to a server, and then updating the UI when the response comes back.

sections.title: A simplified interaction

sections.text: This is deliberately incomplete. There is no server request yet, no error state, and no retry behavior. Those are later topics. For now, notice the division of responsibility: JavaScript handles the browser-side behavior and visible state change.

sections.title: Human beings are also stateful
sections.text: Click Save → 'Saving...' → 'Saved'. That little sequence is already a state machine, even though nobody gave it a fancy architecture diagram. Frontend engineering is full of these tiny state transitions hiding inside apparently simple interactions.
What JavaScript Does Not Replace
JavaScript does not make HTML and CSS obsolete. A strong frontend engineer uses all three together.

sections.title: Keep the responsibilities straight
sections.code:
HTML
→ structure and meaning

CSS
→ presentation and layout

JavaScript
→ behavior, logic, and dynamic changes

sections.text: A common beginner mistake is trying to solve every problem with JavaScript. That usually creates more code and less clarity.

sections.title: The 'JavaScript can do it' trap
sections.text: Yes, JavaScript can change styles. That does not mean it should manually calculate every margin and color on your page. Let CSS do CSS's job. Let JavaScript handle behavior and logic.
Why Timing Matters
JavaScript can only interact with elements that exist in the DOM when the code tries to access them. That is why timing becomes important in browser programs.

sections.title: A future bug you will meet
sections.code:
const button = document.querySelector('#save-button');
button.addEventListener('click', handleSave);

sections.text: If the button does not exist yet, querySelector may not find it, and the next line can fail. You will study this kind of DOM timing problem more deeply in the Browser and Debugging module. For now, the important idea is that browser JavaScript runs inside a changing environment.
Practice: Predict the Interaction
Do not write new code yet. Read the example and predict what will happen.

sections.title: Predict first

sections.text: Question: before the button is clicked, what does the paragraph say? After the button is clicked, what changes? Which part of the program waits, and which part runs after the event?

sections.label: Explain in your own words what JavaScript contributes to a browser application, distinguish HTML/CSS/JavaScript responsibilities, and describe the sequence from a user event to a visible DOM change.
sections.hint: Use this structure: something exists in the DOM → an event happens → JavaScript responds → the DOM may change → the browser updates what the user sees.

sections.text: Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'What does JavaScript do in the browser?' A strong beginner answer is: 'JavaScript provides programming logic and behavior in the browser. It can listen for events, read application or DOM state, perform logic, communicate with other services, and update the page based on what happens.'

A likely follow-up is: 'How does JavaScript change what the user sees?' A strong answer is: 'The browser exposes the DOM to JavaScript. JavaScript can find DOM nodes, read their state, and modify properties or content. The browser then reflects those changes in the rendered page.'

Another follow-up: 'Does JavaScript always run from top to bottom once and finish?' The better answer is: 'The statements execute in program order when they run, but browser applications are event-driven. Code can register callbacks that run later when events, timers, or other asynchronous operations occur.'
Reflect
Think about an interface you used today. Pick one interaction: opening a menu, liking something, submitting a form, changing a quantity, or switching a tab.
Describe it in four steps: What exists in the HTML? What event occurs? What does JavaScript need to decide or change? What does the user see afterward?

sections.title: The frontend detective question
sections.text: Whenever something on a webpage suddenly changes, ask: 'What event caused this, what code responded, and what state changed?' That question will take you surprisingly far.
What You Should Take Away

JavaScript adds programming behavior to browser interfaces. It responds to events, performs logic, interacts with the DOM, and can change what the user sees. HTML provides structure, CSS provides presentation, and JavaScript provides behavior and dynamic logic. The next lesson moves from this mental model into the first concrete JavaScript building block: variables and values.

options: A database stored on the server.

A CSS property for controlling layout.

quiz.explanation: The DOM is the browser's object representation of the document and provides the structure JavaScript can work with.

options: CSS changes → DNS lookup → HTML disappears → JavaScript exits.

CSS

summary: JavaScript brings programming behavior to the browser. It responds to events, performs logic, interacts with the DOM, and can change the live interface. HTML supplies structure, CSS supplies presentation, and JavaScript supplies behavior. Browser applications are event-driven, so code can be registered to run later when user or browser events occur.

title: Variables and Values
description: Learn how let and const give JavaScript names for values, how reassignment works, and why choosing the right declaration makes code easier to reason about.
mastery: The learner can declare variables with let and const, read and update values appropriately, distinguish reassignment from mutation at a beginner level, choose const versus let for a simple situation, and explain why var is not the default choice in modern JavaScript.
learningObjectives: Declare variables using let and const.
Explain that a variable provides a name through which a value can be accessed.
Read a variable's current value and use it in an expression.
Reassign a let variable when a value needs to change.
Explain why a const variable cannot be reassigned.
Choose const or let appropriately in simple situations.
Avoid using var for the modern beginner-level examples in this curriculum.

sections.text: Give Your Values a Name

In the last lesson, JavaScript was the part of the browser that could respond, make decisions, and change what the user sees. But there is an obvious problem: your program needs somewhere to keep the information it is working with.
That is where variables come in. A variable gives your program a name through which it can access a value.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: Think of a variable as a labeled reference in your program. Instead of repeatedly saying 'that string I created three lines ago,' you can give it a name and use the name.

sections.title: A named value
sections.code:
const learnerName = 'Ada';

console.log(learnerName);

sections.text: The program creates a variable named learnerName and gives it the string value 'Ada'. Later, the program can use learnerName instead of repeating the value directly.
const: The Default Choice
Use const when the variable should not be reassigned after it has been initialized.

sections.title: A const variable
sections.code:
const courseName = 'Frontend Engineering';
const lessonCount = 8;

sections.text: These variables can be read and used throughout the rest of the code, but you cannot later assign a new value to the variables themselves.

sections.title: This is not allowed
sections.code:
const courseName = 'Frontend Engineering';

courseName = 'JavaScript Fundamentals';

sections.text: The problem is reassignment. The variable was declared with const, so JavaScript does not allow you to point that variable at a different value later.

sections.title: Do not confuse 'const' with 'nothing can ever change'
sections.text: const prevents reassignment of the variable. It does not mean every object or array connected to that variable becomes a magical frozen artifact. That distinction becomes important later. For now, focus on the simpler rule: const means the variable itself cannot be reassigned.
let: When the Variable Needs a New Value
Use let when the variable needs to be reassigned.

sections.title: A value that changes

sections.text: The same variable name now refers to different values over time. The current value of score is 20.

sections.title: A browser-style example

sections.text: This is a simple example of why reassignment exists. The program needs a piece of data whose current value changes as the application does something.
const or let?
A useful rule is simple: start with const. Change to let only when you know the variable needs to be reassigned.

sections.title: Choose intentionally

sections.text: username and maxAttempts do not need reassignment, so they use const. attempts changes, so it uses let.

sections.title: Why this helps
sections.text: const communicates an expectation to the next developer: 'This name will keep pointing at the same value.' let communicates: 'This value is expected to change.' Clear expectations make code easier to read and safer to modify.
A Variable Is Not the Same Thing as the Value
This distinction is worth learning early. The variable is the named binding. The value is the data currently associated with it.

sections.title: The name and the value
sections.code:
let points = 100;

points = 125;

sections.text: The variable is still named points. What changed is the value associated with that variable.
Expressions Can Use Variables
Variables become useful when your program combines them with other values and operations.

sections.title: Using named values

sections.text: The expression price * quantity uses the current values stored in those variables and produces a new value. The variable total then gives that result a useful name.
Interactive Practice: Change the Values
This is your first real JavaScript playground exercise. Change the values, predict the result, then run it. The goal is to see variables as live pieces of program state rather than vocabulary words.

sections.title: Variables Playground
sections.instructions: Change the values of learnerName, completedLessons, and lessonPrice. Predict the output before running the program. Then change completedLessons so it increases and observe how the calculated progress value changes. Finally, change attempts from const to let and make it increase without causing an error.

sections.text: Predict Before You Run
A good JavaScript developer does not need to execute every line to know what every line probably does. Build that instinct now.

sections.title: What will this print?

sections.text: The first output is 25 because score was reassigned. The second output is 30 because total is calculated from the current score and bonus values.
The Classic const Mistake

sections.title: A variable that changes should not be const
sections.code:
const attempts = 0;

attempts = attempts + 1;

sections.text: The program is trying to reassign attempts, but const does not allow reassignment. The correct declaration for this particular requirement is let.

sections.title: The corrected version
sections.code:
let attempts = 0;

attempts = attempts + 1;

sections.title: The compiler error is useful
sections.text: When JavaScript tells you that a const variable cannot be reassigned, it is not personally attacking you. It is catching a mismatch between what your declaration promised and what your code tried to do.
What About var?

You will encounter var in older JavaScript code. This curriculum uses let and const as the default modern declarations because they make reassignment intent clearer and behave differently around scope in ways that will matter later.

You do not need to master var, hoisting, or block scope yet. Those details belong later in the Modern JavaScript module. For this lesson, recognize var when you see it, but build new beginner code with const and let.

sections.title: Scope is coming later
sections.text: JavaScript variable declarations have scope rules, and let/const have important behavior around blocks. We are intentionally not opening that door yet. You have enough doors open already.
Practice: Choose the Declaration
For each situation, decide whether the variable should be const or let. The important part is not memorizing the answer. It is explaining whether reassignment is required.

sections.title: Make the call
sections.code:
A. The name of the current course never changes.
B. The number of completed lessons increases.
C. The maximum number of retries is fixed.
D. The current progress percentage changes as the learner completes lessons.

sections.text: A and C are natural const cases. B and D need let because their variables must be reassigned as the program state changes.

sections.label: Declare variables with let and const, correctly reassign let variables, explain why a const variable cannot be reassigned, and choose const or let based on whether reassignment is required.
sections.hint: Ask one question: will this variable need to point to a different value later? No → const. Yes → let.

sections.text: Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'What's the difference between let and const?' A strong beginner answer is: 'Both create variables with block scope, but const prevents reassignment while let allows reassignment. I normally start with const and use let when the variable needs to change.'

A likely follow-up is: 'Why not just use let for everything?' Because const communicates that reassignment is not expected. That makes the program's intent clearer and prevents accidental reassignment.

Another follow-up is: 'What about var?' For modern beginner code, use let and const instead. var has older scoping and hoisting behavior that you will study later rather than mixing into your first variable lesson.
Reflect

Look at a small program and circle every variable that changes over time. Ask whether each declaration communicates that fact clearly. If a value never needs reassignment, const is usually the clearer signal.
Good variable declarations tell a tiny story before you read the rest of the program. const says 'stable name.' let says 'this one is going somewhere.' Your future self appreciates the spoiler.
What You Should Take Away

Variables give JavaScript values useful names. Use const when the variable should not be reassigned and let when the variable needs a new value later. Start with const by default, switch to let when reassignment is genuinely required, and treat var as legacy syntax you will study in more depth later. The next lesson builds on variables by introducing JavaScript's data types and operators.

exercises.brief: Modify a small JavaScript program using const and let. Predict the output before running it, then change a value and observe how the calculated result changes.

exercises.title: Choose const or let
exercises.brief: Classify real program values as const or let and explain whether reassignment is required in each case.

quiz.question: What is the main reason to use a variable?
options: To give a value a name so the program can refer to it.
To automatically convert HTML into CSS.
To force the browser to reload the page.
To prevent every value from changing.
quiz.explanation: Variables give values names that the program can use to read, calculate with, and otherwise work with those values.

quiz.question: Which declaration is appropriate when a variable needs to be reassigned?
options: const
let
Both are identical.
Only var can be reassigned.
quiz.explanation: let allows the variable to be reassigned. const does not.

options: score becomes 20.
JavaScript creates a second score automatically.
The reassignment is not allowed because score was declared with const.
The browser converts score to let automatically.
quiz.explanation: A const binding cannot be reassigned after initialization.

quiz.question: Which is the best default choice when you are declaring a new variable and do not expect to reassign it?
options: var
let
const
No declaration is needed.
quiz.explanation: Start with const when reassignment is not required. Use let when the variable genuinely needs to change.

summary: Variables give JavaScript values useful names. const creates a variable that cannot be reassigned, while let allows reassignment. A strong beginner habit is to start with const and choose let only when the variable needs to point to a new value later. var exists in older JavaScript code but is not the default declaration used in this curriculum.

title: Data Types and Operators
description: Learn the core JavaScript data types and the operators used to calculate, compare, and combine values, with special attention to strict equality and type coercion.
mastery: The learner can identify the common primitive data types used in beginner JavaScript, use arithmetic, comparison, and logical operators in simple expressions, predict the result of those expressions, and explain why === is generally preferred over == when comparing values.
learningObjectives: Identify common JavaScript primitive values such as strings, numbers, booleans, null, and undefined.
Use arithmetic operators to calculate new values.
Use comparison operators to produce boolean results.
Use logical operators to combine or invert conditions at a basic level.
Explain the difference between == and ===.
Use === and !== for predictable strict comparisons.
Predict the result of simple expressions before running them.

sections.text: Values Have Different Kinds
Last lesson taught you how to give values names. Now we need to look more closely at the values themselves.
JavaScript values have different types. A person's name, a lesson count, whether a lesson is complete, and the absence of a value are all different kinds of information.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: A variable gives a value a name. The value's type tells JavaScript what kind of thing it is dealing with and influences what operations make sense.
The Core Types You Need First

sections.title: Common beginner values

sections.text: Here we have a string, a number, a boolean, null, and undefined. These values are enough to build a surprisingly large amount of beginner JavaScript.

sections.title: Checking types

sections.text: The typeof operator can help you inspect the type of a value. You will use it when debugging and when you need to understand what kind of data your program is actually holding.

sections.title: One weird JavaScript fact to remember later
sections.text: typeof null returns 'object'. That is a historical quirk of JavaScript, not a reason to abandon the language and become a lighthouse keeper. Learn the common types first; the language's historical oddities can come later.
Numbers and Arithmetic
JavaScript provides arithmetic operators for working with numbers.

sections.title: Basic arithmetic

sections.text: The familiar operators are +, -, *, and /. You can also use % to get a remainder.

sections.title: Remainder
sections.code:
console.log(10 % 3); // 1
console.log(8 % 2);  // 0

sections.text: The remainder operator is useful for questions such as 'Is this number even?' or for repeating patterns.
Strings Are Data Too
Strings represent text. The + operator can concatenate strings.

sections.title: Combining strings

sections.text: String concatenation becomes especially useful when combined with variables. Later you will also use template literals for cleaner string construction.
Comparisons Produce Booleans
Comparison operators ask a question and produce a boolean: true or false.

sections.title: Comparison operators
sections.code:
console.log(10 > 5);   // true
console.log(10 < 5);   // false
console.log(10 >= 10); // true
console.log(8 !== 3);  // true

sections.text: These results become extremely useful once programs need to make decisions. That is the next lesson's job, but you need to understand the boolean results first.
The Big One: == vs ===
JavaScript has both loose equality, ==, and strict equality, ===. They are not interchangeable.

sections.title: The surprising comparison
sections.code:
console.log('5' == 5);  // true
console.log('5' === 5); // false

sections.text: The loose equality operator can perform type conversion before comparing. Strict equality does not convert values just to make the comparison work. If the types differ, strict equality returns false.

sections.title: The rule Forge wants you to build
sections.text: For ordinary JavaScript comparisons, prefer === and !==. They make the comparison's expectations explicit and avoid many surprising coercion cases.
This is not because == is illegal. It is valid JavaScript. The problem is that implicit type conversion can make behavior less obvious when you are still building your mental model.
Logical Operators Combine Conditions
The logical operators &&, ||, and ! let your program combine or invert logical expressions.

sections.title: Basic logical reasoning

sections.text: At this stage, think of && as 'and', || as 'or', and ! as 'not'. JavaScript's logical operators have additional behavior beyond simple boolean algebra, but that deeper truthiness and short-circuiting discussion belongs later.

sections.title: Boundary for this lesson
sections.text: You only need the basic logical model here. Do not jump ahead into short-circuit evaluation, truthy/falsy edge cases, nullish coalescing, or operator-precedence puzzles. Those are useful later, but they are not prerequisites for learning today's core operators.
Interactive Practice: Type and Operator Lab
Now put the pieces together in one live example. Change the values, predict every output, then run the program and compare your prediction with the result.

sections.title: Type and Operator Lab
sections.instructions: Change the supplied values and predict the results before running the program. Test arithmetic, string concatenation, comparisons, strict equality, loose equality, and basic logical operators. Then intentionally make one comparison use == and one use === with values of different types. Explain the difference you observe.

sections.text: Predict Before You Run
The habit we want is simple: make a prediction, then verify it. That turns the console into a laboratory instead of a slot machine.

sections.title: Round one

sections.text: The results are 15, true, false, and true. The last two lines are deliberately different because one comparison is strict and the other allows type conversion.
Practice Drill: Fix the Comparison
A learner wrote this code to determine whether the current lesson number is the expected number.

sections.title: The comparison

sections.text: The code happens to enter the branch because == converts the values during comparison. But the program is comparing a string with a number. Ask whether that mismatch should really be accepted.

sections.title: Strict Equality Fix
sections.instructions: Replace the loose equality comparison with a strict comparison. First predict what the result will be and explain why. Then decide whether the underlying values should also be made the same type before comparing them.

sections.text: Practice Drill: Read the Expression
Translate each expression into plain English before running it.

sections.title: What is JavaScript asking?
sections.code:
score >= 70

isLoggedIn && hasPermission

completedLessons !== totalLessons

!isPaused

sections.text: These mean, respectively: 'Is score at least 70?', 'Is the user logged in and do they have permission?', 'Are the completed and total lesson counts different?', and 'Is the program not paused?'
Don't Confuse Assignment With Comparison

You learned assignment with = in the previous lesson. Comparison uses operators such as === and !==. These symbols look related because JavaScript enjoys making punctuation do overtime, but they perform completely different jobs.

sections.title: Different jobs
sections.code:
let score = 70;       // assignment

score === 70;         // comparison
score !== 50;         // comparison

sections.title: This mistake will follow you into the next lesson
sections.text: If you accidentally write = when you mean to compare, your code may behave very differently from what you intended. JavaScript is not going to send a tiny warning fairy. Learn to visually distinguish assignment from comparison now.
What Should You Use in Real Code?

A useful beginner policy is: use +, -, *, /, and % for straightforward arithmetic; use comparison operators when you need a boolean answer; use &&, ||, and ! to combine basic conditions; and prefer === and !== for equality checks.
The goal is not to memorize an operator table. The goal is to look at an expression and understand what value it produces.

sections.label: Identify common beginner JavaScript data types, use arithmetic/comparison/logical operators, predict the result of simple expressions, and correctly explain why === and !== are generally preferred over == and !=.
sections.hint: Ask two questions: what type is each value, and what kind of result does this operator produce?

sections.text: Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'What's the difference between == and ===?' A strong beginner answer is: 'Both compare values, but == allows type coercion while === compares without converting values. In normal application code, I generally prefer === because it makes type expectations explicit and avoids surprising coercion.'
A likely follow-up is: 'What does a comparison operator return?' The answer is a boolean result: true or false.
Another follow-up: 'What is the difference between = and ===?' = assigns a value to a variable. === compares two values using strict equality.
Reflect

Take three expressions from the lesson and translate them into ordinary language. If you cannot explain an expression without looking at the operator table, keep practicing the meaning rather than memorizing the symbols.
Operators are tiny words wearing punctuation costumes. Once you can read them as ordinary questions and actions, JavaScript starts feeling much less cryptic.
What You Should Take Away

JavaScript values have different types, including common primitives such as strings, numbers, booleans, null, and undefined. Arithmetic operators calculate values, comparison operators produce booleans, and logical operators combine basic conditions. Most importantly, strict equality === and strict inequality !== compare without the type conversion performed by == and !=, making them the preferred choice for ordinary equality checks.

exercises.brief: Modify a live JavaScript example containing strings, numbers, booleans, arithmetic, comparisons, and logical expressions. Predict the output before running each change.

quiz.question: What type of value does a comparison such as 10 > 5 produce?
options: A string
A number
A boolean
An object
quiz.explanation: Comparison operators produce a boolean result: true or false.

quiz.question:
What is the result of this expression?

'5' === 5
options: true
false
undefined
quiz.explanation: The values have different types: one is a string and the other is a number. Strict equality does not convert them, so the result is false.

quiz.question: Why can '5' == 5 evaluate to true?
options: Because strings and numbers are always the same type.
Because loose equality may perform type conversion before comparing.
Because === is used automatically.
Because JavaScript ignores the quotes.
quiz.explanation: Loose equality can convert operands of different types before performing the comparison.

quiz.question: What does && mean in the basic logical model taught here?
options: Or
And
Not
Assign
quiz.explanation: At this level, && can be read as 'and' when combining conditions.

quiz.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes = from ===?
options: = compares values and === assigns values.
= assigns a value and === performs a strict equality comparison.
They are two names for the same operator.
=== is only used for strings.
quiz.explanation: = is the assignment operator. === is the strict equality comparison operator.

summary: JavaScript works with values of different types, including strings, numbers, booleans, null, and undefined. Operators let programs calculate values, compare them, and combine simple conditions. Equality deserves special attention: == can perform type conversion, while === performs strict equality without converting different types, so === and !== are generally preferred for ordinary comparisons.

title: Conditions and Decisions
description: Use if, else if, else, and switch to make JavaScript choose what to do based on conditions.
mastery: The learner can write simple branching logic with if/else and switch, correctly use comparison results inside conditions, predict which branch executes, and avoid accidentally using assignment instead of comparison inside a condition.
learningObjectives: Use if statements to run code when a condition is true.
Use else and else if to represent alternative decisions.
Use switch for a small set of discrete values.
Use comparison expressions as conditions.
Predict which branch will execute before running the code.
Recognize and correct the mistake of using = when === was intended.

sections.text: Make the Program Choose
You already know how JavaScript stores values and compares them. Now the program gets to make a decision.
A condition produces a result that JavaScript can use to decide which code should run. This is the basic idea behind branching: if this is true, do this; otherwise, do something else.

sections.title: The rule in one breath
sections.text: A condition asks a question. if chooses a path when the condition is satisfied. else provides another path. else if gives you another question when the first one was not satisfied.
Drill 1: One Decision
Start with the smallest useful example: one condition, one possible action.

sections.title: Run when the condition is true

sections.text: The condition is score >= 70. It evaluates to true, so the code inside the braces runs.

sections.title: Pass or Fail
sections.instructions: Change score several times and predict the output before running the program. Try a value above 70, exactly 70, and below 70. Then add an else branch that prints 'Try again' when the learner does not pass.

sections.text: Drill 2: More Than Two Possible Paths
When there are several possible ranges or states, else if lets the program check another condition only when the previous one was not satisfied.

sections.title: Three outcomes

sections.text: The order matters. JavaScript checks the conditions from top to bottom and stops at the first matching branch.

sections.title: Grade the Learner
sections.instructions: Complete the branching logic so 90+ prints 'Excellent', 70–89 prints 'Passed', and anything below 70 prints 'Needs more work'. Test boundary values such as 90, 89, 70, and 69.

sections.title: The boundary trap
sections.text: Always test the edges. A condition that works for 85 can still be wrong for 90 or 70. Boundary values are where tiny logic mistakes tend to stop hiding.
Drill 3: When switch Fits Better
switch is useful when one value needs to be matched against several specific cases.

sections.title: A discrete set of choices

sections.text: Here the program is choosing between specific known values of status. break prevents execution from continuing into the next case after a match.

sections.title: Lesson Status Router
sections.instructions: Complete the switch so draft prints 'Not started', in-progress prints 'Learning', complete prints 'Completed', and any unknown value prints 'Unknown status'. Test every case and one value that is not listed.

sections.text: The Bug You Need to Catch
You learned in the previous lesson that = assigns a value and === compares values. That distinction matters even more inside conditions.

sections.title: Do not confuse assignment with comparison

sections.text: The programmer intended to ask whether status was equal to 'published'. Instead, the code assigns 'published' to status. That is a completely different operation.

sections.title: Catch the Condition Bug
sections.instructions: Find the bug in the condition and correct it so the message only appears when status is exactly 'published'. Test both 'draft' and 'published'.

sections.text: Final Drill: Build a Real Decision
Now combine the skills. Build a small course-access decision using conditions rather than hard-coding the final answer.

sections.title: Requirements
sections.code:
If the learner is not logged in:
→ print 'Please log in'

If the learner is logged in but has not completed the prerequisite:
→ print 'Finish the prerequisite first'

If the learner is logged in and has completed the prerequisite:
→ print 'Lesson unlocked'

sections.title: Unlock the Lesson
sections.instructions: Write the if/else logic that produces the required result. Test at least three combinations of isLoggedIn and prerequisiteComplete. Make sure your conditions compare values rather than assigning them.

sections.text: Debugging Habit: Test the Branches
A branch is not finished because one example worked. Test every meaningful path.

sections.title: Branch test checklist
sections.code:
1. Test the obvious true case.
2. Test the obvious false case.
3. Test boundary values.
4. Test the fallback/default path.
5. Check that you used comparison operators, not assignment.

sections.text: This habit will matter when your conditions become longer and your programs start making real decisions.

sections.label: Complete all branching drills using if/else, else if, and switch; correctly predict branch outcomes; test boundary and fallback cases; and identify the assignment-versus-comparison mistake inside a condition.
sections.hint: Trace the condition from top to bottom. Ask which branch is reached first, and check every comparison carefully.

sections.text: Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'How does an if statement work?' A strong beginner answer is: 'The condition is evaluated first. If the result is truthy, the code in the if branch runs. Otherwise, JavaScript checks an else if branch if one exists, and eventually the else branch if no earlier condition matched.'

A likely follow-up is: 'When would you use switch instead of if/else?' A good answer is: 'I would consider switch when one value is being matched against several discrete cases. For ranges or more complex conditions, if/else is often clearer.'
Another likely follow-up: 'What is the classic condition bug?' Watch for = when the intention was a comparison such as ===.
Reflect

Take one real decision from an application: whether a button is enabled, whether a lesson is unlocked, whether a user is allowed to continue. Write the decision in plain English first, then translate each sentence into a branch.

Good branching code reads like a conversation: Is the learner logged in? Yes. Did they finish the prerequisite? No. Then show the prerequisite message. When conditions become readable questions, the code becomes much easier to reason about.
What You Should Take Away

Conditions let programs choose between different paths. Use if for a decision, else if for additional alternatives, else for a fallback, and switch when one value is being matched against several discrete cases. Test every meaningful branch and remember that = assigns while === compares.

exercises.title: Grade the Learner
exercises.brief: Build a three-way grading decision using if, else if, and else. Verify the boundary values for every branch.

exercises.title: Lesson Status Router
exercises.brief: Use switch to map several discrete lesson-status values to user-facing messages, including a default case.

exercises.title: Catch the Condition Bug
exercises.brief: Find and fix an assignment used where a strict comparison was intended. Test both sides of the decision after the fix.

exercises.title: Unlock the Lesson
exercises.brief: Build a small access-control decision using login state and prerequisite completion. Test every meaningful combination.

quiz.question: What happens when an if condition evaluates to a truthy value?
options: The code inside the if branch runs.
The else branch always runs too.
The entire program stops.
JavaScript automatically converts the condition to a string.
quiz.explanation: When the if condition is truthy, JavaScript executes the associated branch.

quiz.question: When does an else branch run?
options: Always.
When none of the preceding if/else if conditions were satisfied.
Before the if branch.
Only when the program has an error.
quiz.explanation: The else branch is the fallback when none of the preceding conditions matched.

quiz.question: Which situation is a natural fit for switch?
options: Checking whether a score is above a numeric threshold.
Matching one known status value against several specific cases.
Repeating an operation ten times.
Transforming every item in an array.
quiz.explanation: switch is useful when one expression or value needs to be matched against a set of discrete cases.

options: It compares too strictly.
It assigns 'published' instead of comparing the current status.
switch should be used instead.
The condition cannot contain strings.
quiz.explanation: = is assignment. A comparison such as status === 'published' would ask whether the values are equal.

summary: Conditional logic lets JavaScript choose what to do based on evaluated conditions. if handles a decision, else if adds alternatives, else provides a fallback, and switch is useful for matching one value against several discrete cases. The main beginner trap is confusing = assignment with === comparison inside a condition. Test every meaningful branch, especially boundaries and defaults.

When would you use else if?
When is switch a good fit?
What is the difference between = and === inside a condition?
How would you test conditional logic thoroughly?
Why are boundary values important when testing conditions?

title: Loops and Repetition
description: Practice repeating work with for and while loops, control iteration safely, and avoid the classic off-by-one and infinite-loop mistakes.
mastery: The learner can write and modify basic for and while loops, predict how many iterations a loop will execute, safely update loop state, and diagnose a simple off-by-one or infinite-loop bug.
learningObjectives: Use a for loop to repeat work over a known range.
Use a while loop to repeat work while a condition remains true.
Predict how many times a basic loop will execute.
Update loop state correctly so a while loop can eventually stop.
Identify and fix a simple off-by-one error.
Identify and fix a simple infinite-loop bug.

sections.text: Do the Same Thing Without Copy-Pasting Yourself Into Oblivion
You know how to make a program choose. Now it needs to do something repeatedly.
Loops let JavaScript repeat a block of code instead of making you write the same instructions over and over again. This is where programs stop being impressed by the fact that you can copy and paste.

sections.title: The rule in one breath
sections.text: A loop asks how long the repetition should continue. A for loop is useful when you can describe the iteration range or count. A while loop is useful when repetition should continue while a condition remains true.
Drill 1: Repeat a Known Number of Times
Start with a for loop. The loop below counts from 1 through 5.

sections.title: A simple for loop

sections.text: There are three important pieces: where the counter starts, when the loop should continue, and how the counter changes after each iteration.

sections.title: For Loop Playground
sections.instructions: Change the starting value, stopping condition, and increment. Before running each version, predict exactly which numbers will print. Then try to make the loop print the numbers 1 through 10.

sections.text: Drill 2: The Off-by-One Trap
A loop can be almost correct and still produce the wrong result by one iteration. This is the classic off-by-one error.

sections.title: One iteration too many

sections.text: This prints 0 through 5, which is six numbers. If the requirement was 'print exactly five numbers starting at 0,' the stopping condition is wrong.
Changing <= to < produces 0 through 4, which is five iterations.

sections.title: Fix the Off-by-One Error
sections.instructions: The requirement is: print exactly five lesson numbers starting at 0. Fix the loop. Then test the result by changing the requirement to exactly eight numbers and updating the loop accordingly.

sections.text: Drill 3: While You Still Have Work To Do
A while loop keeps running while its condition is true.

sections.title: A while loop

sections.text: The important part is that the condition depends on state that changes. Once attempts reaches 3, the condition becomes false and the loop stops.

sections.title: While Loop Playground
sections.instructions: Change the starting value and stopping condition. Then modify the loop so it counts down from 5 to 1. Before running it, predict every value that will print.

sections.text: Catch the Infinite Loop
Here is the bug you must learn to recognize immediately.

sections.title: This loop never changes its condition

sections.text: count never changes. It stays 1 forever, so count <= 5 stays true forever. The loop has no path to termination.

sections.title: The infinite-loop checklist
sections.text: Whenever you write a while loop, ask: what value does the condition depend on, and where does that value change? If the answer to the second question is 'nowhere,' you should expect trouble.

sections.title: Stop the Infinite Loop
sections.instructions: Fix the loop so it prints 1 through 5 and then stops. Identify exactly which line makes termination possible.

sections.text: Final Drill: Loop Through Real Data
Now use a loop for an actual frontend-style task: printing the lesson numbers a learner has completed.

sections.title: The requirement
Print the Completed Lessons
sections.instructions: Use a loop to print one completion message per finished lesson. Test the program with 0, 1, 4, and 10 completed lessons. Make sure the loop does not print a lesson that has not been completed.
sections.initialCode:
const completedLessons = 4;

// Write the loop here.

sections.text: Choosing Between for and while
For beginner code, use for when the iteration has a clear counter or range. Use while when the loop should continue based on a condition whose state changes over time.

sections.title: A useful first rule
sections.code:
Known range or count
→ for

Continue while a condition remains true
→ while

sections.text: There are situations where either can work. The point is to choose the form that makes the loop's intention easiest to read.
Test the Loop Before You Trust It
Loops are excellent at multiplying mistakes. A typo inside one iteration becomes the same typo over and over again.

sections.title: Loop testing checklist
sections.code:
1. What value does the loop start with?
2. When does the loop stop?
3. How does the loop move toward stopping?
4. How many iterations should occur?
5. What happens at the first and last iteration?
6. What happens when the input is empty or zero?

sections.title: The professional habit
sections.text: Do not only test the happy path. Test zero, one, the normal case, and the boundary. Loops have a suspicious relationship with the number one.

sections.label: Complete all loop drills, correctly predict iteration counts, fix the off-by-one example, and identify the missing state update that causes an infinite while loop.
sections.hint: For every loop, identify the starting state, stopping condition, and state change.

sections.text: Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'What's the difference between a for loop and a while loop?' A strong beginner answer is: 'Both repeat code while a condition allows them to continue. I typically use for when the iteration has a known counter or range, and while when the loop should continue until a changing condition becomes false.'
A likely follow-up is: 'What causes an infinite while loop?' The common cause is that the state used by the condition never changes in a way that can eventually make the condition false.
Another follow-up: 'What is an off-by-one error?' It is when a loop runs one iteration too many or too few because the start, end, or increment condition is slightly wrong.
Reflect

Take one repetitive task from everyday software: rendering five cards, checking a list of records, counting attempts, or processing lessons. Decide whether you would naturally describe it with a known range or a condition that changes over time.
A loop is basically your program saying, 'I refuse to type this twelve times.' That is good. Just make sure it also knows when to stop.
What You Should Take Away

Loops repeat work. Use for when a counter or range naturally describes the iteration, and while when repetition continues while a changing condition remains true. Always verify the starting value, stopping condition, state update, and boundary behavior. The biggest beginner traps are off-by-one errors and loops whose condition never becomes false.

exercises.brief: Modify a for loop's start, end, and increment values, predict the output, and make it produce a requested sequence.

exercises.title: Fix the Off-by-One Error
exercises.brief: Correct a loop that runs one iteration too many, then adapt it to a new iteration count while preserving the intended range.

exercises.title: While Loop Playground
exercises.brief: Modify a while loop that counts upward and then downward. Predict the output before running each version.

exercises.title: Stop the Infinite Loop
exercises.brief: Identify the missing state update in an infinite while loop and add the smallest fix that guarantees termination.

exercises.title: Print the Completed Lessons
exercises.brief: Use a loop to generate one completion message per completed lesson. Test zero, one, normal, and larger input values.

quiz.question: Which situation is a natural fit for a for loop?
options: Repeating while a changing condition remains true and the number of iterations is unknown.
Repeating over a clearly defined counter or range.
Reacting to a click event.
Comparing two strings.
quiz.explanation: A for loop is a natural choice when a counter or iteration range describes the repetition clearly.

options: The loop cannot use numbers.
count never changes, so the condition can remain true forever.
while loops always run exactly once.
The console prevents the loop from stopping.
quiz.explanation: The loop condition depends on count, but count is never updated, so the loop has no path toward termination.

quiz.question: What is an off-by-one error?
options: A syntax error caused by using one variable.
A loop running one iteration too many or too few because its boundaries are slightly wrong.
A loop that always runs forever.
A mistake in a CSS selector.
quiz.explanation: Off-by-one errors occur when loop boundaries produce one more or one fewer iteration than intended.

quiz.question: What should you identify first when debugging a loop?
options: The font used by the console.
The starting state, stopping condition, and state update.
The browser's color theme.
The number of files in the project.
quiz.explanation: Those three pieces explain how the loop begins, progresses, and eventually terminates.

summary: Loops let JavaScript repeat work without duplicating code. Use for when a counter or known range describes the repetition and while when a changing condition controls whether repetition continues. The critical debugging questions are: where does the loop start, what makes it stop, and what changes each iteration? Off-by-one errors and infinite loops are the classic beginner traps.
interviewQuestions: What is the difference between a for loop and a while loop?
What causes an infinite loop?
What is an off-by-one error?
How do you determine how many times a loop will execute?
What would you check first when debugging a loop?

title: Functions
description: Learn how functions package reusable logic, accept inputs through parameters, and produce results through return values.
mastery: The learner can declare and call functions, pass arguments into parameters, return values for other code to use, and explain the difference between returning a value and merely logging one.
learningObjectives: Explain why functions are useful for packaging reusable logic.
Declare and call a basic JavaScript function.
Define parameters and pass arguments into a function.
Return a value from a function and use that value elsewhere.
Distinguish return from console.log.
Apply a function to a small realistic frontend-style problem.

sections.text: Stop Writing the Same Logic Twice
You have variables, values, decisions, and loops. Your programs can now store information, choose paths, and repeat work.
But there is another problem: what happens when the same piece of logic needs to happen in several places?
You could copy and paste it. JavaScript will allow this. Your future self will not be impressed.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: A function packages a piece of logic behind a name so you can call it when you need it. Parameters let you provide inputs. return lets the function hand a result back to the code that called it.
A Function Is a Reusable Piece of Logic

sections.title: Your first function

sections.text: The function declaration defines the logic. The call sayHello() tells JavaScript to execute that logic.
Defining a function does not mean its body immediately runs. You define it first, then call it when you want its behavior.
Functions Can Accept Inputs
A function becomes more reusable when it can work with different input values. Parameters are the named inputs declared by the function.

sections.title: A function with a parameter

sections.text: name is the parameter. 'Ada' and 'Grace' are arguments passed into the function when it is called.

sections.title: Parameter vs argument
sections.text: The parameter is the function's named input slot. The argument is the actual value you pass into that slot. Think 'parameter = placeholder, argument = thing I brought to the party.'
Functions Can Return Results
Logging a result is useful while debugging, but most reusable functions should produce a value that other code can actually use.

sections.title: Returning a value
