title: The this Keyword
description: Learn why this is determined by how a regular function is called, how method calls differ from plain function calls and arrow functions, and how to avoid losing the intended this context in callbacks.
mastery: The learner can predict the value of this in common regular-function call patterns, explain why method calls provide their object as this, distinguish arrow functions from regular functions in their treatment of this, and fix a callback that loses the intended object context.
learningObjectives: Explain that this in a regular function is determined by the call site.
Predict this for a simple object method call.
Distinguish a method call from a plain function call.
Explain the useful difference between regular functions and arrow functions when this is involved.
Recognize why passing a method as a callback can lose its original this context.
Fix a simple this-related callback bug using an appropriate modern pattern.
Avoid treating this as a variable that simply refers to the object where the function was written.

sections.text: The Most Misunderstood Word in Beginner JavaScript
You have already learned scope and closures. Now JavaScript gives you a different kind of context-sensitive rule: this.
The dangerous part is that this does not simply mean 'the object this function belongs to.' For regular functions, its value depends on how the function is called.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: For regular functions, ask 'How was this function called?' rather than 'Where was this function written?' The call determines the this value.
Start With a Method Call

sections.title: this refers to the object at the call site

sections.text: The function is called as learner.introduce(). In this call, this refers to learner, so this.name gives 'Ada'.

sections.title: Read the call, not the function name
sections.text: The important part is learner.introduce(). The object before the dot is what provides this for this particular method call.
A Different Call Can Change this

sections.title: Extract the method

sections.text: The function is no longer being called as learner.introduce(). It is being called as introduce(). That changes the call context, so this is no longer automatically the learner object.
In strict mode, which modern JavaScript modules use, a plain function call gives this the value undefined.
The Call-Site Rule

sections.title: A practical first model for regular functions
sections.code:
object.method()
→ this is the object used for the method call

plainFunction()
→ this is not supplied by an object call
→ in strict mode, this is undefined

new Thing()
→ this is the newly created instance

sections.text: There are additional call forms such as call, apply, and bind, which explicitly control this. For now, the call-site model is the foundation you need.
Interactive Practice: Predict this

sections.title: this Predictor
sections.instructions: For each call, predict what this refers to before running the program. First run the method directly. Then extract it and call it as a plain function. Explain why the result changes.

sections.text: Why Callbacks Cause Trouble
Frontend JavaScript frequently passes functions to other code: event listeners, timers, array methods, and browser APIs all do this.

sections.title: The method gets detached

sections.text: The timer receives a function reference. It does not preserve the learner.introduce() method call syntax. The function can therefore run without the learner object providing this.

sections.title: The classic misconception
sections.text: A regular function does not permanently remember its this from the place where it was written. Closures retain lexical variables. this in a regular function is a separate mechanism determined by how the function is called.
One Fix: Wrap the Call

sections.title: Preserve the intended receiver explicitly

sections.text: The arrow function closes over learner from the surrounding scope. When the callback runs, it explicitly performs learner.introduce(), so the regular method call supplies the intended this.
Arrow Functions and this
Arrow functions do not create their own dynamic this binding. They capture this from their surrounding lexical context.

sections.title: Arrow functions capture surrounding this

sections.text: Here, the arrow function does not create a new this. It uses the this from start(), where the method call established this as learner.

sections.title: Regular vs arrow
sections.text: Regular function: this is determined by the call. Arrow function: this is inherited from the surrounding lexical context. That difference is more important than memorizing a list of syntax rules.
Do Not Replace Every Method With an Arrow Function
A common beginner reaction is to use arrow functions for everything. That is not the lesson.

sections.title: A method using regular function syntax

sections.text: Regular method syntax is often exactly what you want when the method should receive its object as this. Arrow functions are useful when you specifically want lexical this from an outer context.
Interactive Practice: Fix the Callback

sections.title: Repair the Callback Context
sections.instructions: The supplied timer loses the intended this context. Fix it without changing the learner object. Use a modern pattern that makes the intended receiver clear.

sections.text: bind: Explicitly Attach this
JavaScript also provides bind, which creates a new function with this permanently bound to the object you specify.

sections.title: Bind the method

sections.text: This can be useful when you genuinely need to pass a method as a callback and preserve its receiver.

sections.title: Three useful callback strategies
sections.text: Call the method directly → learner.introduce(). Wrap the call in an arrow function → () => learner.introduce(). Or explicitly bind the method → learner.introduce.bind(learner). Choose the clearest pattern for the situation.
this Is Not Lexical Scope
This distinction connects directly to the closure lesson. Closures are about retaining access to lexical variables. Regular-function this is about the call context.

sections.title: Two different mechanisms

sections.text: The arrow callback inherits this from show(), while the ordinary variable name is resolved through lexical scope. Those are two different mechanisms working at the same time.
A Practical Frontend Example

sections.title: Component-like object

sections.text: The start method gets this from the method call. The arrow callback keeps that surrounding this, so the delayed log can still access this.title.
Practice Drill: Explain Before Fixing

sections.title: this Diagnosis Lab
sections.instructions: The code below does not print the expected learner name. Before changing anything, explain how save is called and what this will be at that call site. Then fix the callback while preserving the method itself.

sections.text: What's Being Deferred?
JavaScript has several more advanced rules around this, including constructors, classes, call, apply, bind, strict mode, DOM event handlers, and framework-specific behavior.
You do not need to master all of those today. The essential foundation is simpler: regular-function this depends on the call; arrow-function this is lexical.

sections.title: Keep the rule small
sections.text: When you see this, first identify the function type. If it is a regular function, inspect the call site. If it is an arrow function, look outward to find the lexical this it inherited.
Checkpoint Practice

sections.title: Predict these
sections.code:
1. obj.method()
→ What is this?

2. const fn = obj.method; fn()
→ What changed?

3. obj.start() where start creates an arrow callback
→ Where does the callback's this come from?

4. obj.method.bind(obj)
→ What does bind do?

sections.text: You do not need to memorize edge cases to answer these. Apply the basic call-site and lexical-this rules.

sections.label: Complete the Playground exercises and correctly predict this for method calls, detached function calls, and arrow callbacks. Fix the supplied callback bug using an appropriate pattern and explain why the fix preserves the intended context.
sections.hint: Regular function → inspect the call site. Arrow function → look at the surrounding lexical this.

sections.text: Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'What is this in JavaScript?' A strong beginner answer is: 'For regular functions, this is determined by how the function is called. In a method call like object.method(), this refers to the object used for the call. Arrow functions do not create their own this; they inherit it from the surrounding lexical context.'

A likely follow-up is: 'Why does a method lose this when passed as a callback?' Because the function is being called later without the original object-method call syntax, so the original receiver is no longer automatically supplied.

Another follow-up is: 'How can you preserve the intended this?' Depending on the situation, call the method from an arrow wrapper, use bind to create a bound function, or structure the callback so it does not depend on dynamic this.
Reflect

Think of a method that you would pass to setTimeout, addEventListener, or another callback API. Ask whether the method relies on this. If it does, what will the callback call site be, and how will you preserve the intended receiver?
When this surprises you, don't ask 'What does this mean?' Ask 'How was this function called?' That question is far more likely to lead you to the answer.
What You Should Take Away

For regular functions, this is determined by the call site. A method call such as object.method() provides the object as this, while a detached plain function call does not preserve that receiver. Arrow functions do not create their own dynamic this; they inherit this from their lexical surroundings. When callbacks detach methods, preserve the intended context explicitly with a wrapper or bind when appropriate.

exercises.title: this Predictor
exercises.brief: Predict the value of this for method and detached-function calls, then verify the behavior.

exercises.title: Repair the Callback Context
exercises.brief: Fix a timer callback that loses its intended method receiver using a clear modern pattern.

exercises.title: this Diagnosis Lab
exercises.brief: Explain why a callback loses this, then repair it without changing the original method's purpose.

quiz.question:
In this call, what does this refer to inside introduce?

learner.introduce()
options: The global object regardless of context.
The learner object used for the method call.
The function itself.
The nearest parent DOM element.
quiz.explanation: For this method call, the object before the dot supplies this.

options: The function becomes an arrow function.
The original method-call receiver is no longer supplied at the call site.
The function automatically binds to learner.
Closures stop working.
quiz.explanation: The function is now called as a plain function rather than as learner.introduce(), so the learner object no longer supplies this.

quiz.question: How do arrow functions treat this?
options: They create a new dynamic this for every call.
They inherit this from their surrounding lexical context.
They always use the global object.
They always use the object before the dot.
quiz.explanation: Arrow functions do not have their own this binding; they capture the surrounding lexical this.

quiz.question:
What does bind do in this example?

const fn = learner.introduce.bind(learner);
options: It creates a new function with this bound to learner.
It turns introduce into an arrow function.
It deletes the original method.
It prevents the function from being called.
quiz.explanation: bind returns a new function whose this value is fixed to the supplied object.

summary: The key rule for regular-function this is call-site based: ask how the function was called. A method call such as object.method() supplies the object as this, while extracting the method and calling it as a plain function loses that receiver. Arrow functions do not create their own this; they inherit it lexically. When callbacks detach methods, preserve the intended context with an explicit wrapper or bind when appropriate.
interviewQuestions: What determines the value of this in a regular function?
What is the difference between object.method() and a detached method call?
How do arrow functions treat this?
Why can passing a method as a callback cause a this bug?
How can you preserve a method's intended this context?
What does bind do?
How is this different from lexical scope and closures?

title: Destructuring and Spread
description: Practice destructuring values from arrays and objects and using spread syntax to expand or copy data concisely in modern JavaScript.
mastery: The learner can destructure common arrays and objects, rename extracted properties when needed, use rest and spread syntax in simple cases, and recognize when a missing property produces undefined.
learningObjectives: Extract values from arrays with destructuring.
Extract properties from objects with destructuring.
Rename a destructured object property when the local variable needs a different name.
Use default values in simple destructuring cases.
Use spread syntax to create shallow copies or combine arrays and objects.
Distinguish spread syntax from destructuring syntax.
Recognize that destructuring a property that does not exist can produce undefined.

sections.text: Stop Writing the Same Property Name Five Times
Modern JavaScript often works with arrays and objects. You already know how to access their values with indexes and property names.
Destructuring gives you a concise way to pull values out of those structures. Spread syntax gives you a concise way to expand or combine them.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: Destructuring says 'take values out of this structure.' Spread says 'take the values from this structure and expand them here.'
Object Destructuring

sections.title: Extract object properties

sections.text: The destructuring pattern creates local variables with the requested property names.
Array Destructuring

sections.title: Extract by position

sections.text: Unlike object destructuring, array destructuring follows position. The first variable gets the first item, the second gets the second item, and so on.
Renaming a Destructured Property

sections.title: Property name vs local variable name

sections.text: name and level are the object property names. learnerName and currentLevel are the local variable names created by the destructuring pattern.
Missing Properties

sections.title: A missing property

sections.text: Because learner does not contain an email property, email becomes undefined.

sections.title: The misconception to catch
sections.text: Destructuring does not magically create missing data. If the property is absent, the extracted variable will normally be undefined unless you provide a default.
Default Values

sections.title: Provide a fallback

sections.text: Now the local email variable uses the fallback because the property was missing.
Drill 1: Destructure the Learner

sections.title: Destructuring Drill
sections.instructions: Extract name, completedLessons, and currentLevel from the learner object. Rename currentLevel to level where appropriate. Then extract the first two lesson titles from the array. Finally, destructure a missing email property and give it a default value.

sections.text: Spread Syntax
Spread syntax uses three dots to expand the contents of an iterable or object into another place where values can be supplied.

sections.title: Copy an array

sections.text: The copied array contains the same item values, but it is a separate array.
Combine Arrays

sections.title: Combine two collections

sections.text: Spread makes the combination readable without manually pushing every item.
Spread Objects

sections.title: Copy and extend an object

sections.text: The spread operation copies the enumerable properties into a new object, after which the new property is added.

sections.title: Order matters with object spread
sections.text: When the same property appears more than once, a later property assignment wins. That makes object spread useful for creating an updated object with a changed property.
Practice: Create an Updated Learner

sections.title: Object Spread Drill
sections.instructions: Create an updated learner object without modifying the original learner. Change completedLessons, keep all existing properties, and add currentLesson. Verify that the original learner remains unchanged.

sections.text: Destructuring and Spread Are Different Jobs

sections.title: Keep the distinction clear
sections.code:
Destructuring
→ extract values from an existing structure

Spread
→ expand values into a new structure or argument list

sections.text: The syntax looks related because both use patterns such as braces, brackets, and three dots. Their jobs are different.
A Useful Combination

sections.title: Extract, then update

sections.text: This pattern appears frequently in modern JavaScript and React: destructure the values you need, then use object spread to create an updated version of the data.
Drill 3: Build a Progress Update

sections.title: Progress Update Drill
sections.instructions: Destructure the learner's name and current lesson. Create a new learner object with completedLessons increased by one and completed set to true. Do not mutate the original learner object.

sections.text: A Small but Important Boundary
Object and array spread performs a shallow copy. Nested objects and arrays inside the copied structure are not recursively cloned.

sections.title: Shallow means shallow

sections.text: The nested preferences object is still the same underlying object. Deep copying is a separate topic and is intentionally outside this practice lesson.

sections.title: Do not overgeneralize spread
sections.text: Spread is useful for shallow copies and composition. It does not automatically deep-clone every nested value.
Quick Recall

sections.title: Before you finish
sections.code:
Object destructuring
→ property-based extraction

Array destructuring
→ position-based extraction

Object spread
→ copy/merge object properties

Array spread
→ copy/merge array items

Missing destructured property
→ undefined unless a default is supplied

sections.label: Complete all Playground drills correctly without hints. Demonstrate object and array destructuring, object and array spread, a default for a missing property, and a non-mutating object update.
sections.hint: Destructuring takes values out. Spread puts values into a new structure.

sections.text: Interview Mode
Imagine an interviewer asks: 'What is destructuring?' A strong answer is: 'Destructuring is syntax for extracting values from arrays or object properties into local variables.'

A likely follow-up is: 'What is the spread operator used for?' A good answer is: 'Spread expands values from an array, iterable, or object into another array, object, or argument position. It is commonly used to copy or combine data shallowly.'
Another follow-up: 'What happens when you destructure a property that does not exist?' The extracted value is normally undefined unless a default value is provided.
Reflect

Look at a function that receives a large object but only uses two properties. Ask whether destructuring would make the code clearer. Then look for code that modifies an object and ask whether spread would make the update easier to reason about without mutating the original.

sections.title: Concise is only useful when it stays obvious

sections.text: Destructuring and spread can make modern JavaScript much clearer. They can also become punctuation soup if overused. Use them when they make the data flow easier to see.
What You Should Take Away

Destructuring extracts values from arrays and object properties. Array destructuring follows position; object destructuring follows property names and can rename local variables or provide defaults. Spread expands array items or object properties and is commonly used for shallow copies and composition. Missing destructured properties normally produce undefined unless a default is provided.

exercises.title: Destructuring Drill
exercises.brief: Extract object properties and array items, rename a property, and provide a default for a missing property.

exercises.title: Object Spread Drill
exercises.brief: Create an updated object with spread while preserving the original object unchanged.

exercises.title: Progress Update Drill
exercises.brief: Combine destructuring and object spread to create a non-mutating learner-progress update.

quiz.question: What does object destructuring use to decide which values to extract?
options: The property's name.
The property's position in the object.
The number of characters in the property value.
The object's CSS class.
quiz.explanation: Object destructuring matches property names.

options: email becomes 'Ada'.
email becomes undefined.
The object is automatically changed to include email.
The code always throws a SyntaxError.
quiz.explanation: The email property is absent, so the destructured local variable is undefined unless a default is supplied.

quiz.question: What is spread commonly used for?
options: Copying or combining arrays and objects shallowly.
Creating a deep clone of every nested object.
Declaring CSS variables.
Changing the value of a const binding.
quiz.explanation: Spread is commonly used to copy or combine array items and object properties at a shallow level.

summary: Destructuring extracts values from arrays and objects, while spread expands values into new arrays, objects, or argument lists. Array destructuring is position-based, object destructuring is property-based, and missing properties normally produce undefined unless a default is supplied. Spread is especially useful for shallow copies and non-mutating object or array composition.
interviewQuestions: What is destructuring?
How does array destructuring differ from object destructuring?
How can you rename a property during object destructuring?
What happens when a destructured property is missing?
What is spread syntax commonly used for?
Does object spread perform a deep clone?
How can destructuring and spread work together in application code?

title: Array Methods
description: Use map, filter, reduce, and find to transform, select, aggregate, and locate data declaratively instead of rebuilding every operation with manual loops.
mastery: The learner can choose and implement map, filter, reduce, and find for common data-processing tasks, predict the resulting value, and explain why each method is appropriate for the operation being performed.
learningObjectives: Use map to transform every item in an array.
Use filter to select items that satisfy a condition.
Use reduce to combine an array into a single accumulated result.
Use find to retrieve the first matching item.
Distinguish transformation, selection, aggregation, and lookup.
Choose an array method based on the result the code needs.
Predict the output of simple array-method chains before running them.

sections.text: Your Loop Can Probably Be More Specific
You already know how to loop through an array. That is an important skill. But JavaScript gives you methods that describe common collection operations directly.

Instead of thinking only in terms of 'loop through everything,' you can start asking a more precise question: am I transforming every item, selecting some items, combining everything into one result, or finding one matching item?

sections.title: The four-question model
sections.text: map → What should every item become? filter → Which items should remain? reduce → What single result can I build from the collection? find → Which first item matches my condition?
map: Transform Every Item

sections.title: Create display labels

sections.text: map creates a new array with one result for each input item.

sections.title: The map test
sections.text: If your intended result has the same number of items as the input and each output corresponds to one input, map is a strong candidate.
filter: Keep Matching Items

sections.title: Keep completed lessons

sections.text: filter creates a new array containing only the items whose callback condition is truthy.
reduce: Build One Result
reduce is useful when many items need to contribute to one accumulated result.

sections.title: Add the scores

sections.text: The accumulator starts at 0. Each score contributes to the running total. The final result is one number rather than another array.

sections.title: The reduce misconception
sections.text: reduce is not 'the advanced version of map.' It solves a different problem. Use it when multiple items need to contribute to one accumulated result.
find: Locate One Matching Item

sections.title: Find a lesson by title

sections.text: find returns the first matching item. If nothing matches, it returns undefined.
The Four Methods Side by Side

sections.title: Choose by result shape
sections.code:
map
→ new array, one result per input

filter
→ new array, only matching inputs

reduce
→ one accumulated result

find
→ first matching item or undefined

sections.text: That result-shape test is often more useful than memorizing method definitions.
Interactive Practice: Change the Data, Predict the Output

sections.title: Array Methods Live Lab
sections.instructions: Change the lesson data and observe how map, filter, reduce, and find respond. Before each change, predict the resulting output. Then verify your prediction.

sections.text: The Classic Mistake: map When You Needed filter

sections.title: Wrong result shape

sections.text: This produces an array with one output position per input item. Items that do not satisfy the condition become undefined. That is not what the requirement 'keep only incomplete lessons' asked for.

sections.title: The correct operation

sections.text: The difference is conceptual: map transforms every item; filter selects which items survive.
Drill 1: Choose the Right Method

sections.title: Method Selection Drill
sections.instructions: For each requirement, choose the array method before writing code. Then implement it. Requirements: create lesson labels, keep high scores, calculate the total score, and find the lesson named 'Testing'.

sections.text: reduce Needs a Clear Accumulator
reduce is powerful because the accumulator can be many shapes: a number, string, array, or object. But that flexibility can also make it harder to read.

sections.title: Reduce to an object

sections.text: This works, but the accumulator is now an object. The more complex the accumulator becomes, the more important it is to explain what the reduction is building.
Drill 2: Build a Progress Summary

sections.title: Reduce Drill
sections.instructions: Use reduce to calculate the total number of completed lessons and the total lesson duration. Return an object with completedCount and totalMinutes. Test the result by changing lesson data.

sections.text: find Is Different From filter
If you need the first matching object, find is usually more direct than filter.

sections.title: Two possible approaches

sections.text: The filter version returns an array. The find version returns the first matching lesson itself or undefined. Choose based on what the caller needs.
Predict Before You Chain

sections.title: A simple chain

sections.text: First filter keeps 75 and 90. Then map transforms those two values into 80 and 95. Breaking a chain into stages mentally makes chained operations much easier to understand.
One Method Per Question

sections.title: Translate requirements
sections.code:
Create a new value for every lesson
→ map

Keep only lessons that are complete
→ filter

Calculate one total from all lessons
→ reduce

Find one lesson by id
→ find

sections.text: This translation habit is the real skill. The syntax becomes much easier once the intended result is clear.
What's Being Deferred?
You will encounter forEach, some, every, flatMap, sorting, grouping, chaining, and more complex reductions in later JavaScript work.
This lesson isolates four foundational methods. The goal is not to memorize the whole Array API. It is to reliably recognize transformation, selection, aggregation, and lookup.

sections.title: Don't use reduce because it looks clever
sections.text: A simple filter plus map can be easier to read than one giant reduce. The best method is the one that communicates the operation clearly.

sections.label: Complete the live Array Methods exercise and all method-selection drills correctly. The learner must choose map, filter, reduce, and find based on the required result rather than by trial and error.
sections.hint: Transform → map. Select → filter. Aggregate → reduce. Locate one → find.

sections.text: Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'What is the difference between map, filter, reduce, and find?' A strong answer is: 'map transforms every item into a new array, filter keeps items that satisfy a condition, reduce combines the collection into one accumulated result, and find returns the first matching item or undefined.'
A likely follow-up is: 'When would you use filter instead of map?' When the requirement is to select a subset of the original items rather than transform every item.

Another follow-up is: 'Why can reduce be harder to read?' Because the accumulator can take many shapes and the callback can contain more complex logic. A simpler combination of methods may communicate the intent better.
Reflect
Take one manual loop you have written before. Describe its purpose in one verb: transform, select, aggregate, or locate. Then ask whether one of today's methods expresses that purpose more directly.

A manual loop often describes how to process every item step by step. Array methods can make the intent more visible: 'give me the completed lessons,' 'give me the labels,' 'give me the total,' or 'give me the first matching lesson.'
What You Should Take Away

map transforms every item, filter selects matching items, reduce aggregates a collection into one result, and find locates the first matching item. Choose the method based on the result your program needs. The main mistake to avoid is using map for selection, which leaves one output slot for every input and can produce undefined values when the callback does not return a result.

exercises.title: Array Methods Live Lab
exercises.brief: Change lesson data in real time and predict how map, filter, reduce, and find change the resulting output.

exercises.title: Method Selection Drill
exercises.brief: Choose the appropriate array method for transformation, selection, aggregation, and lookup requirements, then implement each one.

exercises.title: Reduce Drill
exercises.brief: Use reduce to build a progress summary containing both a completed count and total lesson duration.

quiz.question: Which method should you choose when every input item should produce one transformed output item?
options: map
filter
reduce
find
quiz.explanation: map creates a new array with one result corresponding to each input item.

quiz.question: Which method should you choose when you want only lessons whose completed property is true?
options: map
filter
reduce
find
quiz.explanation: filter keeps only the items that satisfy its condition.

quiz.question: Which method is best suited to calculating one total from an entire collection?
options: map
filter
reduce
find
quiz.explanation: reduce is designed to accumulate many inputs into one result.

quiz.question: What does find return when no item matches?
options: An empty array
false
undefined
quiz.explanation: find returns the first matching element or undefined if no match is found.

options: map cannot work with objects.
map preserves one output position per input, so non-matching items can become undefined instead of being removed.
map only works with numbers.
map automatically sorts the array.
quiz.explanation: The requirement is selection, so filter is the clearer method. map always creates one output position per input item.

summary: Array methods provide declarative ways to process collections. map transforms, filter selects, reduce aggregates, and find locates the first matching item. Choose by the result shape you need rather than by whichever method you remember first. The important habit is to describe the operation in plain language and then choose the method that expresses that operation directly.
interviewQuestions: What is the difference between map, filter, reduce, and find?
When should you use map instead of filter?
What does reduce do?
What does find return when nothing matches?
Why can map produce an array containing undefined values?
When might a manual loop be clearer than a complex reduce?
How do you decide which array method to use for a requirement?

title: Modules and Imports
description: Practice using ES modules to split JavaScript into reusable files with explicit imports and exports, and learn to diagnose default-versus-named export mistakes.
mastery: The learner can create named and default exports, import them with the matching syntax, explain why a mismatch causes an import error, and organize a small feature across multiple modules with explicit dependencies.
learningObjectives: Export a value or function using named export syntax.
Import a named export with matching import syntax.
Create and import a default export.
Distinguish named imports from default imports.
Diagnose a mismatch between the way a value is exported and the way it is imported.
Use modules to keep a small feature split into focused files.
Explain why explicit module dependencies make code easier to reason about.

sections.text: Stop Putting the Entire Application in One File
Your JavaScript programs are getting more capable. That also means they are getting longer.
Modules let you split related code into separate files and explicitly state which pieces each file depends on.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: export makes a value available from a module. import asks another module for that value. The import syntax has to match the kind of export that was created.
Named Exports

sections.title: lessonProgress.js

sections.text: This module exposes two named exports: calculateProgress and passingScore.
Import Named Exports

sections.title: dashboard.js

sections.text: The names inside the braces identify the named exports you want to import.
Default Exports

sections.title: formatLesson.js

sections.text: A module can have one default export. The importing module does not use braces for a default import.

sections.title: Import the default
sections.code:
import formatLesson from './formatLesson.js';

console.log(formatLesson('Modules'));

sections.title: The mismatch that breaks everything
sections.text: Named export → named import with braces. Default export → default import without braces. Mixing those forms causes import errors.
Drill 1: Match the Export and Import

sections.title: Export / Import Matching Drill
sections.instructions: Repair the imports so every exported value is imported with the correct syntax. Test both a named export and a default export. Before running the code, predict which line is currently mismatched.

sections.text: Named Imports Can Be Renamed
A named import can use a local alias when the imported name is awkward or conflicts with another local name.

sections.title: Alias a named import
sections.code:
import { calculateProgress as getProgress } from './lessonProgress.js';

console.log(getProgress(3, 4));

sections.text: The export is still named calculateProgress. Only the local imported name changes.
Drill 2: Split a Small Feature

sections.title: Build the Lesson Modules
sections.instructions: Complete the three-module feature. Keep the calculation in progress.js, the formatting in summary.js, and the application entry point in app.js. Use named exports for the calculation and a default export for the summary formatter.

sections.text: The point is not the number of files. It is the dependency relationship: app.js needs the calculation and summary behavior, while those implementation details stay in their own modules.
The Common Import Error

sections.title: When the forms do not match

sections.text: The module exported one default value. The importing code asked for a named export called formatLesson. Those are different module contracts.
Do Not Blame the File Path First
When an import fails, check the export/import contract before randomly changing the path. A broken path and a mismatched export are different problems.

sections.title: A useful import-debugging checklist
sections.code:
1. Does the source module actually export the name?
2. Is it a named export or the default export?
3. Does the import syntax match?
4. Is the path correct?
5. Is the file being loaded as a JavaScript module?

sections.text: Drill 3: Diagnose the Module Error

sections.title: Module Import Debugger
sections.instructions: The application fails to load. Determine whether the problem is the export type, import syntax, or file path. Fix only the actual mismatch, then verify both imported values work.

sections.text: Modules Make Dependencies Visible
One of the most useful benefits of modules is that a file's dependencies are visible at the top of the file.

sections.title: A readable dependency boundary

sections.text: A developer reading this file can immediately see which pieces it expects from elsewhere. That is easier to reason about than relying on hidden global variables.

sections.title: Explicit dependencies reduce surprises
sections.text: Modules make relationships visible. When a file needs something, it imports it. That makes the boundaries between pieces of the application easier to understand.
What's Being Deferred?
Larger JavaScript projects introduce dynamic imports, module bundlers, package resolution, circular dependencies, and build tooling.
Those details are intentionally deferred. The essential foundation is the module contract: export what a file provides and import it using matching syntax.

sections.label: Complete all module drills correctly without hints. Demonstrate named and default exports, matching imports, and a working multi-file dependency structure.
sections.hint: Named export → import with braces. Default export → import without braces.

sections.text: Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'Why use ES modules?' A strong answer is: 'Modules let me split code into focused files and make dependencies explicit through import and export, which improves organization, reuse, and maintainability.'

A likely follow-up is: 'What's the difference between a named and default export?' A named export is imported by its exported name, usually inside braces. A default export is the module's default value and is imported without braces.
Another follow-up is: 'What do you check when an import fails?' Check the export type, import syntax, exported name, path, and whether the code is being executed as a module.
Reflect
Think about a growing JavaScript file you have written. Identify one group of functions that could live in its own module. What would that module export, and what would the original file import?

sections.title: The module boundary is a design decision

sections.text: A module should expose what other code actually needs and keep unrelated implementation details inside. The goal is not to create dozens of tiny files; it is to create understandable boundaries.
What You Should Take Away

ES modules let you split JavaScript into focused files with explicit dependencies. Named exports are imported with matching names in braces; default exports are imported without braces. Most import errors begin with a mismatch between what a module exports and what another module expects. Keep module boundaries focused and expose only what other code actually needs.

exercises.title: Export / Import Matching Drill
exercises.brief: Repair mismatched named and default imports and verify the imported functions work.

exercises.title: Build the Lesson Modules
exercises.brief: Split a small learner-progress feature across focused modules with explicit named and default exports.

exercises.title: Module Import Debugger
exercises.brief: Diagnose whether a module failure comes from export type, import syntax, or path and fix only the actual issue.

quiz.question: How do you import a named export called calculateProgress?
options: import calculateProgress from './progress.js';
import { calculateProgress } from './progress.js';
import default calculateProgress from './progress.js';
require calculateProgress from './progress.js';
quiz.explanation: Named exports are imported by name using braces.

quiz.question: How do you import a default export?
options: import { formatLesson } from './formatLesson.js';
import default formatLesson from './formatLesson.js';
import formatLesson from './formatLesson.js';
import * default formatLesson from './formatLesson.js';
quiz.explanation: A default export is imported without braces.

quiz.question: A module has export default function formatLesson() {}. What is wrong with import { formatLesson } from './formatLesson.js'?
options: Nothing; named and default imports are interchangeable.
The import asks for a named export, but the module provides a default export.
The function cannot be imported from another file.
The module must export a variable instead.
quiz.explanation: The export type and import syntax do not match.

quiz.question: What is a major benefit of modules?
options: They make all variables global.
They make dependencies explicit and help separate responsibilities across files.
They remove the need for functions.
They prevent code reuse.
quiz.explanation: Modules provide explicit dependency boundaries and make larger codebases easier to organize.

summary: ES modules let JavaScript code be split into focused files with explicit dependencies. Named exports are imported with matching names in braces, while default exports are imported without braces. The most common beginner module error is mixing those two forms. Good module boundaries expose what other code needs while keeping unrelated implementation details private.
interviewQuestions: Why are ES modules useful?
What is the difference between a named export and a default export?
How do named exports need to be imported?
How do default exports need to be imported?
How would you debug an import error?
What makes a good module boundary?
Why are explicit dependencies useful?

title: Promises
description: Understand how Promises represent future asynchronous results, work with pending, fulfilled, and rejected states, and chain asynchronous operations with then and catch.
mastery: The learner can explain the three Promise states, create or consume a Promise, use then and catch to handle fulfillment and rejection, return a Promise from a then callback to preserve sequencing, and diagnose a broken chain caused by failing to return the next Promise.
learningObjectives: Explain a Promise as a representation of a future asynchronous result.
Distinguish pending, fulfilled, and rejected Promise states.
Consume a Promise with then.
Handle rejected Promises with catch.
Return a Promise from a then callback to continue a chain correctly.
Predict the order and values produced by a simple Promise chain.
Recognize why forgetting to return a Promise breaks sequencing in a chain.

sections.text: The Result Is Coming Later
Up to now, most of your JavaScript examples have produced a value immediately.
Browser applications regularly need to do things whose results arrive later: request data, wait for a timer, read from a service, or perform some other asynchronous operation.
A Promise gives your code an object representing that future result.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: A Promise is a placeholder for a future result. It starts pending, then becomes fulfilled with a value or rejected with a reason. You attach code that should run when one of those outcomes happens.
The Three States

sections.title: Promise lifecycle
sections.code:
pending
→ operation is still in progress

fulfilled
→ operation finished successfully and produced a value

rejected
→ operation failed and produced a reason

sections.text: A Promise settles once. It can move from pending to fulfilled or from pending to rejected. It does not go back to pending or switch from fulfilled to rejected.
Create a Simple Promise

sections.title: Resolve after a delay

sections.text: The Promise starts pending. After the timer finishes, resolve changes it to fulfilled with the value 'Lesson loaded'.

sections.heading: Consume the Fulfilled Value
sections.text: Use then for success

sections.title: Read the future value

sections.text: The callback passed to then runs when the Promise fulfills. The resolved value becomes the callback's argument.
Handle Failure With catch

sections.title: A rejected Promise

sections.text: When the Promise rejects, the catch handler receives the rejection reason.

sections.title: Read the chain as a sentence
sections.text: then means 'when this succeeds, do this.' catch means 'if the chain fails, handle that failure here.'

sections.text: Promises Can Be Chained
A major reason Promises are useful is that one asynchronous operation can lead into another.

sections.title: A simple chain

sections.text: Each then callback receives the result produced by the previous step. The chain makes the sequence explicit.
The Most Important Chain Rule
When a then callback starts another asynchronous operation, return that Promise from the callback if the next step needs to wait for it.

sections.title: Correct Promise chaining

sections.text: The second then waits for loadProgress because the first callback returned its Promise.

sections.title: The chain-breaking mistake
sections.text: Starting a Promise inside then but forgetting to return it disconnects that asynchronous operation from the rest of the chain. The next then can run without waiting for the result you intended it to receive.
Drill 1: Repair the Broken Chain

sections.text: then Always Creates Another Promise
A useful mental model is that calling then gives you another Promise representing the result of that handler. What the handler returns determines what that next Promise becomes.

sections.title: Returning a value

sections.text: The first handler returns 20, so the next Promise fulfills with 20 and the next then receives 20.

sections.title: Returning a Promise

sections.text: When a handler returns a Promise, the next step waits for that Promise to settle.
Errors Propagate Through the Chain

sections.title: One catch can handle a rejected step

sections.text: A rejected Promise or thrown error moves the chain into rejection until a catch handler handles it.

sections.text: Do Not Confuse a Promise With Its Result
Calling an asynchronous function can give you a Promise object immediately even though the actual result arrives later.

sections.title: The placeholder is not the data

sections.text: result is a Promise, not the lesson object itself. You need to consume the Promise to get the eventual value.
Predict the Chain

sections.title: Follow the values

sections.text: Predict the output before running it. First 5 becomes 7. Then 7 becomes 14.
A Small Realistic Workflow

sections.title: Load data in sequence

sections.text: This is the shape to recognize: one asynchronous result feeds the next step, and one catch handles a failure path.
What's Being Deferred?
You will use async/await in the next lesson because it provides another way to write Promise-based code. This lesson deliberately stays with the Promise object and its state/chaining model.
Promise.all, Promise.race, Promise.allSettled, cancellation patterns, and more advanced concurrency strategies also come later. First make individual Promise chains predictable.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: Do not jump straight to saying 'Promises are just callbacks.' A Promise is an object representing a future result with a defined state model and chaining behavior. The next lesson will show how async/await sits on top of this model.

sections.label: Complete the Promise state, chaining, and error-path exercises. The learner must correctly return a Promise from a then callback and pass the applied Promise quiz item.
sections.hint: Pending → fulfilled/rejected. then handles the success path. catch handles rejection. Return the next Promise when the chain must wait for it.

sections.text: Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'What is a Promise?' A strong answer is: 'A Promise represents the eventual result of an asynchronous operation. It can be pending, fulfilled with a value, or rejected with a reason, and I can use then and catch to handle those outcomes.'

A likely follow-up is: 'Why do you return a Promise from a then callback?' Because returning it connects the asynchronous operation to the next Promise in the chain, so the next step waits for the returned Promise and receives its eventual result.
Another follow-up is: 'What happens when a Promise rejects?' The chain follows the rejection path and a catch handler can handle the failure.
Reflect

Think of a frontend workflow that must happen in stages: load the learner, then load lessons, then calculate progress, then display the result. Which step should return the next Promise, and where would you handle a failure?

When asynchronous code feels confusing, separate two things: the Promise object you have now and the value it will eventually settle with. That distinction clears up a surprising amount of JavaScript.
What You Should Take Away

A Promise represents a future asynchronous result and moves from pending to fulfilled or rejected. Use then to handle fulfillment and catch to handle rejection. Promise chains work because each then produces another Promise, and returning a value or Promise determines what the next step receives. The critical chaining rule is to return a Promise when the next step must wait for that asynchronous operation. Async/await is deferred to the next lesson.

quiz.question: Which sequence describes the normal Promise state lifecycle?
options: pending → fulfilled or rejected
fulfilled → pending → rejected
rejected → pending → fulfilled
pending → fulfilled → pending
quiz.explanation: A Promise begins pending and eventually settles as fulfilled or rejected.

quiz.question: What does then receive when a Promise fulfills?
options: The fulfilled value.
The original source code.
The Promise constructor.
The browser window.
quiz.explanation: The fulfillment value is passed to the callback supplied to then.

options: So the next step can wait for loadProgress and receive its result.
So the Promise becomes global.
So the browser can cache the function.
Because then only accepts numbers.
quiz.explanation: Returning the Promise connects that asynchronous operation to the next Promise in the chain.

quiz.question: What happens if a then callback starts a Promise but does not return it?
options: The next chain step may run without waiting for that Promise.
The original Promise becomes pending forever automatically.
The browser cancels the Promise.
The Promise becomes a synchronous value.
quiz.explanation: Without returning the Promise, the asynchronous operation is disconnected from the chain's sequencing.

quiz.question: What does catch provide?
options: A way to handle rejected Promises or errors propagated through the chain.
A way to turn every Promise into a fulfilled Promise.
A way to remove all asynchronous behavior.
A way to access the DOM automatically.
quiz.explanation: catch handles rejection in the Promise chain.

summary: Promises represent future asynchronous results. They begin pending and settle as fulfilled or rejected. then handles successful results, catch handles rejection, and each then returns a new Promise whose state depends on the callback result. Returning the next asynchronous Promise is essential when the chain needs to wait for it. Async/await is deliberately deferred to the next lesson.

title: Async and Await
description: Use async functions and await to write Promise-based asynchronous code in a readable, sequential style while preserving the underlying Promise model.
mastery: The learner can declare an async function, use await to receive a fulfilled Promise value, explain that async functions return Promises, predict what happens when await is omitted, and use async/await to sequence multiple asynchronous operations.
learningObjectives: Explain async/await as syntax built on top of Promises.
Declare an async function.
Use await to pause an async function until a Promise settles successfully.
Explain that an async function always returns a Promise.
Distinguish a resolved value from the Promise returned by the async function.
Predict the behavior of code when await is omitted.
Use multiple await expressions to sequence asynchronous operations.

sections.text: The Same Promise, a Different Way to Read It
You already learned Promises and .then(). async/await does not replace Promises. It gives you another syntax for working with the same asynchronous model.
The biggest benefit is readability. A sequence of asynchronous operations can look more like ordinary step-by-step code while still being asynchronous.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: async marks a function as Promise-based. await waits for a Promise inside that async function and gives you its fulfilled value. The function itself still returns a Promise.
Your First async Function

sections.title: An async function

sections.text: Even though the function returns a string in its source code, calling loadLesson() gives you a Promise because async functions always return a Promise.
await Reads the Fulfilled Value

sections.title: Wait for a Promise

sections.text: getLesson() returns a Promise. await waits for that Promise to fulfill and gives the function the fulfilled value, 'Lesson loaded'.

sections.title: await is not returning a Promise
sections.text: Inside the async function, await gives you the fulfilled value. The async function itself still returns a Promise to its caller.
The Classic Mistake: Forgetting await

sections.title: Promise instead of value

sections.text: lesson is a Promise, not the resolved lesson object. Trying to read lesson.title therefore does not give you the data you intended.

sections.title: The corrected version
The misconception to kill
sections.text: await is not optional decoration. If the next line needs the fulfilled value of the Promise, you generally need to await that Promise before using the result.
Interactive Practice: Toggle await

sections.title: Async / Await Live Lab
sections.instructions: Toggle whether await is used. Predict what each variable contains before running the example. Then observe the difference between receiving a Promise and receiving the fulfilled value.

sections.text: Multiple await Steps Read Like a Sequence

sections.title: Load the dashboard in stages

sections.text: The sequence is easy to read: get the user, then get their lessons, then calculate progress. Each step waits for the previous Promise.
async Functions Still Return Promises

sections.title: The caller still gets a Promise

sections.text: result is a Promise. To access the eventual 75, another async context can await it or a Promise handler can consume it.

sections.title: Consume the async function

sections.text: Drill 1: Convert a Promise Chain

sections.title: Convert to async / await
sections.instructions: Rewrite the supplied Promise chain as an async function using await. Preserve the same order and final output. Do not change the underlying functions.

sections.text: await Only Pauses the Current async Function

A common beginner interpretation is that await freezes the entire browser. It does not. It pauses the execution of the current async function while the Promise settles, allowing the rest of the program to continue.

sections.title: The surrounding program keeps running

sections.text: The output is A, then C, then B. await pauses run(), not the entire JavaScript environment.

sections.title: The browser does not freeze
sections.text: await gives asynchronous code a sequential reading style. It does not turn asynchronous work into blocking browser code.
Sequential vs Parallel Work
One important design question is whether asynchronous operations depend on each other.

sections.title: Sequential
sections.code:
const user = await fetchUser();
const lessons = await fetchLessons(user.id);

sections.text: This is sequential because the lessons request needs the user's id.

sections.title: Independent operations

sections.text: The requests can begin without waiting for each other. More deliberate concurrency techniques such as Promise.all are useful when multiple operations are independent.
Those concurrency patterns are not the focus of this lesson. The key point is to avoid assuming that every await automatically means 'the whole feature must wait for everything else.'
Drill 2: Find the Missing await

sections.title: Missing await Debugger
sections.instructions: The dashboard summary is receiving a Promise instead of the resolved data. Locate the missing await, add it, and verify that the summary receives the actual lesson object.

sections.text: Predict the Order

sections.title: What prints first?

sections.text: The correct order is A, C, B. Predicting this correctly means you understand that await pauses the current async function rather than freezing the entire program.
Error Handling Comes Next
When an awaited Promise rejects, the async function's execution follows the rejection path. The next lesson focuses on handling those failures cleanly with try/catch and .catch().
For now, focus on recognizing the successful flow and understanding what await actually gives you.

sections.title: Boundary
sections.text: Do not mix this lesson with every advanced async pattern. Promise.all, cancellation, retries, race conditions, and complex concurrency strategies belong later. First make async/await predictable.
Quick Mental Checklist

sections.title: When you see async/await
sections.code:
Is the function marked async?
→ It returns a Promise.

Is await used on a Promise?
→ The async function waits for that Promise and receives its fulfilled value.

Is await missing?
→ The variable may hold the Promise itself instead of its resolved value.

Are there multiple awaits?
→ Ask whether the operations depend on one another or can begin independently.

sections.label: Complete the live async/await example and missing-await exercises. The learner must correctly predict the output difference when await is removed and pass the applied quiz item.
sections.hint: async function → Promise. await → fulfilled value inside the async function. No await → you still have the Promise object.

sections.text: Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'What is async/await?' A strong answer is: 'async/await is syntax built on Promises that lets asynchronous control flow be written in a more sequential style. An async function returns a Promise, and await waits for a Promise inside that function and gives you its fulfillment value.'
A likely follow-up is: 'What happens if you forget await?' The variable receives the Promise rather than its resolved value, so using it like the final data can produce incorrect results.
Another follow-up is: 'Does await block the browser?' No. It suspends the current async function until the Promise settles; it does not freeze the JavaScript environment.
Reflect

Think about a feature that loads several pieces of data. Which operations truly depend on earlier results? Which ones could start independently? The distinction will become important when you start working with more advanced asynchronous workflows.
async/await makes asynchronous code look sequential. It does not make the underlying operation synchronous. Keeping that distinction clear will save you from a lot of debugging later.
What You Should Take Away

async/await is syntax built on top of Promises. An async function always returns a Promise. Inside it, await waits for a Promise to settle successfully and provides its fulfillment value. Forgetting await means your variable may contain the Promise itself rather than the resolved data. await pauses only the current async function; it does not freeze the browser or the rest of the program.

quiz.question: What does an async function return?
options: Always a Promise.
Always a string.
Only the final resolved value.
Nothing.
quiz.explanation: An async function always returns a Promise.

quiz.question: What does await give you inside an async function when the Promise fulfills?
options: The Promise object itself.
The fulfilled value.
A callback function.
The browser window.
quiz.explanation: await evaluates to the fulfillment value of the Promise.

options: fetchLesson can never return a Promise.
lesson is probably a Promise rather than the resolved lesson object.
async functions cannot contain const.
The browser automatically converts the Promise into an object.
quiz.explanation: Without await, the variable receives the Promise itself instead of its eventual fulfillment value.

quiz.question: What does await actually pause?
options: The entire browser.
The entire JavaScript runtime.
The current async function until the awaited Promise settles.
Every event listener on the page.
quiz.explanation: await suspends execution of the current async function; it does not block the rest of the JavaScript environment.

quiz.question: Why might you avoid blindly putting await before every asynchronous operation?
options: await is invalid more than once in a function.
Some operations are independent and can begin concurrently rather than unnecessarily waiting for each other.
await always creates errors.
Promises cannot be used more than once.
quiz.explanation: Independent asynchronous work may be started without serializing it unnecessarily; more advanced concurrency patterns build on this idea.

summary: async/await provides a readable syntax for working with Promises. async functions always return Promises, while await pauses the current async function until an awaited Promise fulfills and gives the function that value. Forgetting await leaves the variable holding the Promise itself. The underlying work remains asynchronous; await does not block the browser. More advanced concurrency and failure handling are deferred to later lessons.

title: Error Handling
description: Practice handling failures in synchronous and asynchronous JavaScript with try/catch and Promise catch, while making sure error handling provides useful recovery or user-facing feedback.
mastery: The learner can use try/catch to handle synchronous failures, use catch for rejected Promise chains, distinguish throwing from handling an error, and provide a meaningful fallback or user-facing response instead of merely swallowing the failure.
learningObjectives: Use try/catch to handle a synchronous JavaScript error.
Use catch to handle a rejected Promise or async failure.
Explain the difference between throwing an error and handling an error.
Provide meaningful fallback behavior when an operation fails.
Preserve useful diagnostic information while handling failures.
Recognize when an error should be allowed to propagate rather than silently ignored.
Handle expected failure states without making the application appear successful when it is not.

sections.text: Your Program Will Fail. Plan for It.
A frontend application depends on things that can go wrong: invalid input, unavailable data, rejected Promises, unexpected values, and operations that simply cannot complete.
The goal of error handling is not to pretend those failures never happened.
The goal is to respond deliberately: recover when recovery is possible, tell the user what matters, and preserve enough information to diagnose what happened.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: try contains code that may fail. catch handles the failure. Your handling should answer a practical question: what should the program do now that this operation did not succeed?
Synchronous Errors: try/catch

sections.title: Catch a synchronous failure

sections.text: The code inside try throws a SyntaxError. Control moves to catch, where the failure can be handled.
catch Receives the Error

sections.title: Inspect the failure

sections.text: The caught value gives you information about what went wrong. In real applications, that information should usually be useful to developers while the user receives a simpler explanation.

sections.title: Catching is not fixing
sections.text: Wrapping code in try/catch and then doing nothing is not meaningful error handling. If the application cannot continue, it should communicate that fact or take an appropriate fallback path.
A Meaningful Recovery

sections.title: Provide a fallback

sections.text: The function does not pretend the input was valid. It logs the real failure and deliberately returns a safe fallback.
Asynchronous Errors: Promise catch

sections.title: Handle a rejected Promise

sections.text: A Promise rejection moves into the catch handler. This is the Promise-chain equivalent of providing a failure path.
async/await and try/catch

sections.title: Handle an awaited rejection

sections.text: Because await works with Promises, a rejected Promise can be caught by wrapping the await operation in try/catch.

sections.title: The three forms to recognize
sections.text: Synchronous failure → try/catch. Promise chain failure → .catch(). async/await failure → try/catch around the awaited operation.
Interactive Practice: Choose the Failure Path

sections.title: Error Handling Live Lab
sections.instructions: Toggle between synchronous and asynchronous failure. Identify which error-handling pattern fits each case, then observe the fallback message. The application should never report success when the operation failed.

sections.text: Don't Swallow the Error

sections.title: Technically caught, practically broken

sections.text: This code is dangerous because a failed save can still produce a success message. The application has hidden the failure instead of handling it.

sections.title: Handle the failure honestly

sections.text: The caller can now distinguish success from failure and decide what the user should see.
Drill 1: Fix the False Success

sections.title: Error Recovery Drill
sections.instructions: The supplied save function incorrectly reports success after a rejected Promise. Fix the function so failure is represented honestly and the caller can show an appropriate message.

sections.text: Throw When the Current Layer Cannot Continue
Sometimes a function should not invent a fallback. It should report the problem to its caller so the appropriate layer can decide what to do.

sections.title: Let the caller decide

sections.text: The lower-level function defines the failure condition. The caller decides how to present or recover from it.

sections.title: Handle at the right layer
sections.text: Do not catch an error merely because you can. Catch it where you can make a meaningful decision about recovery, fallback, logging, or user feedback.
Drill 2: Propagate the Right Failure

sections.title: Error Propagation Drill
sections.instructions: The parser should reject invalid lesson data, but the UI layer should decide what message to show. Make the lower-level function throw and let the caller handle it.

sections.text: Error Messages: Developer vs User
A technical error message such as 'Unexpected token } in JSON at position 14' may be useful to a developer but is not a good user-facing message.

sections.title: Two layers
sections.code:
Developer information
→ exact error, stack, request details, diagnostic context

User information
→ what happened and what they can do next

sections.text: A robust application often records the technical details while presenting a concise, useful message to the user.
Do Not Hide Unexpected Bugs
There is a difference between handling an expected operational failure and silently catching every unexpected programming error.

sections.title: Too broad and too quiet

sections.text: This can make real bugs harder to discover because the failure disappears without useful evidence.
A better approach is to handle failures where the application has enough context to respond meaningfully and preserve diagnostics for unexpected conditions.
A Practical Error-Handling Checklist

sections.title: Before you catch
sections.code:
What can fail here?

Is the failure expected or exceptional?

Can this layer recover?

Should the error be propagated to a caller?

What should the user see?

What information does a developer need to diagnose the failure?

After handling it, is the program still telling the truth about its state?

sections.text: That last question is particularly important. If saving failed, do not show 'Saved.' If loading failed, do not render an empty success state and pretend nothing happened.
What's Being Deferred?
More advanced applications need patterns for retries, cancellation, custom error classes, error boundaries, global error reporting, and network-specific recovery strategies.
Those are deliberately deferred. This lesson is about the core decision: catch a failure where you can do something useful, otherwise let the failure propagate to a layer that can.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: Error handling is not 'make the red message disappear.' It is a control-flow decision about what the application should do when the expected operation does not succeed.

sections.label: Complete all error-handling drills correctly without hints. The learner must handle both synchronous and asynchronous failures and demonstrate meaningful recovery or propagation rather than swallowing the error.
sections.hint: Handle where you can make a useful decision. Preserve diagnostic information. Never report success when the operation failed.

sections.text: Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'How do you handle errors in JavaScript?' A strong answer is: 'For synchronous failures I can use try/catch. For rejected Promise chains I can use catch, and for async/await I can wrap awaited operations in try/catch. I handle the error at the layer that can make a useful recovery or user-facing decision, while preserving diagnostic information.'

A likely follow-up is: 'Should you catch every error?' No. Catching every error and doing nothing can hide programming bugs. Catch where you can recover meaningfully or where the application needs to turn the failure into a deliberate result.

Another follow-up: 'What is a bad error-handling pattern?' Catching an error and then reporting success anyway, or silently ignoring the failure so neither the user nor the developer can tell what happened.
Reflect

Think about a failed network request in a learning application. What should the developer see? What should the learner see? What should happen to the current UI state? A good error-handling design answers all three.

sections.title: Make the application tell the truth

sections.text: The simplest reliable rule is this: after an error, the application should represent reality. Failed is failed. Loading is loading. Success is success. Good error handling helps the interface stay honest.
What You Should Take Away

Use try/catch for synchronous failures and for rejected Promises when working with async/await; use .catch() for Promise chains. Catch errors where you can make a meaningful decision, provide useful recovery or user feedback, and preserve diagnostic information. Do not swallow failures or report success after an operation failed. Error handling is about deliberate control flow, not merely hiding error messages.

.catch()
finally only
switch only

quiz.question: Where should an error generally be handled?
options: Anywhere, as long as it disappears.
At the layer that can make a meaningful recovery, fallback, or user-facing decision.
Only at the deepest function possible.

quiz.explanation: Handling is most useful where the application has enough context to decide what to do with the failure.

Why is this error handler a problem?

It silently swallows the failure and gives no recovery or useful diagnostic path.
catch automatically retries the operation.

quiz.explanation: An empty catch hides the failure without deciding how the application should recover or communicate it.

quiz.explanation: The user should receive a useful action-oriented message rather than a technical parser detail or a false success message.

summary: Error handling is deliberate control flow. Use try/catch for synchronous failures and awaited Promise failures, and .catch() for Promise chains. Handle errors at the layer that can recover or communicate the failure meaningfully. Preserve useful diagnostic information for developers, give users understandable feedback, and never allow the application to report success when an operation actually failed.

→ data calculations and selection

tracker.js
→ private interaction state

summary.js
→ readable summary generation

app.js
→ orchestration and user-facing output

sections.text: You may choose slightly different boundaries, but every module should have a reason to exist. Do not create tiny files simply to prove that you know import syntax.
Stage 2: Build the Progress Functions

sections.title: progress.js — starter

sections.text: Choose array methods based on the result required. Do not force every operation through reduce just because this is a JavaScript capstone.
Stage 3: Add Private Interaction State

sections.title: tracker.js — starter

sections.text: The interaction count should not be a global variable. The returned function should be the controlled interface for changing and reading the private state.
Stage 4: Build the Summary

sections.title: summary.js — starter

sections.text: Notice the destructured parameter. The summary function receives a configuration object rather than a long list of positional arguments.
Stage 5: Orchestrate With async/await

sections.title: app.js — starter
Keep the async flow simple
sections.text: The app entry point should read like orchestration: load → calculate → select → track → summarize. Let the specialized modules do the work.
Stage 6: Add Honest Failure Handling

sections.title: The required failure boundary

sections.text: Test the failure path deliberately by calling fetchLessons(true). The application must not print a normal success summary after the load fails.
Stage 7: Verify the Required Array Methods
