sections.code:
Incomplete lessons
→ filter

Lesson by id
→ find

Transform lesson data for display
→ map

Overall duration / total calculation
→ reduce where it is actually useful

sections.text: You do not have to force all four methods into nonsense roles. The capstone should demonstrate that you understand their different result shapes.
Stage 8: Use Spread Without Mutating Source Data

sections.title: Create an updated lesson view

sections.text: This creates a new object while preserving the source object. Use spread where it communicates a real data transformation rather than adding it merely to satisfy a checklist.
Final Build Workspace

sections.title: Modern JavaScript Challenge
sections.instructions: Complete the Forge Lesson Progress Manager. You are responsible for the final implementation. The finished program must load asynchronously, calculate progress, identify incomplete lessons, find a lesson by id, preserve private interaction state through a closure, use focused modules, and handle a failed load honestly. Test both success and failure paths.

sections.text: Required Output

sections.title: Your program should communicate
sections.code:
Learner: Ada
Progress: 2 / 5
Progress percentage: 40%
Selected lesson: The this Keyword
Incomplete lessons: 3
Interactions: 1

Then, when the load fails:
Could not load the lesson dashboard: Lesson service unavailable

sections.text: The exact wording can differ. The important part is that the data is correct, the success path is coherent, and the failure path is truthful.
Code Review Pass

sections.title: Review your own implementation
sections.code:
MODULES
□ Does each module have a clear responsibility?
□ Are named/default imports matched correctly?

CLOSURE
□ Is interaction state actually private?
□ Can outside code modify it directly?

ARRAY METHODS
□ Did I choose methods based on result shape?
□ Did I avoid unnecessary reduce complexity?

ASYNC
□ Is async/await used consistently?
□ Did I avoid forgetting await?
□ Did I test the failure path?

ERROR HANDLING
□ Does failed loading stay visibly failed?
□ Did I preserve useful diagnostics?

DATA
□ Did I avoid unnecessary mutation?
□ Did I use destructuring/spread where it improves clarity?

sections.text: Architecture Review

Now pretend another developer inherits the project. Can they find the data source? Can they find the async boundary? Can they locate the progress calculation? Can they understand where the interaction count lives?
A capstone is not only proof that the program works. It is proof that the concepts can coexist without turning the code into a single enormous function.

sections.title: Avoid the mixed-async soup
sections.text: Do not use callbacks in one line, Promise chains in another, and async/await for the next operation just because all three are available. Pick a coherent style for the feature and use it consistently.
Debugging Prompts

sections.title: When your implementation breaks
sections.code:
Import error?
→ Check named vs default export syntax.

Selected lesson is undefined?
→ Check find and the id being passed.

Progress is wrong?
→ Inspect the input collection before changing the calculation.

Summary receives a Promise?
→ Find the missing await.

Failure prints success?
→ Inspect the catch path.

Interaction count resets?
→ Check whether the closure is recreated on every call.

sections.text: These debugging prompts intentionally point back to the lessons you just completed. The challenge should make you retrieve those concepts rather than presenting them as isolated trivia.
Project Rubric

sections.title: Evaluation
sections.code:
FUNCTIONALITY — 30%
- Loads lesson data.
- Calculates correct progress.
- Finds the requested lesson.
- Lists incomplete lessons.
- Produces the required summary.

JAVASCRIPT CONCEPTS — 30%
- Closure is used for private interaction state.
- Array methods match the tasks.
- Destructuring/spread are used appropriately.
- ES modules are used correctly.

ASYNC + ERRORS — 25%
- async/await is used coherently.
- Missing await bugs are avoided.
- Failure is handled without false success.

CODE QUALITY — 15%
- Modules have clear responsibilities.
- Names are understandable.
- No unnecessary complexity.
- The implementation is explainable to another developer.

sections.text: Root-Cause Reflection
After the feature works, identify one bug you encountered during the build and explain it using the debugging pattern from Module 1-4.
Interview Mode

Imagine the interviewer asks: 'Walk me through your architecture.' You should be able to explain why the asynchronous data access is separated from data calculations, why the interaction tracker uses a closure, why each array method was chosen, and why the entry point owns the orchestration.

A likely follow-up is: 'Why didn't you keep all the code in one file?' The answer is not 'because modules are modern.' It is because each responsibility has a useful boundary and explicit dependencies make the feature easier to understand and change.

Another follow-up: 'Why use async/await rather than mixing Promise styles?' Because consistency improves readability. The feature has one clear asynchronous control-flow style, while the underlying operations remain Promise-based.
Module Reflection

Module 2-2 began with individual language mechanics and ended with a feature built from them. That progression is deliberate. Knowing what a closure is matters less than being able to use one when a feature needs private state. Knowing map exists matters less than choosing it because the feature needs transformation.
The goal is not to collect syntax. It is to build the habit of choosing language features because they solve a specific problem.

sections.title: Module 2-2 complete
sections.text: You can now combine modern JavaScript language features into a coherent feature: organize code with modules, preserve state with closures, transform data with array methods, manage asynchronous operations with async/await, and handle failure deliberately.

sections.label: Submit the completed Modern JavaScript Challenge. The project must meet the functionality, concept, async/error-handling, and code-quality rubric and include a root-cause reflection for one bug encountered during the build.
sections.hint: Build in layers. Make each module work independently, then connect them through app.js.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

Modern JavaScript becomes valuable when the features work together. Modules create boundaries, closures preserve private state, array methods express data operations, destructuring and spread keep data flow concise, async/await coordinates asynchronous work, and error handling keeps the application truthful when something fails. The capstone is about combining these tools deliberately rather than demonstrating syntax in isolation.

options: To make it a global variable.

To make the count reset on every call.
Because closures are required for array methods.

options: Which method has the shortest name.
The result the operation needs to produce.

quiz.explanation: Choose map, filter, find, or reduce according to the transformation, selection, lookup, or aggregation result required.

quiz.explanation: The user-facing application needs to represent failed loading honestly and provide an appropriate response.

summary: The Modern JavaScript Challenge combines the module's core concepts into one realistic feature. The learner builds explicit module boundaries, uses a closure for private interaction state, applies array methods according to result shape, uses destructuring and spread appropriately, coordinates asynchronous work with async/await, and handles failed loading honestly. The final goal is not syntax coverage but deliberate feature design and explainable code.

title: Why Version Control Exists
description: Understand why developers use version control to track change history, collaborate safely, roll back mistakes, and work on parallel changes through branches.
mastery: The learner can explain what version control is, describe how change history and rollback help development, explain why Git is more than a backup system, and connect branches to parallel work and collaboration.
learningObjectives: Explain what version control tracks.
Explain why a project benefits from a history of changes.
Describe how version control supports rollback and recovery.
Explain how version control supports collaboration.
Explain the role of branches in parallel development.
Distinguish version control from simply keeping backup copies.
Explain why version control is especially valuable in frontend projects.

sections.text: What Happens When Your Code Changes Every Day?
A project starts with a working version. Then you add a feature. Then you redesign a component. Then you try another approach. Then someone says, 'The version from yesterday was actually better.'
Without a reliable history, you are left trying to remember what changed, which files were involved, and which version was working.
Version control exists to make that history part of the development process.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: Version control records meaningful changes to a project so you can understand how the project evolved, return to earlier states, and coordinate work with other developers.
Think of It as a Timeline, Not a Backup Folder
Imagine keeping copies of your project like this:

sections.title: The backup-folder approach
sections.code:
project-final.zip
project-final-2.zip
project-final-new.zip
project-final-new-real.zip
project-final-new-real-USE-THIS.zip

sections.text: You have copies, but you do not have a useful model of how the project changed.

A version-control system records a sequence of intentional changes. That history can answer questions such as: what changed, when did it change, who changed it, and what was the project state before the change?

sections.title: The misconception
sections.text: Git is not just a smarter backup system. Backups protect files. Version control gives developers a structured history of changes and tools for collaborating, comparing, branching, and recovering.
Why History Matters
Suppose a new UI change introduces a serious regression. A useful version-control history gives the team a way to identify the change and restore an earlier known-good state.

sections.title: A simplified project timeline
sections.code:
Version A
→ login page works

Version B
→ added lesson dashboard

Version C
→ changed navigation

Version D
→ navigation regression discovered

Version E
→ fix applied

sections.text: The important part is not simply that five copies exist. The sequence tells a story about the project.
Rollback Is a Development Tool
When a change causes a problem, version control can make recovery much safer than trying to reconstruct the previous code by hand.

sections.title: Professional development includes recovery
sections.text: The goal is not to write code that never needs to change. The goal is to make change safe enough that the team can experiment, detect problems, and recover without panic.
Why Collaboration Changes Everything
A solo project can already benefit from history. A team needs it even more.
Two developers may need to work on different features at the same time. Without a shared version-control model, coordinating those changes becomes much harder.
Branches Let Work Develop in Parallel
A branch provides a separate line of development within the repository's history. Teams can use branches so a feature can be developed without immediately changing the main line of work.

sections.title: Parallel development
sections.code:
main
│
├── feature/login
│   └── login changes
│
└── feature/progress
    └── progress dashboard changes

sections.text: The branches can later be integrated into the main line using the team's chosen workflow.

sections.title: Branching is about managing change
sections.text: A branch is not merely a second copy of the project. It is a separate line of development that lets changes evolve independently before they are integrated.
Version Control Makes Collaboration Traceable
In a shared project, it matters that changes have context. A team should be able to understand which change introduced a feature or a bug rather than relying entirely on memory.

sections.title: Useful history questions
sections.code:
What changed?
Who made the change?
When was it made?
Why was it made?
What was the project like before it?

sections.text: Those questions become increasingly important as a project grows.
Why Frontend Developers Need This
Frontend work changes quickly. A seemingly small CSS or JavaScript modification can affect many parts of an interface.
Version control gives frontend developers a safety net for those changes while also creating the collaboration structure used by professional teams.

sections.title: Frontend example
sections.code:
Monday
→ refactor lesson cards

Tuesday
→ update responsive Grid

Wednesday
→ redesign button states

Thursday
→ regression appears in mobile layout

Version history helps identify which change needs investigation.

sections.text: What Version Control Does Not Replace
Version control is powerful, but it does not replace backups, testing, code review, deployment practices, or good communication.

sections.title: Different tools, different jobs
sections.code:
Version control
→ history, collaboration, branching, recovery

Backups
→ protection against loss or infrastructure failure

Testing
→ evidence that behavior still works

Code review
→ another human checks a proposed change

sections.text: A professional development workflow uses these ideas together rather than treating Git as the solution to every project-management problem.
A Useful Analogy

sections.title: Think of a project's history like a film editing timeline
sections.text: The project is the film. Each intentional change is an editing decision. Version control lets the team understand the sequence of edits, compare states, develop alternative cuts, and return to an earlier point when necessary.
Recall Check

sections.title: Answer these without notes
sections.code:
1. What problem does version control solve?
2. Why is Git more than a backup system?
3. How does version history help when a bug appears?
4. Why are branches useful to a team?

sections.text: A strong answer connects all four: version control records project history, makes changes traceable, supports recovery and rollback, and allows different lines of development to progress in parallel.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'Why do developers use Git?' A strong answer is: 'Git gives the team a history of project changes, makes collaboration safer, supports parallel development through branches, and provides ways to compare or recover earlier states.'
A likely follow-up is: 'Is Git just a backup tool?' No. Backups protect copies of files, while Git provides structured change history and collaboration workflows.
Another follow-up is: 'Why use branches?' Branches let developers work on changes independently and integrate those changes into the main development line later.
Reflect

Think about a project where you have ever been afraid to change working code because you might break it. What would change psychologically if you knew you had a trustworthy history and could identify or recover the previous state?

sections.title: The deeper reason Git exists
sections.text: Version control makes change less frightening. Teams can experiment because changes are traceable, collaboration has structure, and recovery is possible.

sections.label: Explain version control in your own words and correctly answer why Git is more than a backup system, how history helps recovery, and why branches support parallel work.
sections.hint: Think: history → traceability → recovery → collaboration → branches.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

Version control records meaningful project changes so developers can understand history, compare states, recover from mistakes, and collaborate safely. Git is more than backup because it provides structured history, branching, and collaboration workflows. Branches allow parallel lines of development, making it easier for teams to develop and integrate changes without constantly disrupting the main line.

exercises.brief: Explain the difference between version control and backups, then describe how history and branches help a team.

exercises.title: Collaboration Scenario

quiz.question: What is the main purpose of version control?
options: To store a second copy of the project with no change history.
To track project changes so they can be understood, collaborated on, and recovered when necessary.
To automatically fix programming bugs.
To replace testing.
quiz.explanation: Version control provides structured change history and supports collaboration and recovery.

quiz.question: Why is Git more than a backup system?
options: It compresses JavaScript better than a ZIP file.
It records structured history and supports comparison, branching, collaboration, and recovery.
It prevents all bugs.
It removes the need for code review.
quiz.explanation: Backups protect copies; version control provides a development history and tools around that history.

quiz.question: Why are branches useful?
options: They allow separate lines of development to progress without immediately changing the main line.
They permanently duplicate the entire team.
They replace commits.
They automatically deploy every change.
quiz.explanation: Branches support parallel development and later integration.

quiz.question: A regression appears after several frontend changes. How can version history help?
options: It guarantees the browser will fix the regression.
It can help the team identify which changes occurred and return to an earlier known state when appropriate.
It automatically identifies the exact CSS selector every time.
It deletes all changes after the regression.
quiz.explanation: History provides a trace of changes that can support investigation and recovery.

summary: Version control records meaningful changes to a project so developers can understand history, compare states, recover from mistakes, and collaborate safely. Git is not simply a backup system: its value comes from structured history, branching, and collaboration workflows. Branches allow parallel development, while version history makes changes traceable and recovery more deliberate.

title: Git Fundamentals
description: Practice the core local Git workflow by initializing a repository, inspecting changes, staging files, creating meaningful commits, and reading project history.
mastery: The learner can initialize a repository, use status to inspect its state, stage the intended changes, create a descriptive commit, and use log to inspect the resulting history while explaining what each step accomplishes.
learningObjectives: Initialize a Git repository.
Use git status to understand the current repository state.
Stage selected changes with git add.
Create commits with descriptive messages using git commit.
Use git log to inspect commit history.
Explain the difference between the working tree, staging area, and committed history.
Choose commit messages that describe the meaningful change rather than vague activity.

sections.text: Now Use Git Instead of Just Talking About It
The previous lesson established why version control matters. Now you are going to perform the smallest useful Git workflow on a local project.
The workflow is deliberately simple:

sections.title: The core local cycle
sections.code:
edit files
   ↓
git status
   ↓
git add
   ↓
git commit
   ↓
git log

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: Git gives you three useful places to think about: the working tree contains your current file changes, the staging area contains changes selected for the next commit, and the repository history contains commits that have already been recorded.
Step 1: Initialize a Repository

sections.title: Start Git tracking
sections.code: git init

sections.text: git init creates the repository metadata needed for Git to start tracking the project. You normally run it once at the root of a project.
Step 2: Ask Git What Is Happening

sections.title: Inspect repository state
sections.code: git status

sections.text: git status is one of the commands you will use constantly. It tells you about the current branch, changes in the working tree, and what is staged or not staged.

sections.title: Use status before making assumptions
sections.text: When you are unsure what Git thinks is happening, run git status. It is usually faster than guessing which files are staged, modified, or untracked.
Step 3: Stage a Change

sections.title: Stage one file
sections.code: git add index.html

sections.text: git add places the selected change into the staging area. Think of staging as choosing what should be included in the next snapshot.
The Staging Area Matters

sections.title: Three places
sections.code:
Working tree
→ files currently changed on disk

Staging area
→ changes selected for the next commit

Repository history
→ commits already recorded

sections.text: This separation gives you control. You can have several changes in your working tree while choosing only some of them for the next commit.
Step 4: Commit the Staged Change

sections.title: Record a snapshot
sections.code: git commit -m "Add lesson dashboard structure"

sections.text: A commit records the staged changes in Git history along with metadata such as the commit message and author information.
Commit Messages Should Tell a Story

sections.title: Vague vs useful
sections.code:
Vague:
fix stuff
changes
update
asdf

Useful:
Add lesson dashboard structure
Fix mobile navigation overflow
Add completed-state styling to lesson cards

sections.text: A useful commit message tells another developer what meaningful change the commit represents.

sections.title: The misconception to kill
sections.text: A commit message is not a diary entry about your mood or a description of every file you touched. It should identify the meaningful change represented by that snapshot.
Step 5: Read the History

sections.title: Inspect commits
sections.code: git log

sections.text: git log lets you inspect the repository history. You can see previous commits, their messages, and other metadata.
Interactive Practice: Live Git State

sections.title: Git Fundamentals Playground
sections.instructions: Use the available controls to simulate editing a project, staging specific files, committing them, and inspecting history. Change 1–2 files at a time and predict what git status and git log should show before checking.
sections.initialCode:
Repository state:

Branch: main
Working tree:
- index.html (modified)
- styles.css (modified)
- app.js (unmodified)

Staging area:
- empty

History:
- Add starter project

Your tasks:
1. Stage only index.html.
2. Commit it with a descriptive message.
3. Inspect the status.
4. Stage styles.css.
5. Commit that change.
6. Inspect the history.

Predict each state change before applying it.

sections.text: Drill 1: The Right Change in the Right Commit

sections.title: Stage Intentionally
sections.instructions: The working tree contains three unrelated edits. Stage only the changes belonging to the lesson-card styling improvement, create a descriptive commit, then confirm the unrelated changes remain outside that commit.
sections.initialCode:
Working tree:

lesson-card.css
→ improved card spacing
→ improved card border

README.md
→ added project description

app.js
→ temporary console.log for debugging

Task:
1. Decide what belongs in one focused commit.
2. Stage only those intended changes.
3. Write the commit message.
4. Explain why the other files should remain uncommitted.

sections.text: Drill 2: Diagnose the Repository State

sections.title: Git Status Investigator
sections.instructions: Read the supplied Git status output and determine which files are untracked, modified but unstaged, and staged for commit. Then decide the safest next command for each file.
sections.initialCode:
On branch main
Changes to be committed:
  modified:   lesson-card.css

Changes not staged for commit:
  modified:   app.js

Untracked files:
  debug-notes.txt

Questions:
1. What is already staged?
2. What is modified but unstaged?
3. What is untracked?
4. Which file should definitely not be committed to the project yet?
5. What command would stage lesson-card.css?

sections.text: Predict the Full Workflow

sections.title: Before you run the commands
sections.code:
You edit app.js.

What should git status show?

You run git add app.js.

What changes?

You run git commit -m "Fix lesson progress calculation".

What changes?

You run git log.

What should you now be able to see?

sections.text: The point of this exercise is to build a mental model rather than memorize command sequences.
A Minimal Real-World Workflow

sections.title: Typical local cycle
sections.code:
git status

# make an intentional change

git status
git add path/to/file
git status
git commit -m "Describe the meaningful change"
git log

sections.text: Notice that status appears before and after staging. That gives you a chance to verify what Git thinks you are about to commit.
Why Small Commits Matter
A commit is easier to understand, review, and potentially revert when it represents one coherent change.

sections.title: Focused history
sections.code:
Add lesson card styles
Fix lesson progress calculation
Add mobile navigation layout
Improve empty state message

sections.text: These commits tell a much clearer story than one enormous commit called 'finish project' that changes thirty unrelated things.
What git add Actually Means
It is tempting to think git add means 'save this file.' It does not. It stages the current content of the selected path for a future commit.

sections.title: A useful sequence
sections.code:
Edit
→ working tree changes

add
→ select current changes for next commit

commit
→ record staged changes in history

sections.text: What's Being Deferred?
Remote repositories, GitHub, branches, pull requests, merging, and conflict resolution come later in this module.
For now, keep the local workflow solid. Branching makes much more sense once you understand what a commit and repository history actually are.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: Do not try to memorize the entire Git command set. Master the core state transition: working tree → staging area → commit history.

sections.label: Complete the Git Playground drills. The learner must correctly predict repository state, stage intentional changes, create a descriptive commit, and interpret git status and git log.
sections.hint: When unsure, inspect the state first. The key cycle is edit → status → add → commit → log.

sections.text: Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'What does git status do?' A strong answer is: 'It shows the current repository state, including changes that are staged, changes that are not staged, and untracked files.'
A likely follow-up is: 'What does git add do?' It stages the selected current changes for the next commit.
Another follow-up is: 'What makes a good commit message?' It clearly describes the meaningful change represented by the commit, rather than using vague messages such as 'fix stuff.'
Reflect
Imagine your project has five unrelated changes in progress. Why might you want to stage and commit them separately instead of committing everything at once?

sections.title: Git is a communication system too

sections.text: A good repository history helps future-you and your teammates understand what changed and why. Every commit is a small piece of communication.
What You Should Take Away

The core local Git workflow is edit → inspect with git status → stage with git add → record a snapshot with git commit → inspect history with git log. The staging area lets you choose which changes belong in the next commit. Small, focused commits and descriptive messages create a useful project history instead of a pile of vague snapshots.

The current repository state, including staged, unstaged, and untracked changes.
Only files already pushed to GitHub.

quiz.explanation: git status gives you a current view of repository and working-tree state.

options: Pushes the code to GitHub.
Stages selected current changes for the next commit.
Creates a branch automatically.
Deletes the working-tree changes.
quiz.explanation: git add places the selected changes into the staging area.

quiz.question: Which commit message is most useful?
options: fix stuff
update
Add lesson card spacing styles
changes
quiz.explanation: A useful commit message communicates the meaningful change represented by the snapshot.

quiz.question: What does git log help you inspect?
options: The project's commit history.
Only untracked files.
The browser console.
The current CSS cascade.
quiz.explanation: git log displays repository history and commit information.

quiz.question: Why is the staging area useful?
options: It lets you select which current changes should be included in the next commit.
It automatically tests every file.
It permanently stores files outside Git.
It replaces branches.
quiz.explanation: The staging area provides control over which changes make up the next commit.

summary: Git's core local workflow is edit → status → add → commit → log. The working tree contains current changes, the staging area contains selected changes for the next commit, and repository history contains recorded commits. Focused commits with descriptive messages make history useful for collaboration, review, debugging, and recovery.

title: Branches
description: Practice creating, switching between, and understanding Git branches so features can be developed independently before being integrated into the main line.
mastery: The learner can explain why branches isolate work, create and switch to a feature branch, make commits on the correct branch, inspect branch state, and explain why working directly on main is risky for feature development.
learningObjectives: Explain why branches are used in Git workflows.
List existing local branches.
Create a new branch from the current commit.
Switch to a branch using git switch.
Create and switch to a new branch in one command.
Verify which branch is currently checked out.
Make a commit on a feature branch without changing the main branch's history.
Explain why feature work should usually happen on a branch rather than directly on main.

sections.text: You Have a Working History. Now Isolate New Work.
You now know how Git records commits. But what happens when you want to try a new feature without immediately putting that unfinished work onto the main line?
That is where branches become useful.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: A branch is a movable name pointing into the commit history. Creating a branch gives you another line of development starting from a particular commit; switching changes which branch your new commits belong to.
See Your Branches

sections.title: List local branches
sections.code: git branch

sections.text: Git lists your local branches and marks the currently checked-out branch. The current branch is the line of history that new commits will normally extend.
Create a Branch

sections.title: Create a feature branch
sections.code: git branch feature/progress-dashboard

sections.text: This creates the new branch at the current commit. It does not, by itself, switch your working tree to that new branch. :contentReference[oaicite:0]{index=0}
Switch to the Branch

sections.title: Switch branches
sections.code: git switch feature/progress-dashboard

sections.text: git switch changes the checked-out branch. New commits you make after switching are added to the tip of that branch. :contentReference[oaicite:1]{index=1}
Create and Switch in One Step

sections.title: The convenient command
sections.code: git switch -c feature/progress-dashboard

sections.text: The -c option creates the new branch and switches to it in one operation. Git's documentation describes this as the convenient equivalent of creating a branch and then switching to it. :contentReference[oaicite:2]{index=2}

sections.title: The habit to build
sections.text: Before starting feature work, confirm where you are. List or inspect the current branch, create the feature branch, switch to it, then make the change and commit.
What Actually Changes When You Switch?

sections.title: Branch movement
sections.code:
main
  A──B
      \
       C──D  feature/progress-dashboard

Your commits C and D belong to the feature branch.
main still points to B until changes are integrated.

sections.text: This is the practical value of isolation. The feature work can develop separately while the main branch remains at its previous state.
Interactive Practice: Branch Playground

sections.title: Branch State Playground
sections.instructions: Simulate creating and switching branches. Before every action, predict which branch will move and which commits will belong to which line of history. Then verify the state.
sections.initialCode:
Repository history:

main
A → B

Current branch: main

Task:
1. Create feature/progress-dashboard.
2. Switch to it.
3. Create commit C.
4. Create commit D.
5. Switch back to main.
6. Predict which commits main contains.
7. Predict which commits feature/progress-dashboard contains.

sections.text: Drill 1: Work in Isolation

sections.title: Feature Branch Drill
sections.instructions: You need to add a mobile progress panel while another developer is preparing a stable main branch. Create a feature branch, make two logical commits on it, then inspect what main contains before integration.
sections.initialCode:
Starting state:

main
A → B

Requirements:
- Create a branch named feature/mobile-progress.
- Switch to it.
- Commit C: Add mobile progress structure.
- Commit D: Add mobile progress styling.
- Switch back to main.
- Explain why C and D are not part of main yet.

sections.text: Drill 2: You Are on the Wrong Branch

sections.title: Branch Safety Drill
sections.instructions: You intended to work on feature/lesson-search, but the repository is currently on main. Do not make a commit on main. Identify the current branch, switch/create the correct feature branch, then make the change.
sections.initialCode:
Current repository state:

* main
  feature/lesson-search

You are about to edit:
search.js

Task:
1. Identify the current branch.
2. Move to feature/lesson-search.
3. Make the search change.
4. Commit it with a descriptive message.
5. Explain why committing before step 2 would be risky.

sections.text: Why Working Directly on main Is Risky
The problem is not that main is cursed. The problem is that teams often treat the main branch as the shared integration line for stable or reviewable work.

sections.title: The risky workflow
sections.code:
main
→ start unfinished feature
→ commit half-finished code
→ another developer pulls it
→ feature is still broken
→ everyone is now debugging shared unfinished work

sections.text: A feature branch gives the work a place to evolve independently before the team decides to integrate it.

sections.title: The misconception to kill
sections.text: Branching is not ceremony for its own sake. The purpose is isolation. If unfinished feature work goes directly onto a shared main branch, the team loses part of the safety that branches are designed to provide.
Branch Names Communicate Intent

sections.title: Useful examples
sections.code:
feature/lesson-search
feature/mobile-progress
fix/navigation-overflow
fix/form-validation

sections.text: The exact naming convention belongs to the team. The useful principle is that a branch name should tell another developer what kind of work is happening there.
Inspect Before You Commit

sections.title: Safety check
sections.code:
git status
git branch

sections.text: The first command helps you understand working-tree state. The second helps you confirm which branch exists and which one is current.
Branch and Commit Are Different Concepts
A commit is a recorded snapshot in history. A branch is a movable reference to a line of commits.

sections.title: Keep the distinction clear
sections.code:
Commit
→ a recorded change in history

Branch
→ a named pointer that moves as new commits are added

sections.text: This distinction becomes important later when you merge branches and work with remote repositories.
What's Being Deferred?
Merging, pull requests, remote branches, and merge conflicts come next. For now, master one question: 'Where should my next commit belong?'

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: Do not think of branches as separate copies you manually synchronize. They are references into the repository history. Git handles the relationship between the working tree, commits, and branch references.
Predict the Repository

sections.title: Without running commands
sections.code:
Start:
main → A → B

Create feature/search from B.
Switch to feature/search.
Commit C.
Commit D.
Switch back to main.

Questions:
1. Where is main pointing?
2. Where is feature/search pointing?
3. Which branch contains C and D?
4. Does creating a branch automatically merge anything into main?

sections.text: The answers should now be predictable: main still points to B, feature/search points to D, C and D belong to the feature line, and creating a branch does not merge it into main.

sections.label: Complete all branch drills without hints. The learner must create and switch to a feature branch, make commits on the correct branch, inspect the branch state, and explain why working directly on main is risky.
sections.hint: Before committing, ask: 'Which branch is currently checked out?'

sections.text: Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'What is a Git branch?' A strong answer is: 'A branch is a named reference to a line of commits. It lets me develop changes independently from another line, such as main.'

A likely follow-up is: 'How do you create and switch to a new branch?' A common modern command is git switch -c feature/name. Git's documentation defines -c as creating the branch and switching to it. :contentReference[oaicite:3]{index=3}

Another follow-up is: 'Why not work directly on main?' Because unfinished feature work can make a shared integration branch unstable. A feature branch isolates that work until it is ready to integrate.
Reflect

Imagine you are about to make a change that could take three days and may require several iterations. Would you rather make those commits directly on the shared main line or on a feature branch? Explain what risk the branch removes.

sections.title: Branching is about permission to experiment

sections.text: A branch gives unfinished work somewhere safe to exist. That makes experimentation normal instead of something you have to hide from the rest of the team.
What You Should Take Away

Branches provide separate lines of development. git branch lists or creates branches, while git switch changes the checked-out branch; git switch -c creates a new branch and switches to it. New commits extend the currently checked-out branch. Feature branches isolate unfinished work so the shared main line can remain stable until the changes are ready to integrate. :contentReference[oaicite:4]{index=4}

exercises.title: Branch State Playground
exercises.brief: Simulate branch creation, switching, and commits while predicting which branch each commit belongs to.

exercises.title: Feature Branch Drill
exercises.brief: Create a feature branch, develop a feature through focused commits, and explain what remains on main.

exercises.title: Branch Safety Drill
exercises.brief: Detect that you are on the wrong branch, switch to the intended feature branch, then make the commit safely.

quiz.question: What does git switch feature/search do?
options: Creates a new commit automatically.
Switches the working tree to the feature/search branch.
Merges feature/search into main.
Deletes feature/search.
quiz.explanation: git switch changes the checked-out branch.

quiz.question: What does git switch -c feature/search do?
options: Deletes and recreates main.
Creates feature/search and switches to it.
Merges feature/search into main.
Pushes feature/search to GitHub.
quiz.explanation: The -c option creates a new branch and switches to it. :contentReference[oaicite:5]{index=5}

quiz.question: Why are feature branches useful?
options: They isolate feature work from the shared main line until it is ready to integrate.
They automatically test every commit.
They replace commits entirely.
They make backups unnecessary.
quiz.explanation: Branches provide a separate line of development for changes that are not yet ready for the main line.

quiz.question: After creating a branch from B and committing C and D on it, what does the original main branch still point to if you have not merged?
options: D
C
B
A
quiz.explanation: The new branch moves forward with C and D, while main remains at B until its history is changed through integration.

quiz.question: What is the safest question to ask before committing feature work?
options: Does Git know my favorite color?
Which branch is currently checked out?
Did I create a ZIP file?
Can I delete the .git folder?
quiz.explanation: Confirming the current branch prevents accidental feature commits from landing on the wrong line of development.

summary: A Git branch provides a separate line of development identified by a movable reference in the commit history. Create branches with git branch or create-and-switch with git switch -c, and switch between existing branches with git switch. New commits extend the currently checked-out branch. Feature branches isolate unfinished work from the shared main line, making parallel development safer and more manageable. :contentReference[oaicite:6]{index=6}
interviewQuestions: What is a Git branch?
Why do teams use feature branches?
What does git branch do?
What does git switch do?
What does git switch -c do?
What happens to main when you commit on a feature branch?
Why is committing feature work directly on main risky?
What is the difference between a commit and a branch?

title: Pull Requests
description: Follow a complete pull request workflow: push a feature branch, open a pull request with a clear description, review the proposed change, respond to feedback, and prepare the branch for integration.
mastery: The learner can explain what a pull request is, reproduce the basic branch-to-PR workflow, write a useful PR description, identify what reviewers need to know, and respond to review feedback without confusing the pull request with the merge itself.
learningObjectives: Explain what a pull request is and why teams use one.
Explain the relationship between a feature branch, a remote repository, and a pull request.
Push a feature branch to a remote repository.
Open a pull request against the intended base branch.
Write a concise PR title and description that communicate intent, scope, and testing.
Read review feedback and make a follow-up change on the same feature branch.
Explain why a pull request is a review and integration workflow rather than simply another name for a merge.

sections.text: Your Feature Branch Is Ready. Now Let Someone Look at It.
You created a feature branch, made focused commits, and kept the unfinished work away from main.
Now the team needs a controlled way to say: 'Here is the change I want to integrate. Please review it before we put it into the shared branch.'

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: A pull request proposes integrating changes from one branch into another. It gives reviewers a place to inspect the change, discuss it, request improvements, and approve or reject the proposed integration.
The Workflow

sections.title: Feature to pull request
sections.code:
1. Create feature branch
2. Make focused commits
3. Push feature branch to remote
4. Open pull request
5. Describe the change
6. Review and discuss
7. Address feedback
8. Get approval / satisfy checks
9. Integrate the branch

sections.text: The important sequence is that review happens before integration in a PR-based workflow.
A Pull Request Is Not the Merge
A pull request proposes a change. The eventual merge or other integration action is what actually incorporates that change into the target branch.

sections.title: The misconception to kill
sections.text: Opening a pull request does not mean the feature is already merged. A PR is the review and coordination mechanism around a proposed integration.
Step 1: Push Your Branch

sections.title: Publish the feature branch
sections.code: git push -u origin feature/mobile-progress

sections.text: The exact remote name and branch name can vary by repository, but the purpose is consistent: publish the local branch so the remote collaboration platform can use it as the source of the pull request.
Step 2: Choose the Base Branch Carefully
A pull request compares a source branch against a target/base branch. In a simple feature workflow, the base is often main.

sections.title: Read the PR direction
sections.code:
base: main
← changes from ←
compare: feature/mobile-progress

sections.text: Always verify the direction. A correct feature branch pointed at the wrong base is still the wrong pull request.
Step 3: Write the Pull Request Description

sections.title: A useful PR description
sections.code:
What changed?
→ Added responsive progress panel.

Why?
→ Learners could not see progress clearly on narrow screens.

How was it tested?
→ Tested at narrow, medium, and wide viewport sizes.

Anything reviewers should know?
→ Uses the existing lesson-card layout system.

sections.text: A reviewer should not have to reverse-engineer the purpose of the branch from the diff alone.

sections.title: The PR description is communication
sections.text: A good PR tells the reviewer what problem you solved, what changed, and what evidence you have that it works.
A Bad PR Description

sections.title: Too vague
sections.code:
Updated stuff.

Please review.

sections.text: That forces the reviewer to discover the purpose, scope, and validation details themselves.
Interactive Walkthrough: Open a PR

sections.title: Pull Request Walkthrough
sections.instructions: Follow the simulated workflow. Start from a feature branch with two focused commits. Push it to the remote, select main as the base branch, write a useful title and description, and inspect the resulting pull request summary.
sections.initialCode:
Repository:

main
A → B

feature/mobile-progress
A → B → C → D

Commits:
C: Add responsive progress structure
D: Add mobile progress styling

Task:
1. Push feature/mobile-progress.
2. Open a PR into main.
3. Write a clear title.
4. Describe what changed, why, and how it was tested.
5. Review the comparison before submitting.

sections.text: Step 4: Review Your Own Diff First
Before asking another person to review the pull request, read the diff yourself.

sections.title: Self-review checklist
sections.code:
Does the diff contain only the intended feature?

Are there temporary console.logs or debug files?

Are unrelated formatting changes mixed in?

Does the code match the PR description?

Did I test the behavior I claim to have tested?

Would I approve this change if someone else submitted it?

sections.text: Review Feedback Is Part of the Workflow
A reviewer may ask for a change. That does not mean the pull request failed. It means the review process found something that should be improved before integration.

sections.title: Example review comment
sections.code:
Reviewer:
'Can we avoid duplicating this spacing value? There is already a shared token for it.'

Your response:
Make the requested code change on the same feature branch,
commit it clearly,
and let the pull request update automatically.

sections.text: New commits pushed to the source branch normally become part of the existing pull request automatically.
Drill 1: Respond to Review Feedback

sections.title: PR Review Response Drill
sections.instructions: The reviewer found two issues: the commit contains an unrelated debug file, and the PR description does not explain testing. Decide what to change, make the follow-up commit, and rewrite the PR description so it accurately reflects the work.
sections.initialCode:
Pull request:

Title: Update progress

Description:
Made some progress changes.

Diff includes:
- progress-panel.css
- progress-panel.js
- debug-notes.txt

Reviewer comments:
1. Remove debug-notes.txt; it is unrelated to the feature.
2. Please describe how the feature was tested.

Task:
1. Decide what belongs in the PR.
2. Make the appropriate follow-up change.
3. Write the commit message.
4. Rewrite the description.

sections.text: Do Not Treat Review as a Personal Attack
Code review is a technical feedback loop. A request to simplify code or add a test is about the change, not a verdict on the developer.

sections.title: Professional response pattern
sections.text: Understand the concern → clarify if needed → make the change → verify it → push the follow-up commit → respond to the reviewer with what changed.
A PR Should Be Reviewable
The reviewer experience depends heavily on the size and focus of the change.

sections.title: Reviewable vs difficult
sections.code:
Reviewable
→ one focused feature
→ descriptive commits
→ clear description
→ relevant tests

Difficult
→ feature + unrelated refactor
→ formatting changes everywhere
→ vague PR title
→ no testing information
→ giant single commit

sections.text: This is why the commit practices from the previous lesson matter here. Good history improves review.
PRs Are Also a Record of Decisions

A good pull request can become useful project documentation. Someone looking back later can understand what problem the change solved, what approach was chosen, what discussion happened, and what was ultimately integrated.
What's Being Deferred?
Merge methods, protected branches, automated checks, review approvals, and more complex team workflows vary by Git hosting platform and organization.
Those details are intentionally deferred. The foundation here is the repeatable workflow: branch → push → PR → describe → review → revise → integrate.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: A pull request is a collaboration workflow, not just a button you click on a website. The technical branch and the human review process are connected.
Walkthrough Check

sections.title: Explain the sequence
sections.code:
You finished feature/search.

What happens next?

1. Push the feature branch.
2. Open a PR against the intended base branch.
3. Explain the problem, change, and testing.
4. Self-review the diff.
5. Receive feedback.
6. Make follow-up commits on the same branch.
7. Update the PR.
8. Integrate when the workflow requirements are satisfied.

sections.label: Reproduce the pull request walkthrough independently on a new scenario. The learner must choose the correct base branch, write a useful PR description, inspect the diff, and respond appropriately to review feedback.
sections.hint: Think: source branch → target branch → purpose → evidence → review → revision.

sections.text: Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'What is a pull request?' A strong answer is: 'A pull request proposes integrating changes from one branch into another and provides a place for review, discussion, testing, and approval before integration.'
A likely follow-up is: 'What makes a good PR description?' It should explain what changed, why it changed, how it was tested, and anything important a reviewer should know.

Another follow-up is: 'What happens when a reviewer requests changes?' You make the changes on the same source branch, commit them, push them, and the pull request updates so the reviewer can inspect the new version.
Reflect
Imagine reviewing a pull request with a title that says 'update stuff' and no testing notes. What information would you want before spending time reviewing the code?

sections.title: The reviewer is another user of your code

sections.text: A good pull request reduces the cognitive load required to understand your change. Clear communication is part of engineering quality.
What You Should Take Away

A pull request proposes integrating a feature branch into a target branch while providing a structured place for review and discussion. The basic workflow is push the branch, open the PR against the correct base, explain what changed and why, describe testing, self-review the diff, respond to feedback with follow-up commits, and integrate only when the team's workflow requirements are satisfied.

exercises.title: Pull Request Walkthrough
exercises.brief: Reproduce the branch-to-pull-request workflow, choose the correct base branch, and write a clear PR description.

exercises.title: PR Review Response Drill
exercises.brief: Respond to review feedback by removing unrelated changes, improving the description, and creating an appropriate follow-up commit.

quiz.question: What is a pull request?
options: A backup copy of a repository.
A proposal to integrate changes from one branch into another, with review and discussion around the change.
A command that automatically creates commits.
A replacement for feature branches.
quiz.explanation: A pull request provides the collaboration and review workflow around a proposed integration.

quiz.question: Why must you verify the PR base branch?
options: Because the base branch determines which target line the proposed changes are being compared against.
Because Git requires every PR to use main.
Because it changes the commit messages.
Because it deletes the source branch.
quiz.explanation: The base branch defines the target context for the proposed change.

quiz.question: What should a useful PR description explain?
options: Only the developer's name.
What changed, why it changed, and how it was tested, plus relevant context.
Only the number of changed files.
Only the final commit hash.
quiz.explanation: Reviewers need intent, scope, and evidence to evaluate the change efficiently.

quiz.question: What normally happens after you address review feedback on your feature branch?
options: You delete the pull request.
You make and commit the changes on the source branch and push them so the existing PR updates.
You create an unrelated new repository.
You edit the main branch directly.
quiz.explanation: The existing PR follows the source branch, so new commits pushed there update the reviewable change.

quiz.question: Why should a pull request be focused?
options: Focused changes reduce reviewer effort and make the intent and risk easier to understand.
Git rejects large files automatically.
Focused PRs are required for every repository.
It prevents branching.
quiz.explanation: A focused change is easier to review, discuss, test, and integrate.

summary: A pull request is a structured proposal to integrate changes from one branch into another. The workflow connects technical Git operations with human collaboration: push the feature branch, open the PR against the correct base, explain the problem and change, describe testing, self-review the diff, respond to feedback with new commits, and integrate when the project's requirements are satisfied.
