title: State
description: Learn how useState gives a React component local changing data, why updating state schedules a re-render, and why directly mutating state does not produce the intended React update.
mastery: The learner can create state with useState, update it with the setter, predict the resulting re-render, distinguish state from props, and diagnose code that mutates state directly instead of using the setter.
learningObjectives: Explain state as information a component remembers between renders.
Create local state with useState.
Read the current state value inside a component.
Update state with the setter function returned by useState.
Predict how a state update changes rendered output.
Explain that a state update schedules another render.
Distinguish component-owned state from parent-provided props.
Recognize why directly mutating state is incorrect.
Use updater functions when the next state depends on the previous state.

sections.text: Props Come From the Parent. State Belongs to the Component.
Props let a parent provide data to a child. But what happens when a component needs to remember something that changes because the user interacts with it?
That is where state comes in.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: State is information a component remembers between renders. When you update state with its setter, React schedules the component to render again using the new state value.
The useState Hook

sections.title: Create local state

sections.text: useState returns two things: the current state value and a function that updates that state.

sections.title: Read the declaration
sections.code:
const [saved, setSaved] = useState(false);

saved
→ current state value

setSaved
→ function used to request a state update

false
→ initial state value

sections.text: Update the State

sections.title: Setter causes the UI to change

sections.text: The click calls setSaved(true). React schedules another render, and the next render sees saved as true. The JSX then describes the Saved version of the button.

sections.title: The cycle
sections.code:
User interaction
      ↓
setSaved(true)
      ↓
React schedules a render
      ↓
component runs again
      ↓
saved is now true
      ↓
UI describes 'Saved'

sections.text: You do not update state by finding the button and changing its text. You update the component's state and let the rendered UI follow from that state.
Interactive Practice: Watch the Re-render

sections.title: State Live Playground
sections.instructions: Toggle the state and predict what the component will render before each click. Then add a second piece of state and make the UI respond to both values.

sections.text: State Is Persistent Across Renders
A component function runs again when React renders it. Ordinary local variables are recreated each time the function runs. State is different: React remembers the state value between renders.

sections.title: Local variable vs state

sections.text: Changing the ordinary variable does not tell React that the UI needs to render again. The value is also recreated the next time the component function runs.

sections.title: State remembers

sections.text: The Most Important Mistake: Mutating State

sections.title: Do not mutate state directly

sections.text: The variable assignment does not use the state setter. You changed a local binding, but you did not request the React state update that drives another render.

sections.title: The misconception to kill
sections.text: Do not mutate a state value directly and expect React to notice. Use the setter returned by useState to request the state update.
Objects and Arrays Make This More Important

sections.title: Bad object mutation

sections.text: The object itself has been mutated, but the state setter was not used.

sections.title: Create a new object

sections.text: The new object preserves the existing fields and changes the completed field. This immutable-update pattern is especially important when state contains objects or arrays.
Use the Previous State When You Depend on It

sections.title: Updater function
sections.code: setCount((current) => current + 1);

sections.text: When the next state depends on the previous state, the updater-function form makes that relationship explicit.

sections.title: Two updates based on previous state
sections.code:
setCount((current) => current + 1);
setCount((current) => current + 1);

sections.text: Each updater receives the relevant previous state value for the update sequence, which is safer than repeatedly reading a captured value when multiple updates are involved.
Drill 1: Repair the Counter

sections.title: State Mutation Debugger
sections.instructions: The counter appears stuck because the code mutates state directly. Repair it using the state setter. Then change the increment logic to use an updater function based on the previous state.

sections.text: State vs Props

sections.title: Ownership
sections.code:
Props
→ parent provides the value
→ child treats it as read-only

State
→ component owns the value
→ component updates it with its setter

sections.text: A component can receive a prop and also have its own state. The key is knowing who owns each value and which mechanism changes it.

sections.title: Props and state together

sections.text: The parent owns title. LessonCard owns expanded. That distinction gives each value a clear owner.
State Can Represent UI Modes

sections.title: Represent an interaction state

sections.text: This connects state to the earlier API lesson. Loading, error, empty, and success are all examples of application conditions that can influence what the UI renders.
Drill 2: Build a Stateful Lesson Card

sections.title: Stateful Lesson Card
sections.instructions: Add local state so the card can expand and collapse its details and toggle a saved status. Keep the lesson title as a prop. The parent should continue to own the lesson data.

sections.text: State Updates Are Requests, Not Immediate Variable Reassignment
When you call a setter, React schedules an update. You should not think of the current render's state variable as immediately changing in place.

sections.title: Current render snapshot

sections.text: The setter schedules the next render. The current function invocation still sees its current render's state value.
A Simple State Debugging Checklist

sections.title: When state does not behave as expected
sections.code:
1. Is the value actually state?
2. Am I using the setter?
3. Am I mutating an object or array directly?
4. Does the next value depend on previous state?
5. Should I use the updater-function form?
6. Which render's state value am I looking at?

sections.text: This checklist catches many beginner React bugs before you need more advanced debugging tools.
State Should Represent Data That Changes
Not every value in a component needs to be state. If a value can be calculated from props or existing state during rendering, you may not need a separate state variable for it.

sections.title: Derived value

sections.text: The percentage does not need its own state here because it can be derived from the inputs.
What's Being Deferred?
Conditional rendering, lists, events, controlled inputs, and effects will build on state in later lessons. More complex state architecture and shared state belong later in the React sequence.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: First master local state: create it, update it correctly, and understand the render cycle. Do not jump to global state libraries before you can reason about useState.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'What is state in React?' A strong answer is: 'State is information a component remembers between renders. I create local state with useState and update it with the setter, which schedules a re-render so the UI can reflect the new value.'

A likely follow-up is: 'Why can't you mutate state directly?' Because React's update mechanism is driven by the state setter. Direct mutation does not properly request the update and can create stale or inconsistent UI.
Another follow-up is: 'When should you use the updater-function form?' When the next state depends on the previous state, such as incrementing a counter or toggling a boolean.
Reflect

Take the Props lesson example. Which values should remain props because the parent owns them? Which values might become local state because the child needs to remember changes caused by its own interaction?
When deciding whether something should be state, ask two questions: who owns this changing information, and what should the UI render when it changes?

sections.label: Complete the live state Playground and both state drills. The learner must correctly use useState and its setter, repair direct state mutation, and use an updater function where the next value depends on previous state.
sections.hint: State belongs to the component. Update it with the setter. For previous-state-dependent updates, use setValue(current => nextValue).

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

State is information a React component remembers between renders. useState provides the current value and a setter that schedules an update. The component renders again with the new state, allowing the UI to reflect the change. Do not mutate state directly, especially objects and arrays; use the setter and create the appropriate next value. Keep props and state conceptually separate: props are parent-owned inputs, while state is component-owned changing information.

exercises.title: State Live Playground
exercises.brief: Change live state values and predict the resulting render, then add another piece of component state.

exercises.title: State Mutation Debugger
exercises.brief: Repair a component that directly mutates state instead of using the setter and then apply the updater-function form.

exercises.title: Stateful Lesson Card
exercises.brief: Add local expansion and saved state while keeping parent-owned lesson data as props.

quiz.question: What does useState provide?
options: A state value and a function for requesting updates to that state.
Only a mutable global variable.
A database connection.
A replacement for props.
quiz.explanation: useState returns the current state value and a setter function.

quiz.question:
Why is this incorrect?

count += 1
options: Numbers cannot be used in React.
It directly mutates a local binding instead of using the state setter to request a React update.
It creates a new component.
It automatically updates the DOM.
quiz.explanation: React state should be updated through the setter returned by useState.

quiz.question:
When should you prefer this form?

setCount(current => current + 1)
options: When the next state depends on the previous state.
Only when the state is a string.
When you want to mutate state directly.
Only inside props.
quiz.explanation: The updater-function form makes the previous-state dependency explicit and reliable.

quiz.question: Which statement best distinguishes props from state?
options: Props are parent-provided inputs; state is component-owned changing information.
Props are always mutable; state is always immutable strings.
They are the same concept with different names.
State can never affect rendering.
quiz.explanation: Props and state have different ownership roles in React's data flow.

summary: State gives a React component information it can remember between renders. useState provides the current value and a setter that schedules another render. The UI is then described from the new state. Directly mutating state does not provide the correct React update mechanism, especially for objects and arrays. Use the setter and prefer the updater-function form when the next state depends on the previous state. Props are parent-owned inputs; state is component-owned changing data.
interviewQuestions: What is state in React?
What does useState return?
What happens when a state setter is called?
Why should you not mutate state directly?
When should you use the updater-function form of a state setter?
What is the difference between props and state?
Why are objects and arrays in state usually updated immutably?
What is meant by state being a component's memory?

title: Conditional Rendering
description: Practice choosing between JSX branches with ternaries, logical &&, and early returns so components display the correct UI for their current state.
mastery: The learner can choose an appropriate conditional-rendering pattern for a UI requirement, implement ternary and && expressions safely, use early returns for larger branches, and avoid accidentally rendering falsy numeric values such as 0.
learningObjectives: Render different JSX based on current component state or props.
Use a ternary expression for two-way UI choices.
Use logical && for optional UI when the condition is guaranteed to be boolean.
Use early returns when different UI branches are large or mutually exclusive.
Choose between ternaries, &&, and early returns based on clarity.
Recognize the JavaScript truthiness behavior that can cause a stray 0 to appear in JSX.
Fix conditional rendering code that produces the wrong UI.

sections.text: Now Practice What You Already Know
You already know JSX, props, and state. Conditional rendering is the next practical step: the component should show different UI depending on those values.
There is no new mental model to memorize here. The job is to choose the clearest rendering pattern for the situation.

sections.title: The basic idea
sections.code:
state or props
      ↓
condition
      ↓
which JSX should appear?

sections.text: Pattern 1: Ternary

sections.title: Choose between two values

sections.text: A ternary is useful when there are two clear alternatives and both belong naturally in the JSX.
Pattern 2: Logical &&

sections.title: Show something only when needed

sections.text: The message appears when saved is truthy. This is useful when the false case should render nothing.
Pattern 3: Early Return

sections.title: Handle distinct whole-component states

sections.text: Early returns are especially useful when the branches represent substantially different UI.

sections.title: Choose for readability
sections.text: Two alternatives → ternary. Optional small piece → &&. Large or mutually exclusive branches → early returns.
Drill 1: Choose the Right Pattern

sections.title: Conditional Rendering Drill
sections.instructions: For each case, choose ternary, &&, or an early return. Then implement the rendering. The goal is to pick a pattern that keeps the JSX readable rather than simply making the condition work.

sections.text: The Classic && Mistake: 0

sections.title: This can render 0

sections.paragraph:
When lessons.length is 0, the expression becomes 0 &&

...

. JavaScript evaluates that expression to 0, and React can render the number 0.

sections.title: The misconception to kill
sections.text: Do not assume that && always produces either the right-hand JSX or nothing. If the left side is a falsy value such as 0, the expression can produce that value.
Fix It With an Explicit Boolean Condition

sections.title: Boolean condition

sections.text: Now the left side is either true or false, so the condition behaves as a clear optional-rendering check.
Drill 2: Repair the Stray Zero

sections.title: Fix the 0 Rendering Bug
sections.instructions: The component accidentally displays 0 when there are no lessons. Repair the conditional expression without changing the intended UI. Test both an empty and non-empty list.

sections.text: Nested Conditions

sections.title: Keep the logic readable

sections.text: This is often easier to read than deeply nested ternaries.
Ternary vs Early Return

sections.title: Compact ternary
Readable early return

sections.text: Both are valid. Once branches become complicated, early returns usually keep the component easier to scan.
Drill 3: Render the Four Data States

sections.title: State-Based Rendering Drill
sections.instructions: Render loading, error, empty, and success states from the supplied state object. Use early returns for the major states and an appropriate conditional for the empty case.

sections.text: A Small Rule That Prevents Big UI Bugs
When a condition controls whether JSX should appear, ask what values the condition can actually be.

sections.title: Before using &&
sections.code:
Can this expression be 0?
Can it be an empty string?
Can it be null or undefined?
Can it be an object or array?

If a falsy non-boolean value can appear,
use an explicit boolean condition when clarity requires it.

sections.text: Don't Make JSX a Puzzle
Conditional rendering is most useful when another developer can quickly understand which UI appears for each state.

sections.title: Readable
sections.code: {isSaving && Saving…}

sections.title: Harder to scan
sections.code:
{isSaving ? (isOffline ?

Offline

: Saving…) : null}

sections.text: When conditions become complicated, move the logic into ordinary JavaScript or use clear early-return branches.
The shortest conditional is not automatically the best conditional. The goal is to make the UI logic obvious.
What's Being Deferred?
Lists and keys are the next practice lesson. Events, forms, effects, and more advanced state patterns come later.
This lesson stays deliberately narrow: choose and apply the correct conditional-rendering pattern.

sections.label: Complete all three Conditional Rendering Playground drills without hints. The learner must correctly apply ternaries, &&, and early returns and eliminate the stray-0 bug.
sections.hint: Two choices → ternary. Optional JSX → &&, but make the condition boolean. Large mutually exclusive branches → early returns.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

Conditional rendering is simply choosing JSX based on current props or state. Use ternaries for two alternatives, && for optional JSX when the condition is safely boolean, and early returns for larger mutually exclusive branches. Be careful with expressions such as items.length && ..., because a zero length can render a visible 0. Keep the logic readable rather than making JSX unnecessarily clever.

exercises.title: Conditional Rendering Drill
exercises.brief: Choose and implement ternaries, &&, and early returns for different UI conditions.

exercises.title: Fix the 0 Rendering Bug
exercises.brief: Repair an && condition that accidentally renders 0 when an array is empty.

exercises.title: State-Based Rendering Drill
exercises.brief: Render loading, error, empty, and success states using clear conditional branches.

quiz.question: Which pattern is a natural choice when you need exactly two JSX alternatives?
options: Ternary expression
map
useEffect
reduce
quiz.explanation: A ternary clearly represents a two-way conditional choice.

quiz.question:
What problem can this create? {items.length &&

Items available

}
options: It always renders the paragraph twice.
When items.length is 0, React can render the value 0.
It deletes the array.
It creates a new state variable.
quiz.explanation: The && expression evaluates to 0 when the array is empty, and that numeric value can appear in the UI.

quiz.question: When are early returns particularly useful?
options: When the component has large, mutually exclusive UI branches.
Only when rendering arrays.
Only when using useState.
When a component has no conditions.
quiz.explanation: Early returns keep larger mutually exclusive rendering branches easy to read.

summary: Conditional rendering lets components choose different JSX from their current state or props. Ternaries work well for two alternatives, && works well for optional UI when the condition is safely boolean, and early returns work well for larger mutually exclusive states. Be careful with falsy values such as 0 when using &&, and prefer readable conditions over clever nested JSX.
interviewQuestions: How do you conditionally render JSX in React?
When would you use a ternary?
When would you use &&?
Why can items.length && ... accidentally render 0?
When are early returns clearer than nested ternaries?
How would you render loading, error, empty, and success states?
How do you keep conditional JSX readable?

title: Lists and Keys
description: Practice rendering arrays of data into JSX with map and learn why each rendered item needs a stable key that identifies the item across renders.
mastery: The learner can render arrays with map, provide stable keys from item identity, explain why keys help React track list items across renders, and diagnose the subtle bugs caused by using array indexes as keys when items can be inserted, removed, or reordered.
learningObjectives: Render an array of data as JSX with map.
Provide a key for each rendered list item.
Explain the purpose of a React key.
Choose a stable item identifier as a key.
Recognize when an array index is an unsafe key.
Explain how reordering can make index keys associate the wrong component state with an item.
Repair a list implementation that uses an unstable key.

sections.text: You Have an Array. Now Render It.
Most real React applications do not render one hardcoded card. They receive arrays of lessons, messages, products, notifications, or search results.
JavaScript's map method gives you the basic transformation you need: take each data item and produce one JSX element.

sections.title: Render a list with map

sections.text: For each lesson, map returns one li. React then uses that collection as part of the rendered UI.
The key Is Not a Visual Attribute
A key identifies an item to React. It helps React understand which item is which when the list changes.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: Think of a key as the item's stable identity in the list. React can use that identity to match the old rendered items with the new rendered items.
Good Key: Stable Item Identity

sections.title: Use the lesson id

sections.text: The id belongs to the lesson itself, so it remains associated with that lesson even when the array changes order.
The Tempting Shortcut: Array Index

sections.title: Looks simple

sections.text: This can appear to work when the list never changes order, but the index identifies the item's position, not the item itself.

sections.title: The misconception to kill
sections.text: Do not treat array index as a universally safe key. If items can be inserted, removed, or reordered, the index can point to a different item on the next render.
Why Reordering Matters

sections.title: Before
sections.code:
index 0 → A
index 1 → B
index 2 → C

sections.title: After inserting X at the beginning
sections.code:
index 0 → X
index 1 → A
index 2 → B
index 3 → C

sections.text: With index keys, the identity formerly associated with A is now associated with X, the identity formerly associated with B is now associated with A, and so on.
That can become a real UI bug when list items contain their own state or other identity-sensitive behavior.
Interactive Practice: Render and Reorder

sections.title: List and Key Playground
sections.instructions: Render the lesson list using map. First use the lesson id as the key. Then intentionally change the implementation to use the array index and reorder the list. Compare the behavior and explain why item identity is affected.

sections.text: Drill 1: Fix the Key

sections.title: Key Repair Drill
sections.instructions: The lesson list uses the array index as its key. Replace it with a stable item identity from the lesson data. Then add a lesson to the beginning of the list and reverse the list to verify that the implementation remains correctly identified.

sections.text: Keys Belong at the Array Mapping Boundary

sections.title: Key where the array is mapped

sections.text: The key is used by React to identify the item in that list. It is not automatically passed to LessonCard as a normal prop.
Do Not Expect key to Be a Prop

sections.title: key is separate from props

sections.text: If the child also needs the identifier as data, pass it explicitly as another prop.

sections.title: Pass id separately
sections.code:
<LessonCard
  key={lesson.id}
  id={lesson.id}
  title={lesson.title}
/>

sections.text: Drill 2: Separate Identity From Data

sections.title: Key vs Prop Drill
sections.instructions: The component needs the lesson id for a button handler, while React also needs a key for list identity. Pass both correctly and explain why key is not read from props.

sections.text: When Is Index Actually Acceptable?
An index can be acceptable in a truly static list where items are never reordered, inserted, removed, or otherwise changed in a way that alters their identity position.
But the important skill is not memorizing 'index is always bad.' It is recognizing whether position is actually a stable identity for the specific list.

sections.title: Ask this question
sections.code:
Can the order change?
Can items be inserted?
Can items be removed?
Can items move between positions?
Does each item have its own state or identity?

If yes, prefer a stable item key.

sections.text: Keys Help React Preserve Item Identity
Suppose each LessonCard eventually has its own expanded state. If the list reorders, React needs to know which rendered component corresponds to which lesson.

sections.title: Stable identity
sections.code:
lesson.id = A
→ LessonCard for A

lesson.id = B
→ LessonCard for B

After reordering:
B, A

React can still match:
B → B
A → A

sections.text: A stable key gives React the identity information needed for that matching.
A Practical Bug Scenario

sections.title: Why the bug can be subtle
sections.code:
List before:
[A expanded]
[B collapsed]
[C collapsed]

Insert X at the top with index keys:
[X]
[A]
[B]
[C]

The component instance associated with index 0
is now rendering X instead of A.

sections.text: This is why index-key bugs can appear only after reordering, insertion, or deletion. A simple static test may not reveal the problem.
What's Being Deferred?
More advanced list behavior, virtualization, drag-and-drop, and state preservation patterns come later. This lesson focuses only on rendering arrays and preserving item identity with keys.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: Do not treat keys as a magical performance setting. Their primary role in this lesson is stable identity for items in a rendered list.

sections.label: Complete all three list/key exercises without hints. The learner must render arrays with map, use stable item identity as keys, distinguish key from props, and repair the index-key implementation.
sections.hint: map creates the elements. key identifies each item to React. If a list can reorder, use item identity rather than position.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

Render arrays with map and give every rendered item a stable key. Keys help React identify which item is which when the list changes. Prefer a stable identifier from the item itself when lists can be reordered, inserted into, or filtered. Array indexes are only reasonable when the list's order and identity are genuinely stable. The key is used by React and is not automatically available as a normal child prop.

exercises.title: List and Key Playground
exercises.brief: Render a list with map, switch between stable IDs and index keys, then reorder the list and compare the behavior.

exercises.title: Key Repair Drill
exercises.brief: Replace an index key with stable lesson identity and test insertion and reordering.

exercises.title: Key vs Prop Drill
exercises.brief: Pass both a React key and a normal id prop correctly when a child needs the item identifier.

quiz.question: Why does React need keys for rendered list items?
options: To style the list item automatically.
To identify items across renders so React can match them correctly.
To make array.map work in JavaScript.
To pass the item's id into the child as a normal prop.
quiz.explanation: Keys provide stable item identity for React's list reconciliation.

quiz.question: Why can array index be a bad key?
options: Indexes are not valid JavaScript values.
When items reorder or are inserted/removed, the same index can represent a different item.
React refuses to render numbers as keys.
Indexes can only be used for strings.
quiz.explanation: Index identifies position rather than stable item identity.

quiz.question: Is key available as a normal prop inside the child component?
options: Yes, props.key always contains the key.
No. If the child needs that identifier as data, pass it separately as another prop.
Only when the key is a number.
Only when using arrays of objects.
quiz.explanation: key is a special React value used for list identity, not ordinary child data.

summary: Use map to turn arrays of data into JSX elements and provide a stable key for each item. A key gives React stable identity so it can correctly associate rendered items across changes. Prefer an item identifier when order can change. Index keys can be acceptable for truly static lists but become risky when items are inserted, removed, or reordered. Keys also do not become normal child props; pass the identifier separately when the child needs it as data.

resources.label: React — Keeping List Items in Order with key

Why does React need keys?
What makes a good key?
Why can array indexes be problematic as keys?
When might an index be acceptable as a key?
Does key become a prop on the child?
What kind of bug can index keys cause when a list reorders?

title: React Mini Project
description: Build a small React application that combines components, props, state, conditional rendering, and lists into one coherent feature.
mastery: The learner can build and explain a small React application using focused components, parent-to-child props, component state, conditional rendering, and list rendering with stable keys, while keeping state and UI responsibilities separated.
learningObjectives: Combine components, props, state, conditional rendering, and lists in one React application.
Create focused components with clear responsibilities.
Pass data from parent components to children through props.
Keep component-owned changing information in state.
Render different UI based on application state.
Render collections with map and stable keys.
Avoid placing all state and UI logic into one component.
Explain the data flow and ownership decisions in the finished project.

sections.text: The Module Capstone
You have now practiced JSX, components, props, state, conditional rendering, and lists with keys. This project combines those ideas into one small application.
There is no new React theory to learn here. The challenge is to decide where each concept belongs and make the pieces work together.

sections.title: The project goal
sections.text: Build a small React learning dashboard with reusable components, parent-to-child data flow, local interactive state, conditional UI, and a list of lessons rendered with stable keys.
Project Brief: Lesson Tracker

Build a mini lesson tracker for Forge Academy. The user should be able to see a list of lessons, expand a lesson to view details, mark lessons as complete, and see an appropriate message when no lessons are available.

sections.title: Required behavior
sections.code:
1. Display a list of lessons.
2. Render each lesson through a reusable component.
3. Pass lesson data from a parent into the lesson component with props.
4. Use stable keys for the lesson list.
5. Let a lesson expand/collapse its details with local state.
6. Let the learner mark a lesson complete.
7. Show different UI for completed vs incomplete lessons.
8. Show an empty state when the lesson collection is empty.
9. Keep responsibilities split across meaningful components.

sections.text: Starter Data

sections.title: Lesson data

sections.text: Suggested Component Structure

sections.title: One possible tree
sections.code:
App
└── LessonTracker
    ├── ProgressSummary
    └── LessonList
        └── LessonCard

sections.text: You do not have to use exactly this tree. The important part is that the responsibilities are meaningfully separated.
Recommended Responsibilities

sections.title: Component responsibilities
sections.code:
LessonTracker
→ owns the lesson collection and coordinates changes

ProgressSummary
→ displays derived progress information

LessonList
→ maps lesson data into LessonCard components

LessonCard
→ displays one lesson and owns its local expanded/collapsed state

sections.text: The exact ownership of completion state can vary. Make the choice deliberately and be able to explain it.
Stage 1: Build the LessonCard

sections.title: Starting point

sections.text: This component demonstrates several concepts together: props provide the lesson data, useState controls local expansion state, && controls optional details, and the completion callback lets the parent own the actual lesson update.
Stage 2: Render the List

sections.title: Map lessons into cards

sections.text: Notice the stable key. The lesson id identifies the item in the list. It is also passed separately because the child needs the id as application data.
Stage 3: Add Parent-Owned State

sections.title: Track the collection in the parent

sections.text: This is the parent/child ownership pattern from the previous lesson: the parent owns the lesson collection, while the child can ask the parent to update it through a callback.
Stage 4: Add the Progress Summary

sections.title: Derived progress

sections.text: The completed count can be derived from the lesson collection, so it does not need a second piece of state.
Stage 5: Add the Empty State

sections.title: Conditional lesson list

sections.text: This uses an early return for the major empty branch and keeps the successful list rendering separate.
Interactive Project Workspace

sections.title: React Mini Project
sections.instructions: Complete the Lesson Tracker. Build the component hierarchy, pass lesson data through props, manage parent-owned completion state, use local state for expansion, render the collection with stable keys, and provide an empty state. Test completing lessons, expanding details, and rendering an empty collection.

sections.text: Required Behaviors to Test

sections.title: Test the whole app
sections.code:
1. Initial render
→ all lessons appear.

2. Expand one lesson
→ only that lesson's details appear.

3. Collapse it
→ details disappear.

4. Mark an incomplete lesson complete
→ its status changes.

5. Progress summary updates
→ completed count reflects the new data.

6. Empty collection
→ a meaningful empty state appears.

7. List rendering
→ every lesson has a stable key.

sections.text: The Important Ownership Decision
The project intentionally includes two different kinds of changing information.

sections.title: Two state boundaries
sections.code:
Lesson completion
→ shared collection information
→ parent-owned state

Expanded/collapsed details
→ local presentation state for one card
→ LessonCard-owned state

sections.text: This is not the only possible architecture, but it is a useful example of separating shared data from local UI state.
Do Not Lift Everything Automatically
A common beginner reaction is to keep every piece of state in the top-level component. That can work, but it often makes the parent responsible for details it does not need to understand.

sections.title: Avoid unnecessary centralization
sections.code:
LessonTracker stores:
- lesson data
- completion data
- expanded state for every card
- every button's local UI state
- every presentation detail

This can make the parent harder to reason about.

sections.text: Use ownership deliberately. Shared application data may need a common owner; local presentation state can often stay close to the component that uses it.
Code Review Pass

sections.title: Review before submission
sections.code:
COMPONENTS
□ Are responsibilities separated meaningfully?
□ Is there one giant component doing everything?

PROPS
□ Does data flow parent → child clearly?
□ Are props treated as read-only?

STATE
□ Is changing data stored in state where ownership belongs?
□ Is local UI state kept local when appropriate?
□ Are state objects/arrays updated without direct mutation?

CONDITIONALS
□ Are completed/incomplete states clear?
□ Is the empty state explicit?

LISTS
□ Is map used for the collection?
□ Does every item have a stable key?

DATA FLOW
□ Does the parent own completion updates?
□ Does the child use callbacks rather than mutating parent data?

sections.text: Common Failure Modes

sections.title: If your project breaks
sections.code:
Cards do not update
→ Check the state setter and immutable array update.

Child data is wrong
→ Check the props passed by the parent.

Expanded state follows the wrong lesson
→ Check the list key.

Completion changes the wrong lesson
→ Check the id passed to the callback.

Empty state never appears
→ Check the lesson collection length and conditional branch.

Parent is enormous
→ Look for local UI state or repeated markup that belongs in child components.

sections.text: Root-Cause Reflection
The strongest project submission includes one bug you can explain clearly. A working app is good; understanding why it works is the deeper objective.
Architecture Review
Look at the finished tree. Can another developer quickly identify where lesson data lives, where completion changes happen, where one lesson is rendered, and where the empty state is decided?
That is the real test of the component boundaries you practiced throughout this module.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'How did you decide where to put state?' A strong answer is: 'The lesson collection is shared by the list and progress summary, so I keep it in their common parent. Expanded state belongs only to an individual lesson card, so I keep it local to that card.'

A likely follow-up is: 'Why not keep expanded state in the parent too?' You could, but then the parent would own presentation state that only one child needs. Keeping it local reduces unnecessary coordination.

Another follow-up is: 'Why does LessonCard receive onComplete instead of changing the lesson itself?' Because the parent owns the lesson collection. The child communicates the user's action upward through the callback while the parent performs the state update.
Reflect

Which concept in the project required the most careful ownership decision: props, state, component boundaries, conditional rendering, or keys? Explain what you would do differently if the feature grew to ten times its current size.

You have now moved from JSX syntax to a complete small React application: reusable components, explicit parent-to-child data flow, local component state, state-driven conditional UI, and stable list rendering.

sections.label: Submit the React Mini Project. The project must meet the functionality and code-quality requirements: reusable components, props, state, conditional rendering, lists with stable keys, clear ownership, and a working empty state.
sections.hint: Build from ownership: shared lesson data in the parent, local expansion state in the card, props down, callbacks up, and stable keys in the list.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

The React Mini Project is about combining the module's core ideas rather than learning another isolated feature. Use components to create meaningful boundaries, props for parent-to-child inputs, state for owned changing information, conditional rendering for UI states, and map with stable keys for collections. The quality of the project comes from clear responsibility and data flow, not from maximizing the number of React features in one file.

quiz.question: Where should the shared lesson collection usually live in this project?
options: Inside every LessonCard.
In a parent that coordinates the lesson list and progress summary.
Inside the key prop.
Only in a local variable that is recreated on every render.
quiz.explanation: The lesson collection is shared application data needed by multiple children, so a common parent is a natural owner.

quiz.question: Why might expanded/collapsed state stay inside LessonCard?
options: Because child components cannot receive props.
Because only the individual card needs that presentation state.
Because state must always be local.
Because parents cannot render lists.
quiz.explanation: Local UI state can remain close to the component that needs it when other parts of the application do not depend on it.

quiz.question: Why does LessonCard receive onComplete?
options: So it can mutate the parent's lesson object directly.
So it can request that the parent perform the completion update.
So React can use the callback as a key.
So the lesson becomes global state.
quiz.explanation: The callback allows the child to communicate the user's action while the parent remains the owner of the shared lesson data.

quiz.question: What is the best reason to keep the project split into multiple focused components?
options: To maximize the number of source files.
To keep responsibilities understandable and make the interface easier to change and reason about.
Because React rejects large components.
Because every JSX element must be its own component.
quiz.explanation: Meaningful component boundaries reduce unrelated coupling and make ownership and UI responsibilities clearer.

summary: The React Mini Project combines JSX, components, props, state, conditional rendering, and lists with stable keys into one small application. The learner must make deliberate ownership decisions: shared lesson data belongs in a common parent, local expansion state can remain in an individual card, props flow downward, callbacks communicate actions upward, and list identity comes from stable keys. The project is assessed on both functionality and code quality.

title: Events in React
description: Wire browser events to React event handlers, pass functions correctly, and practice updating component state in response to user interactions.
mastery: The learner can attach event handlers to JSX, pass a function reference correctly, use an event object when needed, and update state from a React event without accidentally invoking the handler during render.
learningObjectives: Attach event handlers to JSX elements.
Pass a function reference to an event prop such as onClick.
Explain the difference between passing a handler and calling it during render.
Write event handlers that update component state.
Access the React event object when event information is needed.
Use inline handlers and named handler functions appropriately.
Identify and repair incorrect event-handler wiring.

sections.text: Your UI Is Now Stateful. Let the User Change It.
The Mini Project gave you state and conditional rendering. The next step is connecting user actions to those state updates.
React event handling is built on familiar browser events, but the JSX syntax has one especially important rule: give React a function to run when the event happens.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: An event handler is a function that React calls in response to a user interaction such as a click, input change, or form submission.
The Basic onClick Pattern

sections.title: Pass the function

sections.text: The important part is onClick={handleClick}. React receives the function and can call it when the button is clicked.
Do Not Call the Handler During Render

sections.title: Incorrect
sections.code:
<button onClick={handleClick()}>
  Save
</button>

sections.text: handleClick() calls the function immediately while the component is rendering. That is not the same as giving React the function to run later.

sections.title: Correct
sections.code:
<button onClick={handleClick}>
  Save
</button>

sections.title: The misconception to kill
sections.text: Do not invoke the event handler when rendering. Pass the function itself so React can call it when the event occurs.
Inline Handlers Are Also Valid

sections.title: Small inline action
sections.code:
<button onClick={() => setSaved(true)}>
  Save
</button>

sections.text: Inline functions are useful when the handler is tiny and the behavior is obvious. For more involved logic, a named function can keep the JSX easier to scan.
Events and State Work Together

sections.title: Click updates state

sections.text: The event itself does not change the UI directly. The handler updates state, and the new state causes the component to render the appropriate UI.

sections.title: The interaction cycle
sections.code:
User clicks
    ↓
onClick handler runs
    ↓
state setter runs
    ↓
React renders again
    ↓
UI reflects new state

sections.text: Interactive Practice: Wire the Button

sections.title: Event Handling Playground
sections.instructions: Wire the buttons so each interaction changes the displayed state. First use named handlers. Then replace one handler with a small inline function. Predict what the UI will show before each click.

sections.text: The Event Object

sections.title: Read event information

sections.text: React passes an event object to the handler when the event fires. You can use it when you need information about the interaction, such as the current input value or the clicked element.
A Common Input Pattern

sections.title: Read the input value

sections.text: Controlled inputs will build directly on this event pattern in the next lesson.
Drill 1: Repair the Handler

sections.title: Event Handler Repair Drill
sections.instructions: The button currently invokes its handler during render. Fix the event wiring, then make the click change the status text without triggering the action before the button is clicked.

sections.text: Pass Arguments With an Inline Function

sections.title: Pass an item id

sections.text: Wrapping the call in an arrow function delays the call until the click happens while still letting you supply the argument.
Do Not Confuse These Two Forms

sections.title: Function reference
sections.code: <button onClick={handleSave}>Save</button>

sections.title: Function call wrapped for later
sections.code: <button onClick={() => handleSave(id)}>Save</button>

sections.text: The first passes an existing function. The second passes a new function that will call handleSave with the desired argument later.
Events Can Call Previous-State Updaters

sections.title: Toggle state

sections.text: This combines two previous skills: event handling and state updates based on the previous value.
Drill 2: Event + State

sections.title: Interaction State Drill
sections.instructions: Build a lesson card with a Save button and an interaction counter. Clicking Save should switch the status to Saved. Clicking the card's action should increment the counter using the previous-state updater form.

sections.text: Prevent Default Browser Behavior

sections.title: Form submission

sections.text: The event object can also be used to control browser behavior when appropriate. Forms and validation receive dedicated treatment in later lessons.
Keep Handlers Focused

sections.title: Focused event handler

sections.text: The handler should perform the behavior associated with that interaction. If it starts accumulating unrelated UI and data concerns, consider whether some responsibility belongs in another component or function.
What's Being Deferred?
Controlled inputs are next, followed by forms and validation. More detailed event patterns such as keyboard interactions and complex event composition will build later on this foundation.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: This lesson is about wiring events to functions and connecting those events to state changes. Input synchronization and form behavior come next.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'How do event handlers work in React?' A strong answer is: 'I pass a function to an event prop such as onClick. React calls that function when the event occurs, and the handler can read the event object and update state.'
A likely follow-up is: 'What's wrong with onClick={handleClick()}?' It calls the function while rendering instead of passing a function for React to call later.
Another follow-up is: 'How do you pass an argument to a handler?' Use a wrapper function such as onClick={() => handleOpen(id)} so the call happens when the event occurs.
Reflect

Take the Lesson Tracker project. Which interactions should update parent-owned lesson data? Which interactions can stay local to a LessonCard? How would the event handler communicate across that boundary?

sections.title: Events are the bridge from user action to state

sections.text: The browser gives you the event. Your handler interprets it. State changes. React renders the new UI. Keep that chain clear.

sections.label: Complete the Event Handling Playground and both drills. The learner must correctly pass handler references, repair premature invocation, use event arguments when needed, and connect events to state updates.
sections.hint: Pass the function, do not call it during render. Use an arrow wrapper when you need to supply arguments.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

React events connect user interactions to component behavior. Pass a function to event props such as onClick, use the event object when you need interaction details, and update state from the handler when the UI should change. Do not invoke handlers during render; pass the function itself or wrap an argument-taking call in an arrow function.

quiz.question: Which is the correct way to attach a click handler?
options: onClick={handleClick}
onClick={handleClick()}
onClick="handleClick"
onClick="handleClick()"
quiz.explanation: React should receive the function so it can call it when the click occurs.

quiz.question: Why is onClick={handleClick()} usually incorrect?
options: It calls the handler during render instead of passing it for the click event.
React does not support functions.
The browser cannot dispatch clicks.
It converts the function into CSS.
quiz.explanation: The parentheses invoke the function immediately.

quiz.question: How can you pass an id to a click handler?
options: onClick={handleOpen(id)}
onClick={() => handleOpen(id)}
onClick={handleOpen.id}
onClick="handleOpen(id)"
quiz.explanation: The wrapper function delays the call until the event occurs.

quiz.question: What commonly happens after an event handler calls a state setter?
options: The state update causes React to render the component again with the new state.
The browser reloads the whole page.
The handler is permanently deleted.
The component becomes a server component.
quiz.explanation: A state update schedules a React render so the UI can reflect the changed state.

summary: React event handling connects user actions to functions. Pass a function reference such as onClick={handleClick}; do not invoke it during render. Use an arrow wrapper when a handler needs arguments, and use the event object when interaction information is needed. Event handlers commonly update state, creating the flow user action → handler → state update → re-render → updated UI.

title: Controlled Inputs
description: Learn how React state drives an input's value and how onChange keeps the DOM input and React state synchronized.
mastery: The learner can build a controlled input with value and onChange, explain the state → input → event → state loop, and repair a frozen input caused by providing a value without wiring an update handler.
learningObjectives: Explain what makes an input controlled in React.
Connect an input's value to React state.
Use onChange to update state from user input.
Explain the state-to-input synchronization loop.
Use event.target.value to read the current input value.
Distinguish a controlled input from an uncontrolled/default-value input.
Diagnose and repair a controlled input that appears frozen.

sections.text: The Input Has a Value. Who Owns It?
A normal HTML input can manage its own current value in the DOM. In a controlled React input, React state becomes the source of truth for that value.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: Controlled input: React state provides the value, and onChange updates that state when the user types.
The Basic Controlled Input

sections.title: State drives value

sections.text: There are two halves. value={query} tells React what the input should display. onChange updates query when the user types.
The Synchronization Loop

sections.title: State ↔ input
sections.code:
React state
   ↓
value prop
   ↓
input displays value
   ↓
user types
   ↓
onChange fires
   ↓
event.target.value
   ↓
state setter
   ↓
React renders again

sections.text: This loop is the core of controlled inputs. The browser reports the user's input, React updates state, and the next render supplies the value back to the input.
The Frozen Input Bug

sections.title: Broken

sections.text: The input has a value controlled by React, but there is no way for typing to update that value. The user can interact with the browser input, but React keeps rendering the same state value.

sections.title: The misconception to kill
sections.text: Providing value alone does not create a usable controlled input. If React owns the value, you need an onChange path that updates the owning state.
Repair It

sections.title: Working controlled input

sections.text: Interactive Practice: Type Into the State

sections.title: Controlled Input Playground
sections.instructions: Type into the live search field and observe the state preview. Then change the initial state, add a character count, and make a clear button reset the input through React state.

sections.text: Read the Current Value From the Event

sections.title: event.target.value

sections.text: For text inputs, event.target.value gives you the current text the user entered. The handler can transform it before putting it into state when the product needs that behavior.
Controlled Inputs Can Transform Data

sections.title: Normalize while updating

sections.text: Because React owns the value, it can intentionally control what gets displayed. Be careful, though: transformations can affect the typing experience if they are too aggressive.
Different Input Types Use Different Values

sections.title: Checkbox example

sections.text: Text inputs commonly use value and event.target.value. Checkboxes commonly use checked and event.target.checked.
Drill 1: Repair the Frozen Search Box

sections.title: Controlled Input Repair Drill
sections.instructions: The search field is frozen because its value is controlled but never updated. Repair it so typing updates the state preview. Then add a clear button that resets the same state.

sections.text: Controlled vs Default Value

sections.title: Default value
sections.code: <input defaultValue="Closures" />

sections.text: defaultValue supplies an initial value without making React state the ongoing source of truth for every change.

sections.title: Controlled value
sections.code:
<input
  value={query}
  onChange={(event) => setQuery(event.target.value)}
/>

sections.text: The controlled version makes React state the authoritative value shown by the input.
When Controlled Inputs Are Useful

sections.title: React needs to know the current value
sections.code:
Search and filtering

Live validation

Conditional UI based on input

Submit buttons that depend on input state

Formatting or normalization

Multi-field forms

sections.text: Controlled inputs become especially valuable once the UI needs to react to the current value before submission.
Drill 2: Build a Small Filter

sections.title: Controlled Search Drill
sections.instructions: Connect the input to React state and use that state to filter the displayed lessons. The filter should update while the user types. Add a message when no lessons match.

sections.text: Do Not Store What You Can Derive

sections.title: Keep the source of truth small

sections.text: The filtered list is derived from query and lessons, so it does not need separate state. This keeps the input state as the source of truth for the filter.
Debugging Controlled Inputs

sections.title: If the field is frozen
sections.code:
1. Is there a value or checked prop?
2. Is there an onChange handler?
3. Does onChange read the correct event property?
4. Does the handler call the correct state setter?
5. Is the component rendering the same value again?
6. Is another piece of logic overwriting the state?

sections.text: Most controlled-input bugs are synchronization bugs. Follow the loop from DOM event → handler → state → render → input value.
What's Being Deferred?
Forms and validation come next. More complicated input patterns, asynchronous validation, and form libraries are intentionally deferred.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: Master the state ↔ input synchronization loop before adding form abstractions. A form library should make a known model easier to manage, not hide the model from you.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'What is a controlled input?' A strong answer is: 'A controlled input gets its current value from React state, and an onChange handler updates that state when the user edits the input.'

A likely follow-up is: 'Why does an input become frozen if you provide value without onChange?' Because React is controlling what value is rendered but you have not provided a path for user edits to update the state that supplies that value.
Another follow-up is: 'How do you read a text input's current value?' Use the event object's target.value in the change handler.
Reflect
Take the Lesson Tracker project and imagine adding a lesson search field. What should be state, what can be derived, and which component should own the search value?
For a controlled input, the state value is the source of truth. The input displays it; events update it; the next render puts the updated value back into the input.

sections.label: Complete the live controlled-input Playground and both repair/filter drills. The learner must keep state and input synchronized, repair the frozen field, and build a working live filter.
sections.hint: value/checked comes from state. onChange reads the event and updates that same state.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

A controlled input uses React state as its source of truth. The component passes the current state through value or checked, and the onChange handler updates that state from the event. This creates a loop where user input produces an event, the handler updates state, React renders again, and the input receives the new value. If value is supplied without a working update path, the field can appear frozen.
