quiz.question: What makes an input controlled?
options: React state drives its current value or checked state.
The input contains a placeholder.
The input uses defaultValue only.
The browser owns the value without React knowing about it.
quiz.explanation: In a controlled input, React state is the source of truth for the displayed value.

quiz.question:
Why does this field appear frozen?

<input value={query} />
options: React cannot render text inputs.
The value is controlled by React but there is no onChange path to update the state.
Inputs cannot use state.
value only works with numbers.
quiz.explanation: The rendered value remains whatever query currently contains because user changes are never written back to state.

quiz.question: How do you normally read the new value from a text input's change event?
options: event.target.value
event.target.checked
event.value.target
event.input.text
quiz.explanation: Text input changes expose the current entered value through event.target.value.

quiz.question: Which is the correct controlled checkbox pattern?
options: checked={completed} and onChange updates completed from event.target.checked
value={completed} without onChange
defaultValue={completed} and no state
checked="completed"
quiz.explanation: Checkboxes commonly use checked for the controlled value and event.target.checked in the change handler.

summary: Controlled inputs make React state the source of truth for an input's current value. The input receives value or checked from state, and onChange updates that same state from the event. This creates a state ↔ UI synchronization loop. A controlled field with a value but no update path can appear frozen. Keep derived values such as filtered results outside state when they can be calculated from the current source data.
interviewQuestions: What is a controlled input?
Why does value without onChange make an input appear frozen?
How does the controlled-input synchronization loop work?
What is the difference between value and defaultValue?
How do you read a text input's current value?
How do you control a checkbox?
Why might filtered results be derived instead of stored in state?
How would you debug a controlled input that is not updating?

title: Forms and Validation
description: Build a controlled React form that validates user input, prevents invalid submission, and gives clear feedback at the right time.
mastery: The learner can build a controlled form, validate its fields before submission, prevent invalid submission, display useful field-level feedback, and choose appropriate validation timing instead of waiting until the final submit action for every error.
learningObjectives: Handle form submission with React.
Prevent the browser's default form submission when appropriate.
Validate controlled input values against explicit rules.
Track validation errors in React state.
Display clear field-level feedback.
Prevent submission when the form is invalid.
Clear or update errors as the user corrects their input.
Choose sensible validation timing for the user experience.
Distinguish validation errors from submission or server errors.

sections.text: Controlled Inputs Become a Form

A controlled input gives React a reliable representation of the user's current value. A form combines several such values and adds a submission boundary where the application needs to decide whether the data is acceptable.
Validation is the process of checking whether the submitted values satisfy the rules the form requires.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: Input state captures what the user entered. Validation checks that state against rules. The UI explains problems clearly. Submission proceeds only when the form is valid.
Start With a Simple Form

sections.title: Controlled form

sections.text: The form's submit handler is the boundary where validation can run before the application performs the intended action.
Validation Is a Rule

sections.title: Example validation rules
sections.code:
Title
→ required
→ at least 3 characters

Duration
→ required
→ positive number

Description
→ optional
→ maximum 200 characters

sections.text: Write the rule in plain language first. Then translate it into JavaScript. This makes validation easier to test and explain.
A Simple Validator

sections.title: Validate form values

sections.text: The validator returns the problems it found. An empty object means no validation errors were detected by these rules.
Store Errors as State

sections.title: Validation error state
sections.code: const [errors, setErrors] = useState({});

sections.text: The form can render the current validation results from that state.
Validate on Submit

sections.title: Prevent invalid submission

sections.text: Submit-time validation gives the form a clear safety boundary: invalid data is stopped before the action proceeds.
But Submit Is Not the Only Useful Moment
A form can also validate while the user is interacting with it. The right timing depends on the kind of rule and the experience you want.

sections.title: Possible validation timing
sections.code:
On submit
→ always useful as final protection

On blur
→ useful when the user leaves a field

During typing
→ useful for some rules such as character counts
→ can be annoying for complex errors if feedback is too aggressive

After a field has been touched
→ often balances early feedback and avoiding premature errors

sections.title: The misconception to kill
sections.text: Do not assume that all validation should happen only on submit. Submit-time validation is necessary, but users often benefit from clear feedback while correcting a field.
Interactive Practice: Validate a Lesson Form

sections.title: Form Validation Playground
sections.instructions: Complete the controlled lesson form. Validate the title and duration, show field-level errors, prevent submission when invalid, and clear an error once the corresponding input becomes valid. Test invalid and valid values before submitting.

sections.text: Field-Level Feedback

sections.title: Show the relevant error near the field
sections.code:
{errors.email && (

{errors.email}

)}

sections.text: Put the explanation close to the field that needs attention. A single generic 'Invalid form' message forces the user to guess what needs fixing.
Drill 1: Stop the Invalid Submission

sections.title: Form Submission Repair Drill
sections.instructions: The form currently submits even when the email is empty and the password is too short. Add validation, display the appropriate field errors, and prevent the successful-submission message until all rules pass.

sections.text: Clear Feedback as the User Fixes the Field

sections.title: Clear a stale error

sections.text: You can also re-run validation on the field after it has been touched. The important UX principle is that the message should not remain visible after the underlying problem has been corrected.
Touched State

sections.title: Remember whether a field has been visited

sections.text: Touched state lets you distinguish 'the user has not interacted with this field yet' from 'the user interacted and currently has an error.'
Do Not Over-Validate
Validation should help the user complete the task. Showing a complex error message after every keystroke can create noise instead of guidance.

sections.title: Useful feedback strategy
sections.code:
Before interaction
→ avoid unnecessary error messages

After blur / interaction
→ show relevant field feedback

On submit
→ validate all required rules

After correction
→ remove stale feedback

sections.text: Client Validation Is Not Security
Frontend validation improves the user experience, but it cannot be the only enforcement layer for rules that must be trusted by a server.
A user can bypass browser code. A server that accepts submitted data still needs to validate the data it receives.
Validation vs Submission Errors

sections.title: Different problems
sections.code:
Validation error
→ user input violates known client-side rules
→ 'Password must be at least 8 characters.'

Submission error
→ request was valid enough to send, but the operation failed
→ 'We couldn't create your account. Try again.'

sections.text: Keeping those concepts separate makes error handling clearer, especially once a form connects to an API.
Drill 2: Build Timely Feedback

sections.title: Validation Timing Drill
sections.instructions: Add touched-state behavior to the form. Do not show field errors before the user has interacted with a field, show the error after blur when invalid, validate everything on submit, and remove the error once the field becomes valid.

sections.text: Keep Validation Logic Testable
A validator that is a plain function is easy to reason about because it does not need the component's rendering behavior to determine whether a value is valid.

sections.title: Pure validation function

sections.text: The component decides when to call the validator and how to display the result. That separation keeps the validation rule easier to change and test.
What's Being Deferred?
The next lesson introduces useEffect. More advanced asynchronous validation, schema libraries, server-side validation strategies, and form libraries come later.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: Master controlled fields, submit handling, validation rules, and useful feedback before introducing abstraction-heavy form libraries.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'How do you validate a controlled React form?' A strong answer is: 'I keep the field values in controlled state, run validation rules against those values, store or derive the current errors, show field-level feedback, and block submission when the form is invalid.'

A likely follow-up is: 'Should validation only happen on submit?' No. Submit-time validation is important, but feedback can also happen after a field is touched or blurred, and some rules can be evaluated while typing when that improves the experience.
Another follow-up is: 'Is client-side validation enough?' No. It is useful UX and early feedback, but trusted validation must also happen on the server for server-enforced rules.
Reflect
Think about a form you have used that gave feedback too early or too late. What timing would have helped you correct the input without feeling interrupted?
The best validation feedback reduces uncertainty: identify the problem, explain what is expected, and make it clear what the user should do next.

sections.label: Complete the form-validation Playground and timing drill, then pass the applied quiz item. The learner must prevent invalid submission, show field-level feedback, and demonstrate useful validation timing.
sections.hint: Keep input state controlled. Validate on submit as the final gate, but use touched/blur feedback when it improves correction.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

A React form combines controlled input state with a submission boundary and explicit validation rules. Validation should prevent invalid submission, explain field-level problems clearly, and update feedback as the user corrects the form. Submit-time validation is a necessary final gate, but feedback does not have to wait until submit. Client-side validation improves UX; it is not a replacement for trusted server-side validation.

exercises.title: Form Validation Playground
exercises.brief: Build validation for a controlled lesson form, show field-level errors, prevent invalid submission, and clear stale errors.

exercises.title: Form Submission Repair Drill
exercises.brief: Repair a signup form that currently accepts invalid email and password values.

exercises.title: Validation Timing Drill
exercises.brief: Use touched state and submit state to provide feedback at useful times rather than showing all errors immediately.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of form validation?
options: To make every form submit immediately.
To check whether input satisfies required rules before the intended action proceeds.
To replace React state.
To prevent all server errors.
quiz.explanation: Validation checks input against rules and prevents invalid data from proceeding.

quiz.question: Why is validating only on submit sometimes a poor user experience?
options: It can delay useful feedback until the user has finished the whole form.
React cannot validate on submit.
Submit validation is never necessary.
It always sends invalid data.
quiz.explanation: Earlier feedback can help users correct a field without waiting until the final submission.

quiz.question: What is a good purpose for touched state?
options: To know whether the user has interacted with a field so feedback can be timed appropriately.
To replace the input's value.
To store server responses.
To prevent the form from rendering.
quiz.explanation: Touched state can distinguish untouched fields from fields the user has interacted with.

quiz.question: Which statement about client-side validation is correct?
options: It is sufficient security for all server operations.
It improves user feedback, but trusted server-side rules still need server validation.
It means API requests never fail.
It replaces authentication.
quiz.explanation: Users can bypass client code, so server-side validation remains necessary for trusted constraints.

summary: React form validation builds on controlled inputs: field values live in state, submit handling provides a final validation gate, and explicit validation rules produce useful feedback. Field-level errors should be clear and should disappear when the underlying problem is corrected. Validation does not have to wait until submit; touched/blur-based feedback can improve the experience. Client-side validation is a UX layer, not a replacement for trusted server-side validation.
interviewQuestions: How do you handle form submission in React?
How do you validate controlled form fields?
Why should invalid submission be prevented?
Should validation happen only on submit?
What is touched state and why is it useful?
How should field-level validation errors be presented?
What is the difference between validation errors and submission/server errors?
Why is client-side validation not sufficient for trusted server-side rules?

title: useEffect
description: Understand when an effect is appropriate, how useEffect synchronizes a component with something outside React, and how dependency arrays determine when the effect is re-run.
mastery: The learner can identify a genuine side effect, implement it with useEffect, provide the dependencies that determine when synchronization should occur, and diagnose missing dependencies or effects that accidentally run in a loop.
learningObjectives: Explain what useEffect is for.
Distinguish rendering calculations from side effects.
Use useEffect to synchronize a component with an external system.
Understand that an effect runs after rendering.
Use a dependency array to describe the values an effect depends on.
Recognize the difference between no dependency array, an empty dependency array, and specific dependencies.
Identify missing dependencies that can create stale values.
Identify dependency choices that can create unnecessary or infinite effect loops.

sections.text: Not Everything Belongs in the Render

A React component's render should describe the UI for the current props and state. Some work, however, interacts with something outside React: a browser API, timer, subscription, network connection, document title, or another external system.
useEffect is the tool for synchronizing the component with that external system.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: Render describes the UI. An effect runs after rendering to synchronize something outside React with the current state or props.
A Simple Example: Document Title

sections.title: Synchronize the browser title

sections.text: The input value is React state. The browser document title is outside React's render output. The effect synchronizes the browser title with the current state after rendering.
Why Not Do It During Render?

sections.title: Avoid side effects in render

sections.text: Putting external side effects directly into rendering mixes two different responsibilities. Rendering should calculate the UI; the effect should handle synchronization with the external world.
The Dependency Array

sections.title: Run when title changes

sections.text: The dependency array tells React which reactive values the effect uses and when the effect needs to synchronize again.
Three Common Forms

sections.title: No dependency array
Empty dependency array
Specific dependency

sections.text: The exact behavior depends on the dependency list. The important skill is to connect the dependency list to the values the effect actually reads.
Interactive Practice: Synchronize the Title

sections.title: useEffect Playground
sections.instructions: Change the lesson title and observe the browser-document synchronization. Then remove, empty, and correct the dependency array and predict when the effect should run.

sections.text: An Effect Should Describe Synchronization

sections.title: Ask the right question
sections.code:
What external thing am I synchronizing with?

What React values determine how it should be synchronized?

What should happen when those values change?

sections.text: If you cannot name the external system, the work may not belong in an effect at all.
Not Every Calculation Needs useEffect

sections.title: Derived data should stay in render

sections.text: The percentage is derived from React values. No external synchronization is happening, so an effect would add unnecessary complexity.

sections.title: The misconception to kill
sections.text: Do not use useEffect for ordinary calculations or values that can be derived during rendering. Effects are for synchronization with something outside React.
Effect Dependencies and Stale Values

sections.title: Missing dependency

sections.text: The effect reads query but the dependency list does not declare query. If the effect is supposed to stay synchronized with changes to query, this creates a stale relationship: the effect does not re-run when that value changes.

sections.title: Correct dependency

sections.text: The Dependency Array Is About the Effect's Inputs

sections.title: A useful question
sections.code:
Which reactive values does this effect read?

Those values determine when synchronization may need to happen.

sections.text: This is where closures matter. The effect callback closes over the values from the render that created it. If the synchronization needs a changing value, the effect must be able to run again when that value changes.
Drill 1: Repair the Stale Effect

sections.title: Dependency Array Repair Drill
sections.instructions: The effect logs the selected lesson but never reacts when the selected lesson changes. Fix the dependency list, then change the selection and verify that the effect runs with the current value.

sections.text: The Infinite Loop Trap

sections.title: An effect that updates its own dependency

sections.text: This effect changes count, but count is also a dependency that causes the effect to run again. The result can be a render-effect-update cycle that continues indefinitely.

sections.title: Think in synchronization, not reaction chains

sections.text: An effect should usually synchronize an external system with React state. If an effect changes a state value that directly causes the same effect to run again, inspect the design carefully.
Drill 2: Break the Effect Loop

sections.title: Infinite Effect Loop Debugger
sections.instructions: Diagnose why the effect loops and redesign the component so the desired initial behavior occurs without repeatedly updating the same dependency that triggers the effect.

sections.text: Effect + External Browser API

sections.title: Window event synchronization

sections.text: This is a genuine effect because the component is synchronizing with an external browser event system. The cleanup function will be the focus of the next lesson.
Effects Run After Rendering

sections.title: Simplified sequence
sections.code:
State / props
    ↓
Render JSX
    ↓
React commits the UI
    ↓
Effect runs
    ↓
External system is synchronized

sections.text: This timing is why effects are suitable for work that should happen after the UI has been rendered.
Do Not Use an Effect to Move Data Between React Values

sections.title: Usually unnecessary

sections.text: If fullName is simply derived from firstName and lastName, calculate it directly instead of introducing another state value and effect.

sections.title: Prefer derived data
sections.code: const fullName = `${firstName} ${lastName}`;

sections.text: This keeps the data model smaller and avoids an unnecessary render-synchronization cycle.
Debugging useEffect

sections.title: Effect debugging checklist
sections.code:
1. What external system is this effect synchronizing?
2. What reactive values does the effect read?
3. Are those values represented in the dependency list?
4. Does the effect update one of its own dependencies?
5. Is this actually derived data that belongs in render?
6. Does the effect need cleanup?

sections.text: This turns the dependency array from mysterious syntax into a reasoning exercise.
What's Being Deferred?
The next lesson focuses specifically on cleanup for subscriptions, timers, and other external connections. Fetching data in an effect comes after that.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: First understand when an effect belongs and how its dependencies describe synchronization. Cleanup and asynchronous effects come next.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'What is useEffect for?' A strong answer is: 'useEffect lets a component synchronize with something outside React after rendering, such as a browser API, subscription, timer, or external data source.'
A likely follow-up is: 'Why is the dependency array important?' It tells React which reactive values the effect depends on so the synchronization can run again when those values change.

Another follow-up is: 'Why can a dependency mistake cause an infinite loop?' If an effect updates a state value that is itself a dependency, the update can trigger another render, which runs the effect again, which updates the state again.
Reflect
Look at the API Integration Project. Which part of that feature genuinely needs an effect? Which values could be derived directly during render instead?
When you are about to write useEffect, say out loud what external system you are synchronizing with. If you cannot name one, reconsider whether an effect is needed.

sections.label: Complete the useEffect Playground and both dependency/debugging drills. The learner must identify a genuine effect, repair a missing dependency, and break the infinite-loop example without replacing the effect with unrelated complexity.
sections.hint: Ask: what external system is being synchronized, what values does the effect read, and what happens when those values change?

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

useEffect is for synchronizing a component with something outside React after rendering. The effect callback reads current props/state values, and its dependency array describes which reactive values should cause synchronization to run again. Missing dependencies can create stale values; careless dependencies can create repeated or infinite effect loops. Ordinary derived calculations should stay in render rather than being pushed through an effect.

exercises.title: useEffect Playground
exercises.brief: Synchronize an external browser value with React state and observe how the dependency array changes effect execution.

exercises.title: Dependency Array Repair Drill
exercises.brief: Fix an effect with a missing dependency so it stays synchronized with the current selected value.

exercises.title: Infinite Effect Loop Debugger
exercises.brief: Diagnose and redesign an effect that updates its own dependency so the required initial behavior occurs without a render-effect-update loop.

quiz.question: What is useEffect primarily for?
options: Synchronizing a component with something outside React.
Replacing all local calculations.
Creating JSX elements.
Passing props to children.
quiz.explanation: Effects handle synchronization with external systems after rendering.

options: It tells React that the effect depends on query and should synchronize again when query changes.
It converts query into JSX.
It prevents the effect from ever running.
It makes query global.
quiz.explanation: The dependency links the effect's synchronization to changes in query.

quiz.question: What is wrong with storing a derived fullName in state through an effect when it can simply be calculated from firstName and lastName?
options: It adds unnecessary state and synchronization complexity.
React cannot store strings.
Effects cannot read props.
Derived values must always use useEffect.
quiz.explanation: Derived values can normally be calculated during render without another state/effect cycle.

quiz.question: Why can an effect cause an infinite loop?
options: Because every effect always loops.
Because the effect can update a state value that causes itself to run again through its dependency list.
Because dependency arrays cannot contain state values.
Because React renders only once.
quiz.explanation: An effect that updates one of its own triggering dependencies can create a repeated render/effect/update cycle.

summary: useEffect synchronizes a React component with something outside React after rendering. Its dependency array describes the reactive values that determine when that synchronization should run again. Effects are appropriate for external systems such as browser APIs, subscriptions, timers, and network synchronization; ordinary calculations and derived values generally belong in render. Missing dependencies can create stale effects, while self-triggering dependencies can create loops.

resources.label: React — You Might Not Need an Effect

interviewQuestions: What is useEffect for?
When should a value be derived during render instead of calculated in an effect?
What does the dependency array represent?
Why can missing dependencies produce stale values?
How can an effect create an infinite loop?
What is the difference between [] and [value] as effect dependencies?
What kinds of external systems commonly require effects?
How would you debug an effect that runs too often?

title: Side Effects and Cleanup
description: Learn why effects that create subscriptions, timers, or external connections must return cleanup functions so resources are released when dependencies change or the component is removed.
mastery: The learner can recognize when an effect creates an ongoing external connection, return a cleanup function that reverses that setup, and explain how missing cleanup can create duplicate subscriptions, timers, or stale external connections.
learningObjectives: Explain why some effects need cleanup.
Identify effects that create subscriptions, timers, listeners, or other ongoing external connections.
Return a cleanup function from useEffect.
Understand that cleanup runs before an effect re-runs with changed dependencies and when the component is removed.
Write setup/cleanup pairs for browser event listeners and timers.
Diagnose duplicate subscriptions caused by missing cleanup.
Explain why cleanup is part of correct effect synchronization.

sections.text: An Effect Can Start Something That Needs to Stop
The previous lesson introduced effects as synchronization with something outside React. Some external systems are not one-time operations: they create ongoing connections.
An event listener stays attached. A timer keeps running. A subscription continues receiving updates. A connection remains active.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: An effect that sets something up should clean it up when that synchronization is no longer needed. Think setup → use → cleanup.
The Setup/Cleanup Pair

sections.title: Window event listener

sections.text: The effect sets up the event listener. The returned function removes the exact listener that was added.
Why Cleanup Matters

sections.title: Without cleanup

sections.text: If the component is repeatedly mounted or the effect is re-run in a situation where a new subscription is created, old listeners can remain attached. The result can be duplicate callbacks, stale behavior, or unnecessary work.

sections.title: The misconception to kill
sections.text: Do not treat cleanup as optional for an effect that creates an ongoing connection. Forgetting cleanup can leave duplicate subscriptions, listeners, or timers running.
Timers Need Cleanup Too

sections.title: Interval with cleanup

sections.text: The interval continues independently of the component's render. clearInterval stops that external timer when the effect is cleaned up.
Cleanup Runs When Synchronization Changes

sections.title: Dependency changes
sections.code:
Render with room = 'A'
      ↓
Effect subscribes to A
      ↓
room changes to 'B'
      ↓
Cleanup removes subscription to A
      ↓
Effect subscribes to B

sections.text: Cleanup is not only about component removal. When dependencies change, React can clean up the previous synchronization before starting the new one.
Interactive Practice: Watch a Subscription

sections.title: Cleanup Playground
sections.instructions: Switch between a listener implementation with cleanup and one without it. Trigger the external event repeatedly and observe the difference. Then change the dependency so the effect synchronizes with a different channel.

sections.text: Cleanup Reverses Setup

sections.title: Think in pairs
sections.code:
addEventListener
↔ removeEventListener

setInterval
↔ clearInterval

setTimeout
↔ clearTimeout

subscribe
↔ unsubscribe

connect
↔ disconnect

sections.text: A strong cleanup function reverses the resource created by the effect. This symmetry makes effects easier to reason about.
Drill 1: Repair the Duplicate Listener

sections.title: Subscription Cleanup Repair
sections.instructions: The component adds a window listener whenever the selected room changes, but never removes the previous listener. Add the cleanup so only the current room receives the event.

sections.text: Drill 2: Clean Up a Timer

sections.title: Timer Cleanup Drill
sections.instructions: The component starts an interval that increments a counter. Add cleanup so the interval stops when the component is no longer using it. Then change the interval duration through state and ensure the previous timer is cleaned up before the new one starts.

sections.text: Cleanup and Dependency Changes Work Together

sections.title: Synchronization lifecycle
sections.code:
Old dependencies
      ↓
Cleanup old external connection
      ↓
New dependencies
      ↓
Setup new external connection

sections.text: This pattern is why cleanup belongs inside the effect that created the connection. The setup and its corresponding teardown stay together.
Do Not Put Unrelated Cleanup Everywhere
Cleanup should reverse what that particular effect set up. Avoid unrelated global cleanup code that makes ownership unclear.

sections.title: Good ownership
sections.code:
Effect A
→ creates timer A
→ cleanup clears timer A

Effect B
→ creates subscription B
→ cleanup removes subscription B

sections.text: Keeping each effect's setup and teardown together makes it much easier to understand what happens when dependencies change.
Cleanup Is Not Only About Unmounting
A common beginner explanation says cleanup means 'when the component unmounts.' That is incomplete.
Cleanup also happens when an effect is about to re-run because its dependencies changed. The purpose is to stop the previous synchronization before replacing it with the new synchronization.
A Practical Example: Selected Room

sections.title: Subscribe to the current room

sections.text: When roomId changes, the old subscription must stop before the component starts listening to the new room.
Cleanup Can Prevent Stale Updates
An old external connection can continue producing events after the component has moved on to a new value. Cleanup prevents those obsolete connections from continuing to influence the application.
What's Being Deferred?
Fetching data in React is the next lesson. That lesson will combine useEffect and useState for asynchronous loading and will address the additional problem of handling async work safely.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: This lesson focuses on synchronous resource setup and cleanup such as listeners, timers, and subscriptions. Fetching and async race/cancellation concerns come next.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'Why does useEffect need cleanup?' A strong answer is: 'If an effect creates an ongoing external connection such as an event listener, timer, or subscription, the effect should return cleanup that reverses that setup so obsolete resources do not remain active.'
A likely follow-up is: 'When does cleanup run?' Cleanup runs when the component is removed and before the effect re-runs because its dependencies changed.
Another follow-up is: 'What is the setup/cleanup pairing?' Examples include addEventListener/removeEventListener, setInterval/clearInterval, and subscribe/unsubscribe.
Reflect
Imagine a chat screen whose roomId changes from A to B. What could happen if the A subscription is never removed? How would you recognize that bug from the interface behavior?

sections.title: Every ongoing connection needs an owner

sections.text: Ask: what did this effect create, and who is responsible for stopping it? The cleanup function should answer both questions.

sections.label: Complete the cleanup Playground and both repair drills. The learner must correctly pair setup with teardown for a subscription and timer, and explain why cleanup runs when dependencies change.
sections.hint: Whatever the effect creates, the cleanup should reverse. Dependency change means old synchronization is cleaned up before new synchronization begins.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

Effects that create ongoing external connections should return cleanup functions. Event listeners, timers, subscriptions, and similar resources need explicit teardown so obsolete connections do not continue running. Cleanup runs when the component is removed and before the effect re-runs because dependencies changed. Keep each setup and its corresponding cleanup together inside the same effect.

exercises.title: Cleanup Playground
exercises.brief: Compare effect behavior with and without cleanup while changing an external subscription target.

exercises.title: Subscription Cleanup Repair
exercises.brief: Add cleanup to an effect that creates a new event subscription whenever a room changes.

exercises.title: Timer Cleanup Drill
exercises.brief: Clean up an interval and ensure the previous timer is removed when the interval configuration changes.

quiz.question: Why does an effect that adds an event listener usually need cleanup?
options: To reverse the setup and remove the obsolete listener.
Because events cannot run more than once.
Because React deletes all browser listeners automatically.
To convert the listener into state.
quiz.explanation: Cleanup removes the external resource created by the effect.

quiz.question: When can an effect's cleanup function run?
options: Only before the first render.
When the component is removed and before the effect re-runs because dependencies changed.
Only when the browser tab closes.
Only after a network request fails.
quiz.explanation: Cleanup is part of ending the previous effect synchronization.

quiz.question: Which is the correct setup/cleanup pairing?
options: setInterval / addEventListener
addEventListener / removeEventListener
subscribe / setState
setTimeout / useState
quiz.explanation: Cleanup should reverse the resource setup performed by the effect.

quiz.question: What problem can missing cleanup cause when a dependency changes?
options: The old external connection can remain active while a new one is created.
React automatically deletes the component.
The dependency array disappears.
The component can no longer render JSX.
quiz.explanation: Without cleanup, obsolete subscriptions or timers can continue alongside newly created ones.

summary: An effect that creates an ongoing external connection should return cleanup that reverses that setup. Event listeners, timers, subscriptions, and connections are common examples. Cleanup occurs when the component is removed and before an effect re-runs because its dependencies changed. Keeping setup and teardown together prevents duplicate subscriptions, obsolete timers, stale external connections, and other resource leaks.

When does an effect cleanup function run?
What is the setup/cleanup pairing for an event listener?
How do you clean up a timer created inside an effect?
What can happen if a subscription is not cleaned up?
Why does cleanup matter when effect dependencies change?
How would you debug duplicate event listeners or timers?

title: Fetching Data in React
description: Combine useEffect and useState to load asynchronous data, represent loading/error/success states, and avoid updating component state after the component is no longer active.
mastery: The learner can load asynchronous data from an API inside a React component, represent loading/success/error states, guard HTTP failures, and prevent obsolete asynchronous work from updating state after the component is no longer using that request.
learningObjectives: Combine useEffect and useState for asynchronous data loading.
Represent loading, success, and error states in a React component.
Call a web API from an effect and handle its asynchronous response.
Check HTTP success before treating returned data as usable.
Parse response data and store it in React state.
Handle request failures without leaving stale UI state.
Recognize why asynchronous work can outlive the render or component that started it.
Guard against applying obsolete asynchronous results to component state.
Explain the relationship between React effects and the API loading state model from Module 2-4.

sections.text: Bring the API Into React
You already know how to fetch data with JavaScript and how to model loading, success, empty, and error states. You also know that effects synchronize React with external systems.
Now combine those ideas: an effect starts the request, state stores the result, and the component renders the correct UI for the request's current state.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: Effect starts the asynchronous synchronization → request resolves or fails → state is updated → React renders the resulting UI state.
The Basic Pattern

sections.title: Load lesson data

sections.text: This combines nearly every API idea from Module 2-4: fetch, HTTP status checking, JSON parsing, loading/error/empty handling, and list rendering.
Why the Request Starts Inside an Effect
The network request is an interaction with an external system. Putting it directly in the component render would cause the request to be tied incorrectly to rendering itself.

sections.title: Correct separation
sections.code:
Render
→ describe current UI

Effect
→ synchronize with API

State
→ remember request result/status

Render again
→ show current result

sections.text: Loading Is State

sections.title: Explicit request state
sections.code: const [status, setStatus] = useState('loading');

sections.text: The request lifecycle should be visible to the component. A successful response, an empty result, and an error are not the same UI state.
Handle HTTP Failure Explicitly

sections.title: Do not trust every response

sections.text: As you learned earlier, fetch can fulfill with an HTTP error response. Checking response.ok keeps the React state machine aligned with the actual HTTP outcome.
Interactive Practice: Change the API Input

sections.title: Fetching Data in React Playground
sections.instructions: Change the endpoint input and observe how the component moves between loading, success, empty, and error behavior. Predict the state before each request. Then change the displayed data mapping to match the actual response structure.

sections.text: The cancelled flag is not a replacement for cancelling the actual network request. It is a simple guard that prevents obsolete asynchronous work from applying state after the component/effect has moved on.
The Main Async Hazard
Asynchronous work does not necessarily finish at the same time that the component's current assumptions remain valid.

sections.title: Potential race
sections.code:
Request A starts
        ↓
Request B starts
        ↓
B finishes first
        ↓
UI shows B
        ↓
A finishes later
        ↓
A overwrites state with stale data

sections.text: This can happen when a dependency changes quickly, such as when a user changes a selected lesson, search query, or profile.
Guard the Result

sections.title: Ignore obsolete results

sections.text: When lessonId changes, the cleanup marks the previous effect as obsolete. Its eventual result is ignored instead of updating state for the newer synchronization.

sections.title: The misconception to kill
sections.text: Starting an asynchronous request inside an effect does not guarantee that its result will still be relevant when it finishes. Protect the component from applying obsolete results after the effect has been replaced or the component is no longer active.
Dependency Changes Restart the Synchronization

sections.title: Selected lesson example
sections.code:
lessonId = 12
→ effect requests lesson 12

lessonId changes to 13
→ cleanup marks lesson-12 synchronization obsolete
→ effect requests lesson 13

Only the current synchronization should update state.

sections.text: Drill 1: Repair Stale Async Results

sections.title: Async Race Repair Drill
sections.instructions: The component fetches a lesson whenever selectedId changes, but a slower earlier request can overwrite a newer result. Add an effect cleanup guard so only the current request can update state.

sections.text: Keep Loading and Error State Consistent

sections.title: Reset request state when starting a new request

sections.text: When a new request starts, the UI should represent that new loading state rather than leaving an old success or error state visible without explanation.
Drill 2: Complete the Data Loader

sections.title: React Data Loader Drill
sections.instructions: Complete the loader so it handles loading, HTTP failure, parsed data, empty results, and obsolete asynchronous results. Then render the four resulting UI states.

sections.text: Use the Previous Module's State Discipline

sections.title: React data-fetching state machine
sections.code:
effect starts
    ↓
loading
    ↓
 ┌───────────────┬───────────────┐
 ↓               ↓               ↓
success + data   success + empty  error
 ↓               ↓               ↓
content          empty UI        error UI

sections.text: This is why Module 2-4 came first. React is not inventing a different API state model; it is giving you a component structure for the same loading/error/empty discipline.
Do Not Put the Whole API System in One Component

For a small exercise, putting the request directly inside the component is acceptable. As the application grows, separate data-fetching responsibilities from presentation when that makes the code easier to reuse or test.

sections.title: A useful boundary
sections.code:
Data access
→ request / response handling

Component
→ request lifecycle + UI state

Presentation
→ render loading / error / empty / data

sections.text: The architecture should remain proportional to the feature. Do not introduce abstractions solely because they look more sophisticated.
What's Being Deferred?

The next lesson is the React Interaction Challenge, where controlled inputs, effects, and data fetching are combined into a complete feature. More advanced request cancellation, caching, query libraries, retries, and reusable data hooks are deferred.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: Master the basic effect → request → state → UI lifecycle and obsolete-result protection before introducing a data-fetching library.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'How do you fetch data in React?' A strong answer is: 'I use an effect to synchronize with the API, keep loading/data/error state in React state, check the HTTP response before accepting the result, parse the response, and guard against obsolete asynchronous results when the effect's dependencies change or the component is no longer interested in that request.'
A likely follow-up is: 'Why not fetch directly in render?' Because rendering should remain a description of the UI; the network request is an external side effect.

Another follow-up is: 'What happens if an earlier request finishes after a newer request?' Without protection, the older result can overwrite current state. Cleanup can mark the previous synchronization obsolete so its result is ignored.
Reflect
Imagine a search screen where the user types or changes filters quickly. Requests for earlier values may finish after later ones. What state should the UI display if the older request finishes last?

sections.title: Only the current synchronization should win

sections.text: When asynchronous work overlaps, correctness means the result that belongs to the current UI state is allowed to update the current UI.

sections.label: Complete the live Fetching Data Playground and both async-race/data-loader drills. The learner must combine useEffect + useState, handle loading/success/error states, check HTTP success, parse data, and prevent obsolete asynchronous results from updating current state.
sections.hint: Effect starts the request. State represents the request lifecycle. Cleanup marks obsolete work so an older result cannot replace the current one.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

Fetching data in React combines useEffect and useState. The effect starts synchronization with the API, state stores loading/data/error information, and rendering reflects the current request state. HTTP success should be checked before data is accepted. Because asynchronous work can finish after the component has moved on, the effect should guard against obsolete results updating state. This connects React's effect model to the loading/error/empty discipline learned in the APIs module.

exercises.brief: Change an API endpoint and observe the React request lifecycle across loading, success, empty, and error states.

exercises.title: Async Race Repair Drill
exercises.brief: Prevent a slower obsolete request from overwriting state produced by a newer request.

exercises.title: React Data Loader Drill
exercises.brief: Complete a reusable loader that handles status, JSON data, empty results, errors, and obsolete asynchronous work.

quiz.question: Why is an API request commonly started inside useEffect?
options: Because network requests are external side effects, not render calculations.
Because React cannot call functions outside render.
Because fetch only works in CSS.
Because state cannot be used with effects.
quiz.explanation: The request synchronizes the component with an external system and therefore belongs in an effect.

quiz.question: What should happen before fetched data is treated as a successful HTTP result?
options: Only check whether JSON exists.
Check response.ok or the response status.
Assume every fulfilled fetch is 200.
Render the data immediately.
quiz.explanation: fetch can fulfill with an HTTP error response, so the response must be inspected.

quiz.question: Why can an older request corrupt the UI?
options: Because JavaScript always executes requests twice.
Because an earlier asynchronous result can finish after a newer request and overwrite current state.
Because useEffect reverses request order automatically.
Because JSON always changes during transport.
quiz.explanation: Overlapping requests can resolve out of order, so obsolete results must be prevented from updating current state.

quiz.question: What does an effect cleanup guard accomplish in an async request?
options: It marks the previous synchronization obsolete so its eventual result can be ignored.
It guarantees the network request is canceled in every browser.
It converts all failures into success.
It prevents the initial request from running.
quiz.explanation: A cleanup guard can prevent an obsolete asynchronous result from updating current component state; it is distinct from actually aborting the network request.

summary: React data fetching combines useEffect and useState with the API state discipline learned earlier. The effect starts the request, state represents loading/data/error, the HTTP response must be checked before accepting the result, and the response body is parsed into JavaScript data. Because asynchronous requests can finish out of order or after the relevant synchronization has changed, cleanup can mark obsolete work so stale results do not overwrite current state.

title: React Interaction Challenge
description: Build a complete interactive React feature that combines controlled inputs, effects, and asynchronous data fetching into one coherent user flow.
mastery: The learner can build and explain an interactive form-driven React feature that synchronizes input state, triggers asynchronous data loading, handles loading/success/empty/error states, and keeps responsibilities separated enough to remain understandable and testable.
learningObjectives: Combine controlled inputs, useEffect, useState, and data fetching in one feature.
Build a form-driven interaction that changes the data requested by the application.
Represent loading, success, empty, and error states.
Handle HTTP failures explicitly.
Prevent obsolete asynchronous results from overwriting current state.
Keep input state, request state, and presentation responsibilities understandable.
Explain the complete interaction flow from user input to fetched data to rendered UI.
Diagnose and fix integration bugs using observable behavior and Network-panel evidence.

sections.text: This Is the Module Capstone
You have practiced events, controlled inputs, validation, effects, cleanup, and fetching data in React. Now combine them into one feature.
The project is intentionally a build challenge rather than another theory lesson. The concepts you need have already been taught.

sections.title: Project goal
sections.text: Build an interactive lesson search feature: the user enters a query, submits or changes the search criteria, the React app requests matching data, and the UI represents the current request state.
Required User Flow

sections.title: End-to-end interaction
sections.code:
User enters search text
        ↓
Controlled input state
        ↓
User submits search
        ↓
Request state → loading
        ↓
useEffect / data request
        ↓
HTTP response
   ┌────┼──────────────┐
   ↓    ↓              ↓
success  empty        error
   ↓    ↓              ↓
results empty UI    error UI

If the search changes:
old synchronization is cleaned up/ignored
and the current search becomes authoritative.

sections.text: Project Brief: Lesson Search
Build a Lesson Search feature for Forge Academy. The user enters a search query, submits it, and sees matching lessons from a real or supplied API endpoint.

sections.title: Functional requirements
sections.code:
1. Search input is controlled by React state.
2. The user can submit the search.
3. Invalid/empty input is handled deliberately.
4. A request begins in a loading state.
5. The API response is checked for HTTP success.
6. JSON data is parsed and displayed.
7. No matching results show a deliberate empty state.
8. Request failure shows a useful error state.
9. A later search must not be overwritten by an older result.
10. The user can perform another search without refreshing the page.

sections.text: Suggested Component Structure

sections.title: Possible architecture
sections.code:
App
└── LessonSearch
    ├── SearchForm
    ├── SearchStatus
    └── LessonResults
        └── LessonCard

sections.text: This is a suggestion, not a mandatory component tree. Choose boundaries that make ownership and responsibilities clear.
State You Will Probably Need

sections.title: Starting point

sections.text: You do not have to use exactly these variables. The design should distinguish the value the user is currently editing from the query the application is currently searching if that separation helps your feature.
Why Separate Query From Submitted Query?

A common design is to keep the user's current input separate from the committed search term. That allows the user to edit the next query without immediately replacing the results from the current query.

sections.title: Two values, two responsibilities
sections.code:
query
→ what the user is currently typing

submittedQuery
→ what the current request is searching for

sections.text: Stage 1: Build the Controlled Form

sections.title: Search form starting point

sections.text: Stage 2: Validate Before Requesting

sections.title: Reject an empty search

sections.text: This combines the form-validation lesson with the data-fetching lesson: reject known invalid input before starting the external synchronization.
Stage 3: Fetch When the Search Changes

sections.title: Effect-driven search

sections.text: This is the core challenge. The effect synchronizes the component with the currently submitted query, and cleanup prevents an obsolete request from applying a result after the query changes.
Stage 4: Render the Request State

sections.title: State-aware results

sections.text: Interactive Project Workspace

sections.title: React Interaction Challenge
sections.instructions: Complete the Lesson Search feature end-to-end. Connect the controlled search field to state, validate submission, trigger the data request through useEffect, handle HTTP and network failures, protect against obsolete results, and render idle/loading/success/empty/error states. Test at least two different searches and one failure scenario.

sections.text: Required Tests

sections.title: Do not stop at the happy path
sections.code:
Test 1 — Empty submit
→ validation prevents the request.

Test 2 — Search with results
→ loading → results.

Test 3 — Search with no matches
→ loading → empty.

Test 4 — HTTP failure
→ loading → error.

Test 5 — Network failure
→ loading → error.

Test 6 — Search again
→ the new query becomes authoritative.

Test 7 — Rapid changes
→ an older result cannot overwrite a newer search.

Test 8 — Clear/edit current input
→ existing results remain understandable until a new search is committed.

sections.text: The Important Architecture Decision

Keep the feature's responsibilities understandable. The form knows how to collect user input. The parent coordinates the submitted query and request lifecycle. The results area renders the current state.

sections.title: Responsibility boundaries
sections.code:
SearchForm
→ input + submit event

LessonSearch
→ query ownership + request effect + result state

SearchResults
→ loading/error/empty/success presentation

sections.text: You can structure this differently, but each responsibility should have a clear home.
Do Not Couple the Fetching to the Input Event

A tempting implementation is to start a request on every keystroke inside onChange. That can be appropriate for autocomplete, but it changes the interaction model and introduces more concurrent requests.
For this challenge, submit is the explicit boundary: edit locally first, then request the submitted query.
Debugging the Challenge

sections.title: Trace the complete path
sections.code:
Input
↓
query state
↓
submit handler
↓
submittedQuery
↓
effect
↓
fetch
↓
HTTP status
↓
JSON data / error
↓
request state
↓
SearchResults

sections.text: When something breaks, find the first step where the expected value or state differs from what you observe.
Common Failure Modes

sections.title: Debugging guide
sections.code:
Typing does nothing
→ Check value/onChange synchronization.

Submit reloads the page
→ Check event.preventDefault().

Request never starts
→ Check submittedQuery and effect dependencies.

404/500 appears as success
→ Check response.ok.

Old search overwrites new search
→ Check cleanup/obsolete-result guard.

No-match result looks like an error
→ Separate success + empty from error.

Searches use stale query
→ Check effect dependencies and which query is actually submitted.

sections.text: Network Inspection

sections.title: Inspect each search
sections.code:
Request URL
→ correct query parameter?

Method
→ expected method?

Status
→ success or failure?

Response body
→ actual data shape?

Timing
→ can requests overlap?

UI state
→ does it match the response?

sections.text: If the API behaves unexpectedly, use the Network panel as evidence rather than changing the component blindly.
Code Quality Review

sections.title: Submission checklist
sections.code:
FUNCTIONAL
□ Controlled search input works.
□ Submit validation works.
□ Loading state works.
□ Success state works.
□ Empty state works.
□ Error state works.
□ New searches work.
□ Obsolete results cannot overwrite the current search.

REACT
□ useEffect has the correct dependency.
□ State ownership is clear.
□ Cleanup/guard behavior is understandable.
□ Props flow cleanly between components.

API
□ response.ok/status is checked.
□ JSON is parsed correctly.
□ Actual response shape is used.

QUALITY
□ No unnecessary duplicate state.
□ No huge monolithic component.
□ No unexplained side effects.
□ UI responsibilities are separated clearly.

sections.text: Root-Cause Reflection
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer asks: 'Walk me through the architecture.' A strong answer is: 'The search field is controlled state. Submit commits the query. An effect synchronizes with the API using that committed query. The component stores request status and results, and the presentation renders idle, loading, success, empty, or error states.'

A likely follow-up is: 'Why separate the typed query from the submitted query?' Because the user may edit the next search while the current result set is still displayed; keeping them separate gives the feature an explicit request boundary.

Another follow-up is: 'How do you prevent an old request from replacing a newer result?' Use effect cleanup to mark the previous synchronization obsolete, and ignore its result when it eventually resolves.
Reflect

Which part of this feature has the most moving pieces: input synchronization, validation, effect dependencies, async results, or UI states? Explain the data flow without referring to individual lines of code.

You can now build an interactive React feature that accepts user input, validates it, synchronizes with an external API, handles asynchronous results safely, and renders appropriate UI for each request state.

sections.label: Submit the React Interaction Challenge. The working artifact must satisfy the controlled-input, validation, effect, data-fetching, loading/error/empty, and obsolete-request handling requirements, and the learner must be able to explain the key architecture decisions.
sections.hint: Trace the entire flow: input → submit → committed query → effect → request → state → UI. Test both success and failure before submitting.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

The React Interaction Challenge combines the entire module into one interactive feature. Controlled inputs manage what the user is editing, submission commits the request criteria, useEffect performs synchronization with the API, state represents the request lifecycle, and the UI renders loading, success, empty, and error states. Cleanup or an obsolete-result guard protects the current interface from stale asynchronous results. The project is successful when the feature works and the learner can explain the data flow and ownership decisions.

quiz.question: Why might a search feature separate query from submittedQuery?
options: So the current input can change without automatically replacing the results for the currently committed search.
Because controlled inputs cannot store strings.
Because effects cannot use state.
So the API never receives query parameters.
quiz.explanation: Separating editing state from committed request state gives the interaction a clear request boundary.

quiz.question: What should happen when a new search is submitted?
options: The previous UI must always remain marked as success.
The request lifecycle should move into loading, then resolve to success, empty, or error.
The page should reload.
The previous request must always be allowed to overwrite the new one.
quiz.explanation: A new request starts a new request lifecycle and should be represented explicitly.

quiz.question: Why is an obsolete-result guard needed in overlapping searches?
options: To ensure an older request cannot overwrite state for the current search.
To make every request return 200.
To prevent the input from changing.
To convert errors into empty results.
quiz.explanation: Asynchronous requests can complete out of order, so an older result may otherwise replace current data.

quiz.question: Which architecture best matches the challenge?
options: Input → render directly → ignore request state.
Controlled input → submitted query → effect/request → state → state-aware UI.
Input → mutate props → global DOM manipulation.
Fetch on every render → update state unconditionally.
quiz.explanation: The project combines controlled inputs, effects, asynchronous state, and state-driven rendering.

summary: The React Interaction Challenge combines controlled inputs, validation, useEffect, cleanup, and data fetching into one interactive feature. The learner must distinguish the user's current input from the committed request, represent the request lifecycle explicitly, check HTTP outcomes, render loading/empty/error/success states, and protect the current UI from stale asynchronous results. The project is a synthesis task rather than a new theory lesson.

title: Thinking in Components
description: Learn to look at a UI before coding, decompose it into meaningful component boundaries, and decide where data and responsibilities should live.
mastery: The learner can take a UI mockup or feature description, identify meaningful component boundaries, sketch a component hierarchy before implementation, and explain why each component exists and what responsibility it owns.
learningObjectives: Explain what it means to think in components before writing React code.
Decompose a UI mockup into a component hierarchy.
Identify repeated, independently meaningful, or behaviorally distinct UI as candidate component boundaries.
Distinguish structural containers from meaningful components.
Estimate where data and state might eventually live without prematurely implementing them.
Explain why component decomposition should happen before detailed implementation.
Recognize over-decomposition and under-decomposition.

sections.text: Stop Coding for a Moment
A common way to start a React feature is to open the editor and immediately write JSX. That feels productive, but it often means the component structure emerges accidentally.
Before writing code, look at the interface as a system of pieces. Ask what the meaningful parts are, how they relate, and which parts might need their own data or behavior.

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: Thinking in React starts with the UI you need to build. Decompose that UI into a component hierarchy before deciding how each component should be implemented.
Start With the UI, Not the File Names
Do not begin by deciding that this must become App.jsx, Dashboard.jsx, Lesson.jsx, and five other files. First identify what the interface is made of.
Draw the Component Tree

sections.title: A first decomposition
sections.code:
App
└── LessonDashboard
    ├── ProgressSummary
    ├── SearchBox
    └── LessonList
        └── LessonCard

sections.text: This tree is a design model. It is not yet implementation. You can change it before writing a single component.
Find Meaningful Boundaries

sections.title: Useful clues
sections.code:
Repeated UI
→ LessonCard

Independent interaction
→ SearchBox

Distinct conceptual section
→ ProgressSummary

Collection structure
→ LessonList

Page-level coordination
→ LessonDashboard

sections.text: A meaningful component usually has a reason to exist beyond 'this div was getting long.' It represents a UI concept, repeated pattern, independent interaction, or responsibility that is useful to name.
The Repetition Test

sections.title: Repeated card structure
sections.code:
Lesson A
→ title
→ duration
→ status

Lesson B
→ title
→ duration
→ status

Lesson C
→ title
→ duration
→ status

sections.text: Repeated UI is a strong signal for a component. Instead of writing the same structure three times, define one LessonCard and render it with different data.
The Responsibility Test
Ask what one part of the interface is responsible for. A search box collects and communicates a search value. A progress summary displays progress. A lesson card presents one lesson.

sections.title: Focused responsibilities
sections.code:
SearchBox
→ search interaction

ProgressSummary
→ progress presentation

LessonCard
→ one lesson's presentation

LessonDashboard
→ coordinate the feature

sections.text: The Misconception to Kill

sections.title: Do not jump straight into code
sections.text: A component hierarchy should be a deliberate design decision, not an accidental result of splitting a huge file after the implementation becomes difficult to manage.
The source plan specifically identifies the common mistake here as jumping straight into code without first identifying the component boundaries.
Do Not Make Every Rectangle a Component

sections.title: Over-decomposition
sections.code:
LessonCard
├── LessonCardArticle
├── LessonCardTitle
├── LessonCardDuration
├── LessonCardStatus
└── LessonCardWrapper

sections.text: If these pieces always belong together and have no independent responsibility, this decomposition may add noise rather than clarity.
Do Not Make the Whole Screen One Component Either

sections.title: Under-decomposition
sections.code:
LessonDashboard
→ navigation
→ search
→ progress
→ lesson list
→ every lesson card
→ every empty/error state
→ every interaction

sections.text: The goal is not maximum or minimum component count. The goal is useful boundaries that make the interface easier to reason about.
Think About Data Flow Before State
Once the component tree exists, ask which pieces need the same information.

sections.title: Example data questions
sections.code:
Who needs the lesson collection?
→ LessonList
→ ProgressSummary
→ maybe SearchBox results

Who needs one lesson?
→ LessonCard

Who needs the search term?
→ SearchBox
→ perhaps the parent that performs filtering

sections.text: You are not required to solve all state ownership yet. The goal is to notice the relationships that will matter in the next architecture lessons.
Interactive Practice: Decompose a Mockup

sections.text: From Mockup to Tree

sections.title: A useful sequence
sections.code:
1. Identify the visible regions.
2. Identify repeated patterns.
3. Identify independent interactions.
4. Name meaningful sections.
5. Build a component tree.
6. Check which data must flow between branches.
7. Only then begin implementation.

sections.text: This sequence prevents implementation details from determining the architecture too early.
The Component Tree Is Not the DOM Tree

A component tree and a DOM tree are related, but they do not have to be identical. A component can return several nested DOM elements, and a component boundary can represent behavior or responsibility rather than a single visual element.

sections.title: Component vs DOM
sections.code:
LessonCard component
└── article
    ├── h2
    ├── p
    ├── button
    └── p

sections.text: The component gives the group a meaningful identity in the React architecture.
Use Design Repetition as Evidence
If a UI pattern appears repeatedly, that is evidence that the repeated structure may deserve a component. But the component should still represent a coherent concept.
Use Behavior as Evidence
A part of the UI with its own interaction often makes a natural component boundary. Search boxes, dialogs, tabs, and interactive cards are common examples.
Use Change as Evidence

Another useful question is: which parts are likely to change independently? If navigation changes frequently while the lesson list changes for different reasons, separating them can make those changes easier to manage.

sections.title: Three signals
sections.code:
Repeated
or
Interactive
or
Conceptually independent

→ candidate component boundary

sections.text: The Tree Should Help You Answer Ownership Questions
A good hierarchy makes later questions easier: where should the state live, which component should receive the data, and which child needs a callback?

sections.title: Architecture leads to data flow
sections.code:
Parent
↓ props
Child
↓ callback
Parent

The exact ownership decision comes next,
but the component tree gives you the map.

sections.text: Drill 2: Plan Before Code

sections.title: UI Planning Drill
sections.instructions: Before writing JSX, design a component hierarchy for the given feature. Include the likely data each component receives, but do not implement state or effects yet.
sections.initialCode:
Feature:
A course page contains:
- course title
- instructor information
- search box
- category filter
- list of lessons
- each lesson has a title, duration, progress state, and expand/collapse details
- a progress summary appears above the list

Your plan:

Component tree:
____________________________
____________________________
____________________________

Repeated components:
____________________________

Independent interactions:
____________________________

Likely shared data:
____________________________

One boundary you deliberately would not create:
____________________________

sections.text: What This Prevents

sections.title: Without planning
sections.code:
Start coding
→ component grows
→ state gets added
→ more conditions appear
→ repeated markup appears
→ props become tangled
→ refactoring becomes necessary

sections.title: With planning
sections.code:
Inspect UI
→ identify concepts
→ define component tree
→ decide data relationships
→ implement smaller pieces

sections.text: Planning does not eliminate refactoring. It gives you a deliberate starting architecture instead of discovering the entire architecture through accidental complexity.
What's Being Deferred?
The next lessons focus on the specific architecture questions that emerge from this tree: what belongs in props versus state, and how to lift shared state to the closest common ancestor.
This lesson deliberately avoids solving every state-ownership question. First build the hierarchy; then reason about data flow.

sections.title: The boundary
sections.text: Component architecture starts with decomposition. Do not jump into state management, context, or abstractions before you understand the UI tree you are trying to build.
Interview Mode

Imagine an interviewer gives you a dashboard mockup and says, 'How would you build this in React?' A strong first step is not immediately writing JSX. Say: 'I'd first decompose the UI into a component hierarchy, identify repeated and independently interactive pieces, and determine which parts need to communicate.'

A likely follow-up is: 'How do you decide whether something should become a component?' Explain that repetition, independent interaction, meaningful conceptual boundaries, and independent change are useful signals.

Another follow-up is: 'Why not make every visual section a component?' Because component boundaries should improve clarity or reuse; arbitrary fragmentation can make the architecture harder to understand.
Reflect

Take the React Interaction Challenge from the previous module. Before looking at your implementation, draw the component tree you think the feature should have. Then compare it with your code. Where did implementation choices force the architecture instead of the UI requirements determining it?

sections.title: Design the tree before the branches

sections.text: A component tree is a reasoning tool. It lets you discuss responsibilities and data flow before syntax, hooks, and implementation details make the design harder to change.

sections.label: Complete the component-tree Playground and both planning drills. The learner must decompose the supplied UI into meaningful components, identify repeated and interactive boundaries, and justify at least one boundary they deliberately do not create.
sections.hint: Start from the UI: visible regions → repetition → interaction → meaningful concepts → component tree.

sections.text: What You Should Take Away

Thinking in Components means decomposing a UI into a meaningful component hierarchy before writing detailed React code. Use repetition, independent interaction, conceptual responsibility, and likely independent change as signals for boundaries. Avoid both one giant component and arbitrary fragmentation. The component tree is the architectural map that makes later props, state, and data-flow decisions easier.

summary: Thinking in Components means planning a component hierarchy from the UI before writing detailed implementation code. Identify visible concepts, repeated patterns, independent interactions, and responsibilities that may change independently. Then create meaningful component boundaries while avoiding both a single monolithic component and unnecessary fragmentation. This hierarchy becomes the map for later decisions about props, state, and shared data.

title: Props vs State
description: Learn to distinguish parent-provided props from component-owned state, decide which values belong in each, and use ownership to make React data flow predictable.
mastery: The learner can identify whether a value should be a prop or local state, explain who owns each value, and recognize when incorrectly storing parent-owned or derived information as local state creates synchronization problems.
learningObjectives: Explain props as parent-provided inputs used to configure a child.
Explain state as component-owned changing information.
Identify the owner of a value in a component tree.
Decide whether a value should be a prop, local state, or a derived value.
Explain why a child should not duplicate parent-owned state unnecessarily.
Recognize synchronization bugs caused by copying props into state without a clear reason.

sections.text: The Same UI Can Use Both Props and State
You already know both concepts individually. Props let a parent provide data. State lets a component remember changing information.
The architecture question is now: which values belong where?

sections.title: The mental model
sections.text: Props flow down from a parent for configuration and input. State belongs to the component that owns and changes that information. The key question is always: who owns this value?
A Simple Example

sections.title: Props plus local state
Ownership
sections.code:
title
→ parent provides it
→ prop

expanded
→ LessonCard owns and changes it
→ state

sections.text: The distinction is about ownership, not about whether a value changes visually.
Props Configure the Component

sections.title: Same component, different inputs
sections.code:
<LessonCard title="JSX" />
<LessonCard title="Props" />
<LessonCard title="State" />

sections.text: The component does not decide its title. Its parent configures that aspect through props.
State Represents Local Memory

sections.title: Local interaction state
sections.code: const [expanded, setExpanded] = useState(false);

sections.text: The parent does not need to know whether this particular card is expanded unless some other part of the application depends on that information.
The Three-Way Decision

sections.title: Ask which category fits
sections.code:
Parent-owned input
→ prop

Component-owned changing information
→ state

Value calculated from existing values
→ derived during render

sections.text: That third category matters. Not every value needs to become state.

sections.title: Derived value

sections.text: percentage is derived from props. Creating separate state for it would introduce another value that can become out of sync.
The Common Anti-Pattern: Copying Props Into State

sections.title: Usually unnecessary

sections.text: Now the component has two values representing the lesson title: title from the parent and localTitle inside the child. If the parent changes title later, localTitle does not automatically follow.

sections.title: The misconception to kill
sections.text: Do not copy props into state just because you want to use the value inside the child. That creates two potential sources of truth. Use the prop directly unless the child intentionally needs an independent local draft or snapshot.
When a Local Copy Can Be Legitimate

sections.title: Editable draft

sections.text: Here the local state has a distinct purpose: it represents an editable draft that can temporarily differ from the parent value. The distinction should be intentional and documented by the interaction.
Interactive Practice: Classify the Values

sections.title: Props or State Playground
sections.instructions: For each value, decide whether it should be a prop, local state, or derived value. Then modify the example so the ownership matches your decision.
sections.initialCode:

Value A
lesson.title
→ parent already owns the lesson
Decision: __________________

Value B
expanded
→ changes when the user clicks Show details
Decision: __________________

Value C

→ calculated from completed and total
Decision: __________________

Value D

→ user edits locally before pressing Save
Decision: __________________

Value E
